name: Point-in-time universe hygiene
one_line: Make the historical and live universe date-aware so delisted or no-longer-tradable names do not leak into selection or volume baselines.
parameter_choices: Remove symbols after their last tradable date; rebuild the universe and relative-volume baselines using only point-in-time membership.
disagreement: None noted; this is a backtest/live-data hygiene issue rather than a strategy dispute.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly warns that the trading universe changes over time and that knowing when a stock no longer trades is important to avoid survivor bias. That is the same underlying point-in-time universe hygiene proposed here, just applied to our ORB bot and its RV baseline.
review.exact_rule_change: This is a data-layer fix, not a trading-rule change: for each replay/live date, include only symbols that had already started trading and have not yet reached their last tradable session; if a symbol has fewer than 10 prior regular-session bars, exclude it until the 10-session relative-volume baseline can be formed. Keep the existing 1.5× RV threshold, top-8 cap, and ORB entry/exit rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: It prevents survivorship/look-ahead leakage from making dead or not-yet-tradable names look like valid 'in play' candidates and from contaminating the 10-session volume baseline. That improves backtest realism and live/backtest consistency, but it does not create a new breakout edge by itself. If anything, it may slightly reduce candidate count and apparent historical edge.
review.data_missing: We do not have a historical point-in-time constituent list, delisting dates, or a complete archive of names that left the universe. With only the current ~55-name archive, we can infer last observed bars for symbols already present, but we cannot fully reconstruct all past universe membership changes or removed symbols.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. This is a validation/data-plumbing fix, not one of the prior entry/exit ideas that were tested and rejected.
review.overfit_note: There are essentially no alpha knobs here. The main risk is accidental hindsight if the universe is defined using present-day membership instead of point-in-time availability, which is exactly what this change is meant to prevent.
review.expected_effect: Mostly neutral on live P&L; the main effect is cleaner validation. On historical runs it may lower apparent edge and slightly reduce trade count by removing impossible or contaminated candidates, but it should not improve costs, targets, or breakout quality on its own.
review.test_protocol: Run an audit replay, not a live alpha test: compare the current backtest against the point-in-time-cleaned version on all archived days. Track (1) days where the 10:00 top-8 in-play set changes, (2) trade-list differences, and (3) any bars/symbols that fall outside their tradable window. If the two runs are identical on the 67 archived sessions, stop there; do not spend scarce unseen days on it. If differences exist, adopt the cleaned data layer for all future strategy tests, but do not treat any P&L change as alpha. Minimum sample: the full archived history plus any later day with actual universe churn.
review.verdict_reason: Good hygiene, but not a standalone trade hypothesis. With our current small, mostly static 55-name universe and no point-in-time membership/delisting dataset, this is unlikely to produce a measurable P&L delta on the existing sample; it mainly fixes backtest realism. Implement it as research infrastructure, not as one of the bot’s scarce strategy tests.

name: Raise the liquidity floor
one_line: Keep only the most liquid names on the watchlist, especially on the short side, to reduce slippage and make exits easier.
parameter_choices: Use a higher minimum 20-day dollar-volume cutoff; or keep only the top half of names by dollar volume; apply the strictest liquidity gate to shorts.
disagreement: The sources agree liquidity matters but do not give one numeric cutoff.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources clearly support the general principle of trading only liquid names and being stricter on shorts, but none gives a numeric cutoff for this bot. The top-half/top-quarter implementation is our own operationalization of that idea.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00, after the existing in-play screen, rank the qualifying names by prior-20-session average regular-session dollar volume (computed from the 5-minute OHLCV bars). Allow longs only if the name is in the top 50% of that rank; allow shorts only if the name is in the top 25%. Keep the rest of the Midas rules unchanged; if fewer than 2 names remain, sit out.
review.mechanism: This is mainly a cost/execution filter: thinner names should have wider effective spreads, worse next-bar fills, and uglier exits, so raising the liquidity floor could reduce slippage and cost-driven stop-outs. It may also remove some noisy fake breakouts, especially on the short side. The trade-off is fewer trades and possibly losing some of the biggest target runners in the play batch.
review.data_missing: No critical data missing for the proxy. We do not have bid-ask spreads, depth, or L2, so we cannot measure liquidity directly; we can only infer it from dollar-volume rank and resulting P&L/fill quality.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule. The closest rejected idea was 'top-5 only' plus price caps, which also shrank the universe, but it was not a liquidity-rank filter and not a stricter short-side liquidity gate.
review.overfit_note: This is only one real knob, but with 67 sessions it is still easy to tune a percentile cutoff to noise. Liquidity is also tangled up with market cap, volatility, and 'stocks in play,' so a win may be regime-specific rather than a true edge.
review.expected_effect: Likely small positive if execution friction is the real problem: fewer thin-name trades, lower slippage, fewer cost-driven stop-outs, and better short survival. It may also be flat or slightly negative if the thinner names were providing the largest breakout targets.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the percentile rule before looking at results. Replay all archived days with a 20-session warmup and compare against baseline on the same days. Primary metrics: net P&L after costs, expectancy per trade, profit factor, max drawdown, and trade count; require improvement in both halves of the sample, not just overall. Do not accept if trade count collapses below about 20 archived trades. If it beats baseline in both halves, confirm on the next 20 unseen sessions without changing anything.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully computable from the existing OHLCV data, cheap to replay, and directly addresses the bot's cost problem. The evidence is only generic liquidity wisdom, not a proven edge, but this is a sensible low-cost test rather than a waste.

name: Exclude sparse opening-range names
one_line: Skip stocks whose opening-range window is too thin to generate meaningful 5-minute bars.
parameter_choices: Require a minimum count of nonzero 5-minute bars during 9:30–10:00; optionally require opening-range volume above a floor.
disagreement: None noted; this is a practical liquidity screen for clock-time bars.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book’s point is that infrequently traded stocks can have empty 5-minute intervals, which supports avoiding sparse opening ranges. It does not state this exact OR bar-count cutoff, so this is an adaptation rather than a direct rule from the source.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a pre-entry liquidity gate: at 10:00 New York, skip any symbol whose 9:30–10:00 opening-range window contains fewer than 6 nonzero 5-minute bars (i.e. any empty 5-minute bar in the OR disqualifies the name).
review.mechanism: This is a hygiene filter, not a new alpha source. It should remove the worst thin/opening-range cases where the OR high/low is stale, the breakout is more likely to be a fake print, and fills are more fragile. Best case: fewer failed-break stops and slightly lower slippage/costs. Realistically, the effect is probably small because the current universe is already screened for liquidity.
review.data_missing: None; the existing 5-minute OHLCV archive is enough to count zero-volume or missing opening bars.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the rejected list. This is a new liquidity-screen variant, not one of the previously rejected overlays or entry/exit tweaks.
review.overfit_note: Only one cutoff, but it is still an arbitrary hard threshold on a 67-session sample. If you start moving the threshold after looking at results, it will overfit fast.
review.expected_effect: Small at best. It may trim a few low-quality mornings and reduce some false breakouts, but because your universe is already fairly liquid, I would not expect a large change in total PnL or trade count.
review.test_protocol: Replay baseline vs. this rule on all 67 archived sessions with the threshold fixed before looking. Compare net PnL/day after costs as the primary metric, plus stop rate and average slippage on affected trades. Keep a guardrail that trade count does not drop by more than 10%. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, and do not promote if the filter changes fewer than about 10 trades total unless the per-trade uplift is clearly large. If it passes archive replay, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and not already tried. I do not expect a big edge, because your universe is already pre-filtered for liquidity, but this is exactly the kind of low-cost hygiene screen that is worth one archived replay before you decide it is noise.

name: Prune expensive / large-cap names
one_line: Bias the in-play universe toward cheaper, more volatile names instead of expensive blue chips that tend to move less cleanly intraday.
parameter_choices: Test a hard price cap at $20; a tighter $2-$10 band; or exclude sub-$5 names. If needed, manually drop obvious mega-cap names from the play list.
disagreement: The books disagree on the low end of the band and on whether the real signal is price alone or a broader size/ownership proxy.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Day Trade (sample)

review.source_support_note: B3 directly argues for a lower-priced universe ($2-$20, especially $2-$10) and against names over $20; B1 separately excludes sub-$5 names and the smallest-cap decile. That supports the general 'cheaper/smaller names may work better' idea, but not this exact ORB setup, and the 'large-cap' part is only a proxy here.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current in-play price filter `yesterday's close ≥ $20` with a fixed price band: only names with `yesterday's close between $5 and $20` may enter the 10:00 in-play list; keep the existing RVOL ≥ 1.5x, top-8 selection, gap filters, stop/target, and exit rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: Cheaper momentum names usually have larger percent intraday range, so the ORB may reach its 2.5R target more often instead of drifting into a flat close. In the best case this should lift target hits and reduce dead flat exits. The downside is that lower-priced names also bring more noise and our fixed $0.02/share slippage hurts more in percentage terms, so the net effect is uncertain.
review.data_missing: We can compute the price band from the daily closes and 5-minute bars we already have. We cannot directly test 'large-cap' or ownership/float effects because we do not have market cap, float, or institutional ownership data; those can only be approximated by price.
review.already_tried_note: The rejected tests were single-name ORB, SPY/QQQ timing overlay, top-5 and price caps ($80/$120), two-close confirmation, and morning fade. None of those tested a cheaper-name price band like $5-$20.
review.overfit_note: There are several plausible cutoffs ($2-$10, $5-$20, $20 cap, plus optional megacap blacklists). With only 67 sessions / 53 trades, it would be easy to pick the band that flatters the archive by chance.
review.expected_effect: If it helps, the main win would be more target hits and fewer flat exits; but the low end may be eaten by slippage and noise, so the after-cost edge could easily be flat or worse.
review.test_protocol: Fix the band at $5-$20 before looking at the replay. Run a side-by-side replay on all 67 archived sessions with no other changes. Score after-cost net P&L, expectancy per trade, profit factor, max drawdown, target rate, and flat-exit rate. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just the full sample, and require at least about 30 trades in the modified run so we are not judging on a tiny sample. If it clears archive and does not concentrate all gains in one half, paper-trade the next ~20 unseen sessions with the same fixed rule.
review.verdict_reason: This is feasible with the data we have, cheap to replay, and not already tried. It is only a price-band proxy for the larger 'smaller names' idea, but that proxy is concrete enough to test. The main caution is cost drag at the low end, so we should test it once, fixed, and reject it fast if the archive does not improve in both halves.

name: Tighten the relative-volume gate
one_line: Require more extreme opening participation before a name can be in play.
parameter_choices: Raise the opening relative-volume threshold to around 2.0x; test a 20-session average baseline; keep the same opening-window definition but make the cutoff stricter.
disagreement: The sources converge on roughly 2x volume, but they do not agree on the exact lookback or baseline window.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Day Trade (sample)

review.source_support_note: One source explicitly recommends high relative volume of at least 2.0, and the other says volume jumping above the long-term average is informative. That supports tightening Midas' existing volume gate, but neither source proves that 20 sessions is the right baseline or that this exact change has edge in this bot.
review.exact_rule_change: Change the 10:00 in-play filter to: a name qualifies only if its 9:30-10:00 volume is at least 2.0x its average 9:30-10:00 volume over the prior 20 sessions. Keep the existing top-8-by-relative-volume rule and all other ORB rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is a blunt quality filter on the universe. If low-energy names are causing many failed breakouts and stop-outs, a stricter opening-volume gate should remove some of those weak setups before entry, which can improve hit rate and reduce commission/slippage drag. The tradeoff is fewer names, more sit-out days, and a real chance of filtering out some of the few winning breakouts too.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: We have already tried the broader idea of shrinking/cherry-picking the universe (top-5 only, price caps) and it starved the bot. This is not the same rule, but it is in the same family of tighter universe selection, so the same starvation risk applies.
review.overfit_note: Two tunable knobs (threshold and lookback) on only 67 days makes this easy to fit to the archive. Even if we fix 2.0x and 20 sessions up front, the result could still be mostly noise because the current sample is tiny and trade frequency is low.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, fewer marginal breakouts, and lower cost drag. It may slightly improve win rate and reduce stop-outs, but the upside is probably modest because it does not change entry logic or exits. Main failure mode: the stricter gate cuts trade count too much and removes the few strong winners along with the junk.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the parameter before looking at results: use 2.0x relative volume with a 20-session baseline. Replay the modified rule and the current baseline on all 67 archived sessions side by side. Primary metric: net PnL after costs per session. Secondary metrics: profit factor, max drawdown, stop-out rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both chronological halves of the archive, not just the full sample, and reject the change if trade count drops by more than about 25-30%. If the archive test is positive, paper trade the fixed rule on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully data-feasible, and the sources do support the basic idea of using stronger relative volume to identify better momentum names. The expected gain is probably small, but this is a clean, low-cost filter change worth replaying before spending live days on it.

name: Require pre-entry momentum
one_line: Only trade breakouts in names that are already drifting up before the ORB trigger fires.
parameter_choices: Use positive 30-minute return, rising VWAP slope, top gainer/loser ranking, or a stronger version like +10% versus the prior close as the momentum gate.
disagreement: The books agree on the concept of 'already rising' but use different proxies and do not standardize the threshold.
books: How to Day Trade (sample)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books support the general idea of starting with names that are already rising and active, and one source explicitly likes shares that are already up a lot on the day. But none of the sources specifies a formal rolling pre-breakout momentum gate for an ORB system, so the exact trigger is our adaptation, not a quoted rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the existing in-play scan and ORB logic, but add a directional pre-entry momentum gate: a long ORB is eligible only if the trailing 30-minute return on the trigger bar is > 0.0%; a short ORB is eligible only if the trailing 30-minute return on the trigger bar is < 0.0%. No other rules change.
review.mechanism: This should filter out names that are merely noisy or high-volume but not yet trending, which is where a lot of failed breakouts and flat closes come from. If the move is already going the right way before the trigger, the breakout has a better chance of continuation, so we may get fewer stop-outs and more 2.5R runners. The side benefit is fewer low-quality trades, which also trims costs a bit on a small book.
review.data_missing: None required for this exact rule. 5-minute regular-session OHLCV is enough to compute the trailing 30-minute return at each trigger bar.
review.already_tried_note: You already tried a different momentum-style confirmation: requiring two consecutive closes beyond the range. That is not the same as a pre-entry trailing-return gate, but it is close enough that this is clearly the same family of idea.
review.overfit_note: There is only one real threshold here if you fix it at 0.0% before looking, but the family of proxies is broad (30-minute return, VWAP slope, top-gainer rank, +10% day gain). The danger is not the rule itself; it is using the replay to shop among variants.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, slightly lower costs, fewer weak breakouts/flat exits, and a higher target-hit rate if the signal is real. If it fails, it will probably fail by cutting too many good mean-reversion-to-breakout setups rather than by not being computable.
review.test_protocol: Replay the fixed 0.0% gate on all 67 archived sessions side by side with the baseline, using the same entry/exit/size/cost model. Compare net PnL after costs, profit factor, win rate, stop rate, target-hit rate, average PnL per session, and trade count. Do not tune the lookback or threshold on these days. Require improvement in both halves of the archive (days 1-33 and 34-67), or at minimum no clear degradation in either half plus a better overall net after costs. If the replay leaves you with fewer than about 25 trades, treat the result as too sparse and confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions before believing it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully computable from the data we have, and plausible for the bot's main weakness. It is not strong evidence, but it is concrete enough to replay now without needing new feeds or a big sample. The main caution is not to over-tune the momentum proxy after the first replay.

name: Beta sensitivity check
one_line: Measure whether ORB expectancy concentrates in a particular beta band before turning beta into a live filter.
parameter_choices: Compute monthly 1-year daily beta versus SPY; test performance by beta decile or coarse high/low beta bands.
disagreement: None noted; this is a validation step, not a recommendation to trade one beta band yet.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports monthly beta sorting using the prior year of daily data, but it is a stock-selection/portfolio sort, not an opening-range breakout rule. Using beta as a conditioning variable for our intraday ORB is our own adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Diagnostic only: at each month start, compute each symbol's beta vs SPY from the prior 252 daily closes and tag every ORB trade into three fixed bands: low beta < 0.9, mid beta 0.9-1.1, high beta > 1.1. Do not change the entry or exit rules yet; just replay the existing bot and measure results by band.
review.mechanism: Beta is a crude proxy for how far a name can actually travel. If the ORB edge depends on names that move enough to pay costs, high-beta names should show fewer flat/time-stop exits and a better chance of reaching target. If low-beta names are the problem, this filter could also cut some failed-breakout losers.
review.data_missing: None beyond the existing daily closes and SPY.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact idea. We have tried an intraday SPY/QQQ overlay, which is different, and the current SPY direction confirmation is not a beta screen.
review.overfit_note: With only 53 trades so far, slicing by beta band is easy to mine. The beta estimate itself is also noisy when based on about one year of daily data, so a 'best' band can be an accident unless it survives out of sample.
review.expected_effect: If it works, the effect should be modest: slightly better average R / net expectancy and fewer low-amplitude, cost-dominated trades. If it does not work, it will mostly just reduce trade count.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the beta definition before looking: trailing 252 daily closes vs SPY, recomputed monthly. Replay all archived sessions side by side with the baseline, first using the three pre-set bands above. Compare net P&L after costs, expectancy per trade, profit factor, win rate, max drawdown, and trade count for each band versus baseline. Treat any band with fewer than 10 trades total or fewer than 5 trades in either half as too sparse to trust. Promote a band only if it improves in both halves of the archive and then holds up on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully feasible with our data and cheap to replay. The academic beta-sort literature gives a real empirical basis for the check, but not enough to live-trade a beta filter blindly. As a sensitivity test, though, it is worth doing now because it can quickly tell us whether beta is informative or just noise.

name: Short-interest squeeze overlay
one_line: If short-interest data is available, favor breakouts in heavily shorted names because squeeze pressure can improve upside follow-through.
parameter_choices: Test days-to-cover thresholds like >=2, >=5, and >=10; optionally rank by short-interest percentile or utilization rather than a hard cutoff.
disagreement: Short-interest data is stale and not always predictive; it can also attract crowded, reversal-prone names.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book excerpt says short interest / utilization / days-to-cover can indicate squeeze potential and a larger possible upside move in heavily shorted names. It does not say to use it as an ORB filter, does not specify a breakout rule, and gives no threshold. Our proposed overlay is an extrapolation, not a direct rule from the source.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a long-side filter only: after the normal in-play selection and ORB setup, take a long breakout only if the symbol’s latest reported days-to-cover is >= 5.0; otherwise skip that long. Shorts unchanged. Default threshold: 5.0 days-to-cover.
review.mechanism: If the short-interest signal is real, it should help the bot keep only long breakouts where forced covering can extend the move, which could raise target hits and reduce flat exits. The downside is that heavily shorted names are also often crowded and reversal-prone, so this could just as easily increase stop-outs and cut trade count.
review.data_missing: We do not have historical short interest, utilization, or days-to-cover in the current dataset. We would need an external short-interest feed with as-of dates that can be aligned to each trading day; 5-minute OHLCV and daily closes are not enough.
review.already_tried_note: Nothing on the rejected list is a short-interest overlay. We have not tested this filter or anything close to it.
review.overfit_note: Even with one threshold, the choice of cutoff is arbitrary and easy to tune on 67 sessions. The signal is stale, sparse, and likely interacts badly with the bot’s existing breakout logic, so it is very easy to fit noise.
review.expected_effect: Best case: a small lift in target rate and average R on a subset of long breakouts. More likely: lower trade count with little or no net improvement, because short-interest alone is too blunt and stale for intraday timing.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend live days on this until a historical short-interest feed is added. If added, fix the rule at DTC >= 5.0 before looking at results, replay the full archive side-by-side with baseline, and compare net PnL per session, expectancy per trade, target-hit rate, stop rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just the full sample. If the filter produces fewer than about 30 qualifying trades in the archive, treat the result as too sparse and reject rather than tune thresholds. Only then allow a 20-day forward paper check.
review.verdict_reason: It cannot be tested with the current data, and the source support is only a generic squeeze interpretation, not evidence that this improves ORB performance. Even if data are added later, the signal is stale and likely too noisy for a small 67-day sample unless it shows a clear archival edge.

name: Familiarity whitelist for expanded universes
one_line: If the universe is expanded, only let in names the bot has already studied enough to understand their ORB behavior and fills.
parameter_choices: Require at least 10/25/50 prior observed sessions or keep only tickers already in the current watchlist until enough history is accumulated.
disagreement: This reduces breadth and may miss fresh movers, but should lower regime noise and execution surprises.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports a familiarity bias in asset choice, but that is a portfolio-behavior claim, not a trading rule for ORB selection or fill quality. The leap from "people prefer familiar stocks" to "our breakout bot should gate new tickers until it has seen them for N sessions" is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a maturity gate before the 10:00 in-play ranking: a symbol is eligible only after it has at least 25 prior regular-session 5-minute sessions in Midas’ own archive; otherwise it is excluded from trading that day. Keep the rest of the ORB recipe unchanged.
review.mechanism: In theory, this could reduce regime noise and surprise behavior from newly added symbols, which might cut a few failed-breakout stops and avoid some bad days when the universe is expanded. In practice, our current universe is already small and liquid, and this gate mostly just removes candidates; it does not target the bot’s main failure mode of breakouts that reverse.
review.data_missing: We can count prior sessions for the current 55 names from our own 5-minute archive, but the intended use-case is newly added symbols, and we do not have 5-minute history for arbitrary new names. Daily closes are not enough to measure ORB behavior, and we still cannot validate the claimed fill-stability benefit from bar data alone.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tried, but it is close in spirit to the rejected universe-thinning ideas (top-5 only, price caps): it narrows the eligible set and risks starving the bot. We have no evidence that narrower breadth helps this bot’s edge.
review.overfit_note: The cutoff is arbitrary (10/25/50 all plausible on paper), and with only 67 sessions / 53 trades it would be very easy to fit a threshold to noise. Any apparent gain could just come from excluding a few early losers.
review.expected_effect: At best a small reduction in bad trades from very new symbols in an expanded universe; more likely a lower trade count with little or no durable improvement in net PnL, drawdown, or costs.
review.test_protocol: If you insist on a replay, precommit to N=25 before looking. Run the exact same ORB logic on all archived days with and without the maturity gate, then compare net after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, and trade count on the full sample and on each half of the archive separately. Only keep it if it improves net after cost materially (say, >20%) without cutting trade count by more than 10% and does not worsen either half. Then confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions. If the filter barely changes the replay, that is itself evidence it is not worth live testing.
review.verdict_reason: This is a weakly supported universe-thinning rule, not a real edge. Our data cannot test the intended "expanded universe" use-case properly, we have no fill/spread data to validate the claimed execution benefit, and on the current bot it mostly adds a redundant filter that is likely to reduce trade count more than it improves expectancy.

name: Low-float filter
one_line: Bias the in-play list toward low-float stocks because limited share supply can produce cleaner momentum and bigger intraday runs.
parameter_choices: Test float caps at under 20M shares, under 50M shares, and under 100M shares.
disagreement: Lower float can improve upside but also increases whipsaws, halt risk, and gap/reversal risk.
books: How to Day Trade (sample)

review.source_support_note: The book explicitly prefers low-float names and even cites <50M shares (and sometimes <20M) as desirable for momentum. That supports the general low-float bias, but it is anecdotal day-trader lore and not evidence for adding this filter to our specific ORB bot.
review.exact_rule_change: New strategy / not a minor tweak: at 10:00 New York, only names with public float <= 50 million shares are eligible for the in-play ranking; then keep the top 8 by 9:30-10:00 relative volume, and still sit out if fewer than 2 names qualify.
review.mechanism: If low-float names really do run further, the main upside for Midas would be more 2.5R winners and fewer flat-at-close exits, because breakouts would have a better chance of traveling far enough before 15:45. The downside is that low-float stocks are also the ones most prone to whipsaws, halts, gap/reversal behavior, and worse fills, so the filter could just swap many small losers for fewer but nastier ones. On this bot, the first-order effect may simply be fewer trades.
review.data_missing: We do not have public float data in the current dataset, so this cannot be computed from 5-minute OHLCV plus daily closes. Low-float names also need better execution data (spreads/halts), which we do not have.
review.already_tried_note: Not this filter directly, but we already tried narrower universe ideas (top-5 only, price caps) and they hurt by starving the bot. A low-float cap is another universe-tightening change with the same risk.
review.overfit_note: One hard threshold plus three candidate caps (20M/50M/100M) on a tiny sample is easy to fit after the fact. With only ~55 liquid names, the filter may leave too few trade days to trust any apparent improvement.
review.expected_effect: Best case: more explosive breakouts and a higher target-hit rate. More likely here: far fewer eligible names, more zero-trade days, and possibly worse realized costs and stop-outs if the remaining names are genuinely low float.
review.test_protocol: Do not live-test until float data is added. If it is, pre-register float <=50M as the primary cap and replay all archived days versus the current baseline. Reject immediately if the cap leaves fewer than about 20 total trades on the archive or materially lowers trade count. Only keep it if net P&L after costs improves and the gain shows up in both halves of the archive, with a better target-hit rate and no DD blow-up. If it passes, forward-test on the next 20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: This is not computable from our current data, and in our mostly high-float/liquid universe it is likely to starve the bot rather than add edge. The support is anecdotal and from a different small-cap momentum context, while our execution-cost model is least reliable on the very names this filter would favor.

name: Broaden the scanner beyond the fixed watchlist
one_line: Scan all liquid U.S. stocks instead of only the frozen 55-name list, while keeping the same in-play qualification rules.
parameter_choices: Define the scan universe as all U.S. stocks with yesterday dollar volume >= $20M and price >= $20, or top-N by dollar volume.
disagreement: This can find more opportunities, but may add noise and worse fill quality versus a curated list.
books: How to Day Trade (sample)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general idea of scanning the whole market instead of a preset list, but it does not show that this improves breakout performance or that it should be paired with our exact $20M/$20 eligibility and 10:00 in-play rules.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the frozen 55-name universe with a market-wide scan: at 10:00 New York, consider every U.S.-listed stock with yesterday close >= $20 and yesterday dollar volume >= $20M, then apply the existing in-play rule (9:30-10:00 volume >= 1.5x its 10-day average; keep the top 8 by relative volume; same ORB entry, stop, target, and time exit rules).
review.mechanism: This could catch real movers that are not in the frozen watchlist, so it may increase the number of tradeable days and occasionally capture a stronger breakout. But on our bot it is just a larger scanner, not a better entry rule: the main effect is likely more noise, more unfamiliar names, and worse fills, which can raise slippage and lower hit rate.
review.data_missing: We do not have 5-minute OHLCV history for the full U.S. market. We also lack the historical daily volume/close coverage for that full universe needed to build the eligibility screen and relative-volume baseline. To test this properly we would need survivorship-free intraday plus daily data for all candidate U.S. equities.
review.already_tried_note: This is not the same as the rejected 'Top-5 only and price caps' test; that narrowed the universe, while this expands it. It is only adjacent in that both are universe-selection changes.
review.overfit_note: There is only one obvious threshold set if we use the $20M/$20 screen, but universe changes are easy to tune to a short sample by cherry-picking. With a small edge and only 67 archived sessions, apparent improvement could easily be regime luck.
review.expected_effect: More candidate names and possibly more trade days, but probably a lower hit rate and worse fills. Best case: you catch some missed leaders. Most likely: little or no net improvement after costs.
review.test_protocol: If full-market data is ever acquired, replay the expanded scanner against the frozen 55-name baseline on all archived days, side by side. Compare net PnL/day after costs, profit factor, win rate, average slippage, and trade count. Require the expanded scanner to improve in both halves of the archive, not just overall. If it only increases trade count while PnL/day or costs worsen, reject. After that, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: Reject for now: this cannot be tested with our current archive, because we only have intraday data for the frozen 55 names. Even if we bought the data, universe expansion is more likely to add noise and execution risk than fix the bot's real problem, which is weak breakout quality and many flat exits.

name: Same-day catalyst requirement
one_line: Only trade breakouts when the stock has a same-day catalyst such as earnings, guidance, FDA, analyst, merger, or sector news.
parameter_choices: Require a binary same-day catalyst flag; optionally test broad buckets like earnings/guidance, corporate news, and sector/news shock days.
disagreement: Catalyst filters can cut false breakouts, but they also require extra data and may reduce trade frequency too much.
books: How to Day Trade (sample)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly says a momentum name should have "news or some other catalyst ... announced today." That is the same rule in substance; the only extrapolation is applying it to Midas' ORB entry filter.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a pre-entry filter at 10:00 NY: only names with catalyst_flag = 1 are eligible for ORB trading. Default: catalyst_flag = 1, meaning a same-day catalyst announced before the trade window (earnings/guidance, FDA/clinical, merger/M&A, analyst action, or major sector/news shock). If no qualifying catalyst, skip the name even if it is in the top-8 by relative volume.
review.mechanism: This tries to replace Midas' crude 'in play' proxy (relative volume) with a real reason for sustained direction. In theory it should reduce failed breakouts and late-day flat exits by keeping us in names with actual news pressure, and may improve 2.5R target hits. The tradeoff is fewer candidates and possibly more volatility around gaps/news.
review.data_missing: We need a timestamped news/catalyst feed or manual daily catalyst labels. Current 5-minute OHLCV and daily closes do not tell us whether a catalyst existed or whether it was announced before the trade window.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. The closest prior filter is volume-based 'in play' selection, but that is not the same as a catalyst requirement.
review.overfit_note: A binary event filter sounds simple, but the definition of 'catalyst' can be widened or narrowed in many ways. With only 67 sessions, it would be easy to tune the label set to flatter the backtest and not generalize.
review.expected_effect: If real catalyst data is available, this could reduce stop-outs and increase target hits on the subset of names that actually have news-driven follow-through. It may also reduce flat-at-close trades. The likely cost is a lower trade count, and if the catalyst definition is too broad, the benefit may disappear.
review.test_protocol: Not testable on the current archive. If you add a timestamped catalyst label, freeze the labeling rules first, replay all archived days side-by-side with the baseline, and compare after-cost expectancy per trade, stop rate, 2.5R hit rate, trade count, and daily P&L in both halves of the sample. Only keep it if it improves both halves, then confirm on the next ~20 qualifying unseen days.
review.verdict_reason: This cannot be computed from the data we currently have, so it is not worth spending replay tests on Midas as-is. It becomes testable only after adding a news/catalyst feed or manual labels.

name: Sector-relative strength filter
one_line: Only take breakouts when the stock is outperforming its sector or same-industry peers during the open.
parameter_choices: Use sector ETF or peer-group comparison; require the name to beat its sector ETF by a small margin over the first 15–30 minutes.
disagreement: This may improve selection quality, but it adds complexity and can exclude good idiosyncratic breakouts.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general idea of narrowing candidates to industry-related names/ETFs, but it does not say to use sector-relative strength as an ORB entry filter. That trading-rule link is our extrapolation from pair-search narrowing.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00, keep the existing ORB setup only if the stock's 9:30-10:00 return is at least +0.25 percentage points above the equal-weight return of its fixed sector/industry peer basket from our loaded universe; otherwise do not arm that symbol for the day.
review.mechanism: This is a quality filter: if a name is already leading its own group during the open, its breakout is more likely to continue instead of faking out and stopping us. That should mainly reduce failed-breakout stops and the flat-at-close no-follow-through trades, with a possible bump in target hits. The trade-off is fewer signals.
review.data_missing: A one-time sector/industry map for the 55 symbols, or sector ETF OHLCV if you want the ETF version. The 5-minute OHLCV we already have is enough once the labels exist; no pre-market, news, float, or L2 is needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact filter. The closest prior rejected idea was an SPY timing overlay, which also added a benchmark confirmation condition. This sector-relative version is different, but it is in the same family of extra confirmation filters.
review.overfit_note: There is at least one new threshold plus an implicit choice of peer grouping. With only 67 sessions and about 53 baseline trades, it's easy to tune the cutoff to the archive and mistakenly believe the filter works.
review.expected_effect: Fewer breakout failures, fewer flat exits, and a modestly higher win/target rate if sector rotation is real. Expect trade count to drop.
review.test_protocol: Fix the threshold at +0.25 percentage points before looking at results. Replay on all 67 archived sessions side by side with the baseline. Judge by net P&L per session after costs, stop rate, and trade count, with the key requirement that performance improves in both halves of the archive. Do not accept the idea if the filtered sample falls below ~30 trades or if trade count drops below 80% of baseline. If the archive looks better, paper-trade the next ~20 unseen sessions without retuning.
review.verdict_reason: Worth checking only after you add a fixed sector/industry map. Without that metadata, it's not directly testable from the current data. Even with the map, it's a secondary confirmation filter that may just shrink an already small sample and duplicate the current SPY-relative filter.

name: Delay first breakout until post-open stabilization
one_line: Push the earliest ORB eligibility later so the opening auction and first burst of post-open noise are excluded.
parameter_choices: Delay eligibility by 15-30 minutes after 9:30; test 10:15 or 10:30 starts; alternative is extending the opening range to 45-60 minutes.
disagreement: Most sources agree the open is noisy, but one cited study says profits cluster in the first and last hour, so the optimal delay may be shorter than the anecdotes suggest.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The quoted sources support the general premise that the first 15–30 minutes after the open are noisier, wider-spread, and more execution-sensitive, and a couple of the source items explicitly suggest delaying ORB-style entries to 10:15/10:30. But none of them directly tests Midas’s exact setup, and the bot already uses a 30-minute opening range, so this is still an adaptation rather than a directly evidenced rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current 9:30–10:00 opening range, in-play selection, SPY filter, size, stop, target, and time exit unchanged, but add a hard entry gate: the first breakout entry is only eligible on the first 5-minute bar ending at 10:15 New York or later. Any breakout that happens before 10:15 is ignored; the first qualifying close above/below the existing OR after 10:15 is the only entry, filled at the next bar open.
review.mechanism: This should cut the ugliest post-open whipsaws and some of the widest-spread fills, so fewer trades get stopped out immediately and some bad early breakouts become no-trades instead of losses. It may also reduce flat-at-close churn from weak entries. The tradeoff is fewer trades and a real chance of missing the few early runners that make the day.
review.data_missing: None for this variant; 5-minute regular-session OHLCV for the symbols and SPY is enough.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact gate. However, the bot already waits through the first 30 minutes to define the OR, so this is only an extra 15-minute delay rather than a brand-new timing regime.
review.overfit_note: One knob on paper, but the cutoff is very easy to sweep on 67 sessions (10:05 vs 10:15 vs 10:30, or even a 45-minute OR variant). If you do not precommit to 10:15 before looking, this turns into data-mining fast.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer failed-break stops and slightly lower slippage, with a modest increase in win rate if the open is the main whipsaw zone. Main downside is fewer trades and possibly fewer full-target winners.
review.test_protocol: Fix 10:15 ex ante. Replay baseline vs variant on all 67 archived sessions. Primary metric: after-cost net P&L per session; secondary metrics: trade-level expectancy, stop rate, target rate, flat-at-close rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both archived halves (days 1–33 and 34–67), not just overall, and do not accept it if trade count collapses by more than about 30% unless expectancy improves materially. If it passes the archive, paper trade the next ~20 unseen sessions before any further tuning.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, fully testable with existing data, and directly aimed at the bot’s known early-whipsaw / cost-drag problem. It is not proven, but it is reversible and worth a single fixed-cutoff replay. Just do not sweep multiple cutoffs on the same 67 days.

name: Restrict entries to the morning window
one_line: Stop taking fresh signals after the first two trading hours and compare that with the current all-day entry window.
parameter_choices: First 2 hours after the open (to 11:30 ET); quoted alternative window is 7:30-11:30 ET.
disagreement: This conflicts with sources that emphasize the last hour as liquid and sometimes profitable, so a morning-only cutoff may miss late-day opportunities.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Day Trade (sample)

review.source_support_note: Two practitioner excerpts explicitly recommend concentrating day trading into the morning window, and one cited research summary says profits cluster in the first and last hour. That supports the general idea that time-of-day matters and that a morning cutoff could help, but it is not direct evidence for this exact ORB rule, and one source conflicts by implying the last hour can also be profitable.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a hard entry cutoff: Midas may open new positions only on signals whose triggering 5-minute bar ends at or before 11:30 ET. After 11:30 ET, ignore all fresh breakout signals. Keep the existing 10:00 ET opening-range completion, SPY confirmation, stop, target, and 15:45 flat rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is mainly a quality filter. It should cut late-day breakout attempts that are more likely to stall, reverse, or drift into a flat exit, which is exactly the failure mode we saw in August. Fewer afternoon entries should also reduce total commissions and slippage a bit. The tradeoff is that we may give up some valid late-day trend continuations, so the expected win is fewer bad trades, not more signals.
review.data_missing: None for the 9:30-11:30 regular-session cutoff. If you want the source's literal 7:30-11:30 window, we would need pre-market bars, which we do not have.
review.already_tried_note: We have tested a time-related SPY/QQQ overlay and rejected it, but we have not tested this specific hard no-new-entries-after-11:30 rule on the ORB bot.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob if fixed at 11:30 before looking, but time-of-day filters are easy to data-snoop on a 67-session sample. If we start searching multiple cutoffs, the overfit risk jumps fast.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, fewer late-day false breakouts, and a smaller flat-at-close share. Win rate may improve a bit if the edge is morning-concentrated, but total P&L could also fall if late-day winners matter. This is a plausible quality filter, not a guaranteed lift.
review.test_protocol: Fix 11:30 ET before looking. Replay all 67 archived sessions with the cutoff on and off, using identical fills and costs. Compare after-cost net P&L, expectancy per trade, profit factor, max drawdown, and the share of flat exits. Split the archive chronologically into two halves and require the cutoff to help in both halves, not just one lucky period. If it survives archive replay, confirm live on the next 20 unseen sessions or 15 trades, whichever comes first.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully testable with our existing 5-minute regular-session data, and directly targets a known weakness of this bot. The source support is only partial, and the last-hour winner risk is real, but that is exactly why it should be replay-tested now rather than argued about.

name: Move the forced flat closer to the close
one_line: Keep winners open into the closing-auction window instead of forcing exits at 15:45.
parameter_choices: Test forced exits at 15:55 or 15:59 versus the current 15:45 flat; optionally compare 15:45/15:55/15:59 variants.
disagreement: Closer-to-close exits may capture more liquidity, but the close can also be noisier and more volatile than mid-afternoon.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book supports the *general execution idea* of trading into the close: it notes explicit on-close order types, that the closing auction is a distinct liquidity window, and that late-day volume/order flow is elevated. It does **not** show that Midas’ opening-range breakout specifically improves by holding to the close, so that performance claim is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Change the forced-flat rule from 15:45 New York time to 15:55 New York time for all open Midas positions; keep every other rule unchanged. Use the 15:55 5-minute bar as the exit proxy (not a true auction model).
review.mechanism: If Midas winners tend to keep trending into the final 10–15 minutes, this can turn some forced flats into larger winners or full targets. The upside bucket is mostly better winner capture / fewer premature flats. The downside is more exposure to end-of-day reversals, so late losers may get worse rather than better.
review.data_missing: We can backtest a later forced exit from 5-minute regular-session bars, but we do not have auction prints, imbalance data, spread, or L2. So we can only proxy the close with the 15:55 bar, not measure actual closing-auction fill quality.
review.already_tried_note: Nothing on the rejection list is the same idea. The bot already has a 15:45 flat, but moving that flat later has not been tested yet.
review.overfit_note: Only one knob, but it is easy to data-mine a 10-minute shift on 67 days, especially if you sweep 15:45/15:55/15:59 and pick the best. Fix 15:55 before replaying and do not optimize the cutoff after seeing results.
review.expected_effect: Maybe a small positive if the edge lives in late-day drift, but it could just as easily be neutral or slightly worse. Best case: fewer premature flats and a bit more winner size. Worst case: more late-day giveback and stopouts. I would not expect a big standalone edge from moving the flat by 10 minutes.
review.test_protocol: Fix 15:55 ex ante. Replay all 67 archived sessions side by side with the current 15:45 baseline, keeping entries, stops, size, and costs identical and changing only the forced-flat time. Compare session-level net PnL after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, and the number of trades that improve versus worsen relative to 15:45. Require the 15:55 version to beat 15:45 in both halves of the archive and not worsen drawdown before promoting it. If it passes, paper-trade the next ~20 unseen sessions unchanged; do not test 15:59 unless 15:55 already wins.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully replayable from the data we have, and directly targets a real weakness of the live bot: too many forced flats. The source support is only partial and the effect may be small, but this is still a sensible one-parameter test rather than a new strategy.

name: Add a simple intraday trend filter
one_line: Only take long ORBs when a fast intraday average is above a slower one, and only shorts when it is below.
parameter_choices: Use either price-vs-MA or fast/slow MA alignment; source examples include 5-minute fast vs slow windows and a 20/100 moving-average crossover.
disagreement: The books use two slightly different mechanisms, price-above-MA versus MA crossover, so test one filter at a time.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books support the general idea of a moving-average timing filter (price above MA, or short MA above long MA), but they do not test this specific overlay on ORB, on 5-minute bars, or on this universe. This is an adaptation, not a directly sourced rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a trend gate to Midas: on the signal bar, take a long ORB only if the most recent completed 5-minute close is above its 8-bar SMA; take a short ORB only if that close is below its 8-bar SMA. If fewer than 8 completed 5-minute bars exist, skip the entry. No other ORB rules change.
review.mechanism: This should mainly filter out breakouts against the local intraday drift, which is where a lot of failed breakouts live. The hoped-for gain is fewer stop-outs and fewer dead-on-arrival trades, with a possible bump in win rate and maybe a small reduction in flat exits and cost drag. The trade-off is fewer trades and the risk of skipping the rare strong early move.
review.data_missing: None for this version. It can be computed from the regular-session 5-minute OHLCV we already have.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is adjacent to other regime/overlay ideas, but we have not tried a 5-minute MA trend gate on the stock-level ORB itself.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob, but the lookback can still be mined on 67 days if we let ourselves tune it. Fix the 8-bar value before looking and do not sweep many lengths.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, fewer failed-breakout stops, and a modestly better win rate if the local trend really matters. Best case: some of the August-style chop disappears. Worst case: we just cut out the best early breakouts and the edge shrinks further.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule at 8 bars. Replay the full 67 archived sessions side by side with baseline. Primary metric: net P&L after all costs per session and per trade; secondary metrics: win rate, stop rate, full-target rate, trade count, and max drawdown. Accept only if it improves the full archive and both chronological halves (early vs late) on net P&L or expectancy, not just on one half. If it passes, paper trade the next ~20 unseen sessions with no retuning.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully computable from current data, and plausibly attacks the bot’s main failure mode (break-and-fail chop). The evidence is only generic MA lore, not specific ORB proof, but this is still worth a single locked-down replay test rather than a long delay.

name: Skip longs and shorts when RSI is extreme
one_line: Do not chase breakouts when RSI says the move is already stretched.
parameter_choices: Skip longs when RSI > 70 and shorts when RSI < 30; the excerpt does not specify the lookback.
disagreement: The threshold is clear but the lookback is not, so the RSI period should be chosen in testing rather than copied from the source.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book explicitly treats RSI > 70 as overbought and RSI < 30 as oversold, so the thresholds themselves are supported. What is not directly supported is using that rule as a pre-entry veto on an opening-range breakout; that is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a pre-entry RSI filter on the symbol’s 5-minute regular-session closes: compute RSI(14) through the signal bar, and skip any long breakout if RSI(14) > 70 or any short breakout if RSI(14) < 30. Keep the rest of the ORB rules unchanged; if a signal is filtered out, continue scanning later bars for the first signal that passes.
review.mechanism: This is a simple anti-chase filter. It may block names that are already stretched when they break the opening range, which could reduce the failed-breakout stop-outs and some of the end-of-day flat exits. It also should cut a few low-quality trades and therefore some costs. The risk is that it removes the small number of strong momentum runners that produce most of the target exits.
review.data_missing: none for the test itself; 5-minute OHLCV is enough to compute RSI(14) on regular-session bars.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the rejected list. The closest prior reject was a failed-breakout fade overlay, which is a different strategy, not this entry filter.
review.overfit_note: RSI is a classic knobbed indicator, and with only 67 sessions/53 trades it is easy to make a simple filter look good by excluding a few bad days. Fix the lookback at 14 before looking and do not tune thresholds or timeframe on the archive.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, a lower stop-out rate, and possibly a small cost reduction. Net P&L could improve if the filter removes tired breakouts, but it could just as easily hurt by filtering out the rare big runners that drive the targets.
review.test_protocol: Fix RSI(14) before looking. Replay the full 67-session archive side by side with the frozen baseline. Compare after-cost net P&L/day, profit factor, win rate, stop rate, target count, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just the full sample. If the filtered replay falls below about 20 trades total, treat it as too sparse to judge. If it helps on the archive, paper it unchanged on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap to replay, feasible with existing data, and it targets the exact failure mode of stretched breakouts. The evidence is weak and the risk of deleting the few winners is real, so it should only be tested with a fixed RSI(14) and no parameter shopping — but it is worth a controlled test now.

name: Skip entries when price is stretched vs Bollinger bands
one_line: Filter out breakouts that are already too far from the local mean.
parameter_choices: Source variants use a 2-sigma envelope or a 10-period band with 1.5 standard deviations and a 20-period SMA.
disagreement: The Bollinger examples use different lengths and widths, so the test should pick one band definition and hold it fixed.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The books support the *general* idea of avoiding stretched prices: one source says to sell above the upper Bollinger band / buy below the lower band, and the other gives an explicit Bollinger example with a 10-bar, 1.5σ setup. But neither source directly tests an ORB entry filter on US equities, so this is an adaptation rather than a quoted rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Add one pre-entry filter to the existing ORB: compute Bollinger bands on the last 10 completed regular-session 5-minute closes (SMA 10, band width 1.5σ). If the breakout trigger bar closes above the upper band, skip the long; if it closes below the lower band, skip the short. If fewer than 10 completed bars exist, do not apply the filter and trade normally.
review.mechanism: This keeps the bot out of breakouts that are already extended away from the local mean, which are the ones most likely to whipsaw into the stop or drift into a flat exit. If it works, the gain should come from fewer failed breakouts and slightly lower cost drag; the trade-off is fewer fills and possibly skipping some of the best trend days.
review.data_missing: none beyond completed regular-session 5-minute OHLCV; no premarket, L2, news, or other extra data needed.
review.already_tried_note: Related in spirit to the rejected failed-breakout fade, but not the same thing: this is a pre-entry stretch gate on the existing ORB, not a separate reversal strategy or consecutive-close rule.
review.overfit_note: This is only one binary gate, so the dimensionality is low, but with just 67 sessions it can still look good by accidentally filtering a few bad trades. Do not scan multiple band lengths/σ values on the archive.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer stop-outs and fewer sloppy flat exits, with a modest lift in net PnL and drawdown. Worst case: it just removes good momentum entries and shrinks trade count without improving expectancy.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the preset before looking: 10-bar, 1.5σ Bollinger bands on 5-minute closes. Replay all 67 archived sessions side by side with baseline. Judge on net $/session after costs as the primary metric, plus stop rate, flat-exit rate, and max drawdown. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just the total, and require trade count to stay at least ~70% of baseline so we are not just starving the bot. If it passes archive replay, paper it on the next 20 unseen sessions with the exact same rule; kill it if the live confirm does not hold up.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully computable from the data we already have, and directly targets a known failure mode. The evidence is weak-to-partial, but the test cost is low enough to justify a fixed-parameter replay. If it only works by cutting trades too much or only in one archive half, reject it fast.

name: Require candle confirmation before entry
one_line: Only enter when the breakout/retest is backed by a strong candle shape instead of a thin wick or tiny body.
parameter_choices: Engulfing confirmation with a minimum gap around 1%; pin/rejection candles with wick-to-body ratio of 3x; some examples also add a body-size threshold around 1%.
disagreement: The books use different candle definitions, so this is a family of confirmation filters rather than one exact pattern.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: The sources do support the general idea of candle-shape confirmation: confirmed breakouts should close beyond prior highs/lows, engulfing patterns need a size filter, and pin/rejection bars should have large wick/body asymmetry. But none of the excerpts validate this specifically for our 5-minute opening-range breakout on US equities; that adaptation is ours.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current ORB trigger, but only enter if the trigger candle is a confirmed engulfing candle and its real body is at least 1.0% of price (body_perc = 0.01). Long: the breakout candle must open below the prior 5-minute close and close above the prior 5-minute open; short: reverse. Keep the existing next-bar-open fill, stop, target, SPY filter, and all other rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could cut thin-wick/tiny-body breakouts that are more likely to fail and snap back into the stop, so it mainly targets fewer failed-breakout losses and less cost drag from low-quality entries. The tradeoff is later entries and fewer trades, so it may also miss some winners and reduce target frequency.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: We already tested a related but different confirmation idea: requiring two consecutive closes beyond the range, which was worse. This is not the same rule, but it is the same broad family of "wait for more confirmation" filters.
review.overfit_note: Candle-pattern rules are easy to overfit because there are many plausible definitions (engulfing, pin bar, body thresholds, wick ratios, etc.). With only 67 archived sessions and a small number of trades, it would be easy to optimize folklore until it fits the sample.
review.expected_effect: Most likely outcome is fewer trades, fewer weak-breakout stop-outs, and lower slippage/commission drag. It could also lower the number of big winners if the filter is too strict, so the net effect is uncertain rather than obviously positive.
review.test_protocol: Freeze this exact rule before looking at results. Replay it on all 67 archived sessions and compare to baseline on after-cost net PnL, expectancy per trade, profit factor, max drawdown, win rate, stop-out rate, and trade count. Require it to beat baseline in both halves of the archive (Jul-Aug vs Sep-Oct), not just in aggregate. If it survives the archive test, paper it on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully computable from existing 5-minute OHLCV, cheap to replay, and directly targets the bot’s main failure mode of weak breakouts. The evidence is only moderate and overfit risk is high, so we should freeze one exact version and test it once, not wander across candle-pattern variants.

name: Use a pullback/reclaim entry instead of the first breakout
one_line: After an initial breakout, wait for a retracement and reclaim rather than buying the first push through the range.
parameter_choices: Fibonacci retracement zones at 38.2%, 50%, and 61.8%; stop beyond the impulse extreme or just below the 100% level; target back toward the breakout high.
disagreement: This is a continuation pullback strategy, not a pure breakout entry, so it will trade differently from the current bot.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: The books support the general idea of Fibonacci retracement zones and breakout retest/secondary entry setups, but only as practitioner opinion and worked examples. None gives an ORB pullback/reclaim rule with performance stats, so the exact Midas rule is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Treat this as a separate ORB variant: after the first 5-minute close outside the opening range, do not enter immediately. For longs, wait for a 61.8% retracement of that breakout leg and then a later 5-minute close back above OR high; enter at the next bar open. Mirror the rule for shorts. Use a stop just beyond the pullback low/high and a target at the prior breakout extreme (the 0% level). Keep the rest of the bot unchanged.
review.mechanism: This tries to avoid paying for the first thrust that often fails and snaps back. A pullback/reclaim entry should only fire when the move can absorb a retracement and hold the range break, which can cut stop-outs and improve average R. The trade-off is fewer fills and more missed runaway moves; it is not mainly a cost-saving idea.
review.data_missing: None for the rule itself; 5-minute regular-session OHLCV is enough to compute the OR, breakout leg, retracement, reclaim, stop, and target.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tried. It overlaps with the rejected two-close confirmation and the failed-breakout family, but it is not the same rule and not the same direction as the fade test.
review.overfit_note: There are many plausible knobs hiding inside this idea: 38.2 vs 50 vs 61.8, stop placement, target choice, and whether to allow long/short symmetry. With only 67 archived days, it would be easy to curve-fit one fib level. Freeze 61.8 before looking and do not shop levels afterward.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, fewer outright stop-outs, and a higher win rate / average R if the pullback version works. It may also miss the strongest momentum days and could lower total PnL if the retracement filter is too strict.
review.test_protocol: Freeze 61.8% before inspecting results. Replay the variant on all 67 archived sessions side by side with the current bot, using the same universe, OR definition, volume filter, SPY filter, sizing, and time exits. Primary metric: net PnL after costs per session; secondary: profit factor, max drawdown, win rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, and do not keep it if it produces fewer than about 25 trades or materially starves the bot. If it clears the archive, shadow it on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with the data we already have, cheap to replay, and directly targets the bot's main failure mode. The evidence is weak and the overfit risk is high, but not high enough to reject outright; it deserves one frozen-parameter backtest, not level-shopping.

name: Filter by higher-timeframe structure
one_line: Only take an intraday ORB when the name is aligned with a daily support/resistance or multi-session breakout.
parameter_choices: 20-day rolling support/resistance with 2-day confirmation; 50-day Donchian-style breakout/low break; test one daily window at a time.
disagreement: One source uses a tolerance-band confirmation while another uses a clean 50-day breakout, so they are similar but not identical filters.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The cited material supports the general higher-timeframe idea: one snippet is a rolling support/resistance confirmation rule on daily bars, and the other is a Donchian/turtle-style daily breakout rule. Neither source directly validates using that daily structure as a gate on a 5-minute intraday ORB, so the link is an adaptation, not a direct claim.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a higher-timeframe gate to the existing ORB: only allow a long entry if yesterday's regular-session close is above the prior 20-session regular-session high; only allow a short entry if yesterday's close is below the prior 20-session regular-session low. Otherwise skip that name for the day. Leave the ORB trigger, stop, target, sizing, and cost model unchanged. Parameter: lookback = 20 sessions.
review.mechanism: This tries to keep us out of intraday breakouts that are happening inside a choppy daily range and only trade names already in a daily breakout state. If it works, it should reduce failed-breakout stop-outs and some flat-at-close exits, and raise the share of trades that reach 2.5R. The main risk is that it also removes too many of the already-scarce good trades, so the book may get quieter rather than better.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: Nothing on the rejected list is this filter. The closest prior test was the SPY half-day overlay, which is a different time-of-day effect, not a higher-timeframe structure gate.
review.overfit_note: Only one obvious knob, but it is easy to tune 20 vs 50 vs confirmation variants on a 67-session sample. Because this is a filter, the danger is not just overfitting P&L but also accidentally fitting a tiny set of trades and then starving the bot.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer trades, lower stop rate, more target hits, and less cost drag from bad breakouts. Worst case: the filter strips out too many trades and leaves us with too little sample to beat costs.
review.test_protocol: Fix the rule first: 20-session prior daily high/low gate, no tolerance band, no extra confirmation. Replay all 67 archived sessions side-by-side against the frozen baseline with identical sizing and costs. Compare net P&L after costs, expectancy per trade, stop rate, target-hit rate, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive (Jul-Aug and Sep-Oct) before trusting it. If the filtered replay ends up with fewer than about 30 trades or only a tiny P&L lift, call it noise and stop. If it survives the archive, forward-test on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: It is computable from the data we already have, cheap to replay, and directly targets failed breakouts. The source only gives a loose analog, so the evidence is weak, but this is still worth one fixed-parameter test because it could reduce the loss-making chop days that are hurting the bot.

name: Rank by morning gap size
one_line: Prefer the biggest gap-up or gap-down names each morning instead of treating all in-play names equally.
parameter_choices: Rank by open-to-previous-close gap and keep the top names; the cited example focuses on the top ten gappers.
disagreement: Gap ranking overlaps with the current relative-volume screen, so it should be tested as a replacement or tie-breaker, not layered blindly.
books: How to Day Trade (sample)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general habit of scanning gappers and paying attention to the top gappers, but it does not explicitly say to replace a relative-volume ranking with gap-size ranking. That part is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the existing universe and 10:00 in-play qualification rules, but replace the current ranking by 9:30-10:00 relative volume with ranking by absolute open-to-previous-close gap % = |today 9:30 open - yesterday close| / yesterday close. Keep the top 8 qualified names by that gap rank; everything else in the ORB recipe stays unchanged.
review.mechanism: This may improve candidate quality by pushing the bot into names that already have the biggest attention and displacement at the open, which can mean stronger ORB follow-through and fewer sleepy flat exits. It could also reduce some failed breakouts if the current weakest names are the small-gap names. The risk is that the biggest gaps are also the most overextended and may reverse harder.
review.data_missing: None. We can compute the gap from the 9:30 open (first 5-minute bar open) and the prior daily close using the data we already have; no pre-market, L2, or news is needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not explicitly tested as a standalone rule, but it is close to the existing morning in-play selection logic, so this is an adjacent universe-ranking tweak rather than a brand-new edge.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob if we pre-fix the cutoff at top 8, but with just 67 sessions it is still easy to tune the cutoff or accidentally fit a regime. Do not search multiple N values or combine it with other filters in the same test.
review.expected_effect: Best case: slightly higher win rate and more target hits, with fewer flat 15:45 exits, because we trade the most attention-grabbing movers. Worst case: the biggest gappers are exhausted and stop out more. Net effect is likely modest, not transformative.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the rule exactly: rank by absolute gap % and keep top 8. Replay all 67 archived sessions side by side against the frozen baseline with the same ORB entry/stop/target/flat rules. Compare post-cost daily expectancy, profit factor, win rate, target hit rate, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive (early and late sample), not just overall. If it wins on archive without a big drop in trade count, forward-test it unchanged on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting it.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and concrete with our current data. The support is only anecdotal and the edge may be weak, but this is a single pre-registered selection tweak that could improve trade quality without adding complexity, so it is worth one controlled replay test.

name: Use a catalyst/news gate
one_line: Only allow ORB trades on names with a same-morning catalyst or clearly news-driven setup.
parameter_choices: Manual catalyst flag; 'ahead of expectations' updates; same-morning company report/news; half-hour rolling sentiment if a feed is added later.
disagreement: This needs a news process we do not yet have, so it is only partly testable until a feed or manual tagging is added.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general idea that early-morning company news and news analytics can help with directional trading, but none of them show that a catalyst gate improves this specific ORB bot. The jump from 'check morning news' to 'only take ORB trades with a catalyst' is our own extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add one new entry filter: CatalystFlag ∈ {0,1}. At the 10:00 ET selection step, allow an ORB trade only if CatalystFlag=1, where CatalystFlag=1 means a company-specific news item or report timestamped before 09:30 ET on the same day (earnings, guidance/trading update, FDA/SEC decision, merger/contract, or major press release). Otherwise skip the name; all other ORB rules stay unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is meant to cut random volume breakouts that reverse into stops and concentrate trades on days with a real information shock, which should improve follow-through, target hits, and maybe reduce the August-style chop. The downside is fewer trades and the risk of starving the bot, since the current relative-volume screen already captures some news-driven names.
review.data_missing: We do not have a timestamped pre-market/news feed, earnings or event calendar, or manual catalyst tags for the archive. Regular-session 5-minute OHLCV alone cannot tell us whether a move was news-driven.
review.already_tried_note: Not explicitly tried. But the existing 'in play' relative-volume filter already acts as a rough proxy for catalyst/news names, so this is a refinement of something partially embedded in the bot, not a brand-new dimension.
review.overfit_note: The gate is binary in theory, but in practice the tagging definition is subjective and easy to tune after seeing results. With only 67 archive days and roughly one trade per day, a catalyst filter can quickly become a sparse-sample cherry-pick.
review.expected_effect: Best case: higher win rate, more target hits, fewer stopouts, and a cleaner equity curve. Most likely case: some improvement on true news days, but not enough to offset the trade-count drop and the fact that the current volume screen already captures part of the same effect.
review.test_protocol: Do not change live trading until the catalyst definition is frozen and the archive is manually tagged. Then replay the full 67-day archive side by side with baseline. Primary metrics: after-cost net per session and expectancy per trade; guardrails: max drawdown and trade count. Require improvement in both archive halves, and do not accept a version that leaves fewer than ~20 archive trades or less than ~60% of baseline trade count unless the per-trade expectancy jump is very large. If it passes archive tests, paper it on the next ~20 unseen sessions before any live deployment.
review.verdict_reason: Plausible in principle, but we cannot test it with the data we currently have because the key variable is missing. Until we add a timestamped news/catalyst log or manual tags, this is not runnable.
