Even then, the idea risks starving an already small system, so it should only be revisited with a frozen tagging rule and enough trades to avoid overfitting.

name: Prefilter by medium-term momentum
one_line: Prefer names with positive multi-month momentum before applying ORB.
parameter_choices: Six-month cumulative return ranking with a one-month skip after formation; test top-decile versus the full universe.
disagreement: The source is monthly and cross-sectional, so the translation to an intraday ORB prefilter is indirect and should be treated as a hypothesis.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source directly supports a six-month cross-sectional momentum sort with a one-month skip, but it does not test an intraday opening-range breakout prefilter. Using that signal to choose ORB names is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00, keep the existing in-play volume screen, then allow long ORB entries only in names whose 6-month cumulative return, computed from daily closes 126 trading days ago through 21 trading days ago (one-month skip), is in the top decile of the 55-name universe; short ORB rules stay unchanged.
review.mechanism: This should mostly cut failed long breakouts. Stocks with strong medium-term momentum are more likely to keep trending after an opening-range break, so the filter may raise long win rate, increase target hits, and reduce the number of long trades that drift back to flat by the close. Keeping shorts unchanged avoids applying a bullish filter to a bearish setup.
review.data_missing: Only daily closes are needed, which we already have. We just need enough history to define the 126-session lookback plus 21-session skip on the first test date.
review.already_tried_note: Not tested directly, but it is structurally similar to the rejected 'top-5 only' universe reduction because a top-decile filter can starve the trade set if the long side is weak.
review.overfit_note: There is only one fixed cutoff, but on 67 sessions a decile screen can still be noise-fitting. Do not start tuning alternative cutoffs or applying it to both sides if the first replay is weak.
review.expected_effect: Slightly fewer long trades, higher follow-through on longs, better win rate/target hit rate, and possibly fewer flat exits. The main risk is that it trims away good long entries or leaves the short side untouched, so the gain has to come from real improvement in long breakouts, not just fewer trades.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule before looking. Replay baseline vs the momentum-filtered version on all 67 archived sessions. Score net P&L after costs, expectancy per trade, profit factor, max drawdown, trade count, and long/short split. Require the filter to improve net P&L in both halves of the archive and not reduce trade count by more than about 30%. If the filtered long side ends up with fewer than ~20 trades in the archive, treat the result as inconclusive. If it passes, run it on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our existing daily closes, cheap to replay, and it targets the bot’s weakest bucket: failed long breakouts. The source is only partial support, but the idea is concrete enough to test without new data. The big caveat is trade starvation, so keep it long-only and require a real lift, not just a lower trade count.

name: Bias toward long-only or tighter shorts
one_line: If shorts are weaker after costs, either disable them or make the short side more selective than the long side.
parameter_choices: Test long-only first; if shorts remain, require an extra confirmation filter beyond the long side.
disagreement: The evidence is old broad-market technical work, so this is a hypothesis about the current stock-in-play universe rather than a general law.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general asymmetry claim that buy signals can outperform sell signals, but it is broad-market, very old, and not specific to intraday opening-range breakouts on a small stock-in-play universe. The move from that evidence to disabling shorts here is our adaptation, not something the source states directly.
review.exact_rule_change: Disable shorts entirely: after 10:00 New York, only take the first valid long breakout above the OR high; ignore all breaks below the OR low. Keep every other Midas rule unchanged (universe, in-play filter, stop, target, sizing, flat time, day halt).
review.mechanism: If the short side is structurally weaker, this should remove a chunk of the worst stop-outs and short-squeeze losses, while also cutting round-trip costs. On a small cost-sensitive book, that can help more than forcing symmetry between a decent long side and a weak short side.
review.data_missing: Nothing extra is needed; this can be computed from the existing 5-minute regular-session OHLCV data plus SPY.
review.already_tried_note: The rejected tests were about a single pet stock, a SPY/QQQ time-of-day overlay, universe caps, double-close confirmation, and morning fade. None of those directly tested long-only versus short-only asymmetry in the current ORB stock-in-play bot.
review.overfit_note: This is only one binary knob, so it is not a sprawling parameter search. But with just 67 archived sessions, the result could easily be driven by a few short-squeeze days or one regime, and long-only may simply be the side that happened to work in sample.
review.expected_effect: Most likely fewer bad short trades and slightly lower costs; downside is fewer total trades and possibly missing some real short edge if it exists. It helps only if shorts are genuinely negative expectancy after costs.
review.test_protocol: Freeze short_enabled=false and replay all 67 archived sessions side by side with baseline. Primary metric: after-cost PnL per session. Secondary metrics: profit factor, max drawdown, and trade count. Require the long-only version to beat baseline in both halves of the archive (split the 67 days into two contiguous halves) on PnL/session, and not worsen max drawdown materially. If the archived replay produces fewer than about 20 total trades or fewer than 0.4 trades/day, treat the result as too sparse to trust. If it passes the archived replay, forward-test unchanged on the next ~20 unseen sessions before adopting it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, feasible with current data, and it targets a real asymmetry that could matter after costs. The evidence is only partial and the fit is not perfect, but this is a single binary rule change worth replaying now rather than overthinking.

name: Scale thresholds by intraday volatility
one_line: Make the breakout or confirmation threshold breathe with the day’s volatility instead of using one fixed rule.
parameter_choices: Use the source recipe stdev_factor = stdev/15; scale entry thresholds and profit-lock thresholds by that factor.
disagreement: The volatility-scaling recipe comes from a different strategy, so the mapping to ORB needs a careful test.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The book supports the general idea of volatility-adjusting entry/exit thresholds, and the APO worked example gives a concrete stdev/15 scaling recipe. But neither source is about opening-range breakouts, so applying it to Midas is an adaptation, not a direct citation.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00 New York, compute vol_factor = (20-bar standard deviation of the last available 5-minute closes) / 15. Keep the existing ORB logic, but require the first long/short close beyond the OR boundary to clear that boundary by at least 0.10 × vol_factor × OR_width before taking the trade. Leave the current stop, 2.5R target, position sizing, SPY filter, gap filter, and 15:45 flat rule unchanged.
review.mechanism: This should mainly cut marginal fake breakouts on noisy sessions, which is where we have been getting stopped out or drifting back to flat. A volatility-buffered trigger may reduce those failed entries and slightly reduce cost drag from bad trades, while still allowing low-vol days to trigger because the buffer shrinks with vol.
review.data_missing: None for the proposed test; the 20-bar rolling volatility can be computed from the existing regular-session 5-minute bars. No L2, news, float, or premarket data is required.
review.already_tried_note: Not the same as the rejected 'two consecutive closes beyond the range' test. This adds a volatility-scaled buffer to the first breakout trigger instead of requiring multiple confirmations.
review.overfit_note: Only one free knob (the 0.10 buffer), but the mapping from the book's APO recipe to ORB is loose and easy to tune to a 67-session sample if we are careless. Do not sweep parameters.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer breakout stop-outs, slightly fewer trades, and lower cost drag on chop days. Risk: we miss some good breakouts and lower trade frequency too much, so total PnL could go down even if win rate improves.
review.test_protocol: Run a fixed replay on all archived days with the buffer locked at 0.10 before looking at results. Compare baseline vs variant on after-cost net PnL per session, profit factor, max drawdown, stop-out rate, and trade count. Require the variant to improve in both halves of the archive (first 33 vs last 34 sessions) rather than just one side. If it survives that, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting. Reject if the gain comes only from trading much less or if drawdown worsens.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap to test, uses only existing data, and directly targets the bot's known failed-breakout problem. The source support is only partial, so this is a low-confidence hypothesis, not a live rule change, but it is worth a deterministic replay test.

name: Stress-test fill latency and next-bar execution
one_line: Measure how much edge disappears if fills are delayed or executed less favorably than the baseline backtest.
parameter_choices: Next-candle-open execution as the baseline; compare against trade_on_close and delayed-fill assumptions.
disagreement: This is not a trading rule change; it is a robustness check on timing sensitivity.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The source is relevant because it states the platform timing convention: decisions in `next()` execute on the next bar open unless `trade_on_close=True`. That supports a fill-sensitivity check. It does not, however, claim that stress-testing latency creates edge; that part is our own validation logic.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to the live Midas recipe. Add a fixed robustness replay for every candidate: keep the baseline fill at `next_bar_open`, then re-run the same signals under (1) `trade_on_close=True` and (2) a conservative `delay_bars=1` stress case (fill at the open of the bar after the normal next-open fill). Do not promote any timing-sensitive tweak unless the edge survives the conservative case.
review.mechanism: This does not directly improve live PnL; it prevents us from mistaking a backtest artifact for a real edge. ORB on 5-minute bars can look good if fills are assumed too optimistically. If performance collapses under a one-bar delay, the setup is too timing-fragile for a small book with real slippage and commissions. If it survives, we gain confidence that the edge is not just an execution illusion.
review.data_missing: We can simulate next-bar-open, bar-close, and one-bar-delayed fills from 5-minute OHLCV. We cannot measure true latency, bid-ask spread, queue priority, partial fills, or intrabar path, so the stress test is approximate rather than execution-realistic.
review.already_tried_note: The team has not listed a fill-latency or delayed-execution robustness test as already tried. The existing baseline already uses next-bar-open execution, but the adverse-fill stress test itself is new.
review.overfit_note: As a fixed diagnostic there are effectively no free knobs. The only risk is cherry-picking whichever fill assumption looks best, so the stress cases must be pre-committed before looking at results.
review.expected_effect: No direct alpha expected. Best case: confirms the edge survives plausible execution drag. More likely: it reduces apparent performance, which is still valuable because it stops us from deploying a timing-fragile, cost-negative variant.
review.test_protocol: Replay all 67 archived sessions with the existing signals unchanged. Compare three fill assumptions side by side: baseline next-bar-open, trade-on-close, and one extra 5-minute bar of delay beyond the baseline. Use net PnL after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, and session-level consistency as the main metrics. Require the edge to keep its sign in both halves of the sample; if the delayed-fill case wipes out most of the PnL or drops PF below 1 in either half, classify the setup as timing-fragile and do not use any timing-optimistic variant live. Then monitor the next ~20 unseen sessions to confirm real fill drift stays inside the stressed range.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible, and useful as a gate. It is not a source of alpha, but it is exactly the kind of diagnostic that prevents us from wasting live tests on an execution-fragile backtest.

name: Recompute the in-play volume baseline on comparable full sessions
one_line: Exclude half-days and shortened sessions from the 10-session relative-volume baseline so the in-play filter is not distorted.
parameter_choices: Use only regular full sessions in the baseline; skip half-days and other shortened sessions; optionally maintain weekday-specific baselines.
disagreement: This is more data hygiene than alpha, but it can materially change who qualifies as in play.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source does not prescribe this exact rule, but it explicitly says session hours, holidays, DST shifts, and weekday effects matter when building intraday volume profiles. Excluding shortened sessions from a 10-session volume baseline is a direct, reasonable adaptation of that guidance.
review.exact_rule_change: Change only the in-play baseline: when computing each symbol’s 9:30–10:00 average volume over the prior 10 sessions, include only prior full regular sessions (defined as 78 regular-session 5-minute bars from 9:30 to 16:00 ET). Exclude holiday-shortened or otherwise incomplete sessions from that baseline. Keep the 1.5x threshold, top-8 ranking, and all other ORB rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is data hygiene, not new alpha. A shortened session is not comparable to a normal day, so including it can distort the relative-volume reference and make the in-play list noisy. A cleaner baseline should make the bot pick more genuinely active names, which could reduce failed-breakout trades and some of the flat, low-quality days; any cost benefit would come indirectly from avoiding marginal setups.
review.data_missing: None. We can detect shortened/incomplete sessions from the 5-minute bar count alone; no pre-market, L2, news, or extra datasets are needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. The existing in-play filter was already used, but this specific baseline-cleanup variant has not been isolated and tested.
review.overfit_note: Very few knobs if we keep it fixed at 'prior 10 full sessions only.' The main risk is not over-parameterization but a tiny effect size, since shortened sessions are rare in a 67-session sample. Do not start adding weekday buckets or tuning the session definition on the archive.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small but plausible cleanup: slightly more stable in-play selection, fewer false qualifiers on odd/holiday weeks, and possibly a modest reduction in bad breakout days. Trade count may fall a bit if the old baseline was admitting marginal names.
review.test_protocol: Run a deterministic side-by-side replay on all archived days with the exact same ORB execution rules. Compare baseline vs this variant on: net PnL after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, and trade count. Require the sign to be consistent in both chronological halves of the archive, not just the full sample. If the variant only helps on days whose lookback windows contain shortened sessions, that is still useful, but only if the total archive result is positive or at least not worse. If it passes, forward-test the fixed rule on the next ~20 unseen sessions with no further tuning.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, fully feasible with existing 5-minute bars, and directly tied to a known source concern about session comparability. It is not a new strategy, not previously rejected, and has only one fixed rule change, so the overfit risk is low. The expected edge is probably small, but this is exactly the kind of hygiene tweak worth testing now rather than guessing about.

name: Normalize intraday volume tempo by symbol
one_line: Scale the in-play and entry timing rules by each symbol’s usual intraday volume pace instead of using one raw threshold for every name.
parameter_choices: Estimate a per-symbol characteristic time or 30-minute volume profile from the last 10-20 full sessions; use it to normalize the 9:30-10:00 volume test and/or morning timing gates.
disagreement: Whether symbol-specific volume tempo is stable enough to improve selection beyond the existing relative-volume filter.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: B1-c001-07 supports the general idea of symbol-specific time-scale normalization; B1-c025-10 supports using 30-minute volume for timing. Neither source directly proposes an ORB in-play filter, so this is an adaptation rather than a direct rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the 10:00 in-play screen with a symbol-specific opening-pace score: opening_share = (9:30–10:00 volume) / average daily volume over the prior 20 full sessions. Keep only names whose opening_share is at least 1.5× their own median opening_share over the prior 20 sessions, rank the top 8 by opening_share, and leave the breakout/stop/exit rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This tries to pick names that are not just active, but unusually active for that symbol’s own normal morning pace. If it works, we should get fewer failed breakouts and fewer dead-flat closes from mediocre names, without adding costs or changing execution.
review.data_missing: None for this regular-session version; 5-minute OHLCV is enough to compute opening_share and the 20-session baseline.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list, but the live bot already uses a related symbol-relative opening-volume filter. This is a refinement of that layer, not a wholly new edge.
review.overfit_note: There are only a couple of degrees of freedom, but it is still easy to invent many near-variants (10 vs 20 sessions, mean vs median, ratio vs percentile) and fit 67 days of noise. Freeze the formula before replaying.
review.expected_effect: Best case: slightly fewer bad breakout entries and a modest improvement in target/stop mix. More likely: a small reshuffle of qualifying names with little net change. It should not materially change costs.
review.test_protocol: Fix the formula above before looking. Replay on all 67 archived sessions side by side with the frozen baseline using the same fills and costs. Compare net PnL after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, stop rate, target rate, flat-at-close rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive and no >20% drop in trade count before spending any unseen days. If it clears that bar, forward-test on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with the data we already have, cheap to replay, and at least directionally aligned with the failure mode we care about. The expected edge is probably small because the current bot already uses a relative-volume screen, but it is worth one fixed archived test before we spend live days.

name: Gate entries with a standardized momentum oscillator
one_line: Require an intraday momentum or attention score to clear a threshold before taking the ORB, instead of relying on price breakouts alone.
parameter_choices: Test a z-score band such as ±1, or an APO-like threshold such as ±10; tune lookback length and threshold walk-forward on unseen days.
disagreement: Whether a standardized oscillator filter adds edge or just reduces signals and delays entries.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The book supports thresholded oscillator entries in general (z-score bands and APO cutoffs), but not ORB gating. The ±1 and ±10 values are explicitly presented as examples/arbitrary, so this is only a generic confirmation-filter analog, not direct evidence for this strategy.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a pre-entry momentum gate: compute the 12-bar z-score of the symbol's 5-minute close using the prior 12 regular-session bars. Take a long ORB only if z >= +1.0 on the breakout bar; take a short ORB only if z <= -1.0. Otherwise skip the trade. Keep every other Midas rule unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could filter out weak, low-momentum breakouts that currently reverse into stops or drift flat by the close. Best case: fewer stop-outs, slightly higher win rate, and lower commission/slippage from fewer marginal trades. Main risk: it just delays entries and removes some of the few target winners, so the gain has to show up as a cleaner stop rate, not just fewer trades.
review.data_missing: None for the z-score version; 5-minute OHLCV is enough. A true 'attention score' based on news/flow is not available in our data.
review.already_tried_note: Not the same rule, but it is the same family of extra confirmation filters. You already tried requiring more confirmation beyond the breakout (two closes beyond range) and it got worse, which is a warning sign that this may just cut the trade stream.
review.overfit_note: Only two real knobs (lookback and threshold), but with 67 days and ~1 trade/day it is very easy to discover a fake sweet spot. Keep the formula fixed, do not tune per symbol, and do not search many thresholds.
review.expected_effect: Most likely effect is fewer trades, lower stop-out count, and possibly a small PF lift if weak breakouts are the problem. If it helps, it should be visible as better per-trade expectancy and a lower failed-breakout rate. If it mostly lowers trade count without improving per-trade PnL, reject it.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the exact filter (12-bar z-score, +/-1.0) before looking at results. Replay it on all 67 archived sessions side-by-side with the frozen baseline, with the same costs and fills. Compare: net PnL after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, trades/session, and stop-out rate. Split the archive into early and late halves; require improvement in both halves, not just the full sample. If the filter leaves fewer than about 25 trades on the archive or only helps by reducing activity, kill it. If it clears the archive test, run the next ~20 unseen sessions before keeping it.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with current data and cheap to replay. The support is only generic thresholded-oscillator logic, not direct ORB evidence, so the odds of a real edge are modest, but this is still testable without new data. The key is to freeze one parameter set and kill it quickly if it fails the archive half-split or starves the trade stream.

name: Enforce anti-chop spacing before same-direction entries
one_line: Require enough swing size and distance from the last same-direction entry so the bot does not keep re-entering the same noisy level.
parameter_choices: Use a minimum pre-entry swing window such as 40-50 bars, a short gap exclusion such as 5-10 candles, and a minimum distance from the last entry of about 0.2-0.3 ATR.
disagreement: Whether the spacing rule improves expectancy or mostly just lowers trade count and turnover.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books support the general pattern of anti-chop filters: a minimum price move from the last buy/sell, plus short gap and lookback thresholds. But those examples are from different indicator-based strategies, not from an ORB bot that already trades only once per day, so the link here is adaptation rather than direct evidence.
review.exact_rule_change: No concrete change to the current Midas recipe as written: with one trade per day and no same-day re-entries, a same-direction spacing rule has almost nothing to act on. To make the idea operative you would need a different strategy: allow repeat same-direction entries and then block them until price is at least 0.25 ATR(14) away from the prior same-direction fill and at least 10 sessions have passed. That is a new strategy, not a small tweak.
review.mechanism: In theory this would cut churn by refusing to trade the same noisy level repeatedly, which could reduce failed-breakout stops and slippage. On Midas specifically, the effect is likely tiny because the bot already takes at most one trade per day, so there is little same-day re-entry to suppress. If it does anything, it will mostly reduce trade count, not create a new edge.
review.data_missing: No external data is required. We can compute it from the existing 5-minute OHLCV plus the bot’s own stored last-entry price/direction and ATR from bars already in the archive.
review.already_tried_note: We already tried a related anti-chop idea: requiring two consecutive closes beyond the range before entry, and that was worse. We have not specifically tested a distance-from-last-entry cooldown, but it is the same family of filter.
review.overfit_note: This is easy to tune on only 67 sessions. With at most a couple of knobs, the danger is that we fit a cooldown that simply removes bad days in sample while also removing good trades out of sample.
review.expected_effect: Most likely outcome: fewer trades and little or no improvement in net P&L after costs. Best case is a small reduction in repeat chop losers; more realistic is that the rule does almost nothing on this bot or quietly starves the few good trades we already get.
review.test_protocol: Do not allocate unseen live days to this idea. If the team insists on checking it, run a frozen archived replay only, comparing baseline vs. the fixed cooldown variant on net P&L after costs, profit factor, stop-out rate, max drawdown, and trade count. Split the 67-day archive into first and second halves and require improvement in both halves before any live test. If the rule barely fires or only reduces trades, discard it.
review.verdict_reason: Reject because the proposed anti-chop spacing is basically a different strategy for this bot. Midas already has one trade per day, so same-direction re-entry spacing is mostly dead code unless we redesign to allow repeat entries. Given the tiny sample and the risk of just lowering trade count, this is not a good use of new tests.

name: Confirm breakouts with classic chart structure
one_line: Only take the ORB when the morning setup also shows a clear support/resistance, neckline, triangle, or reversal-structure confirmation.
parameter_choices: Define pattern windows over roughly 20-60 bars, require a neckline or triangle close rather than a wick break, and allow retest-based confirmation where appropriate.
disagreement: Whether chart-structure filters improve the bot enough to justify lower frequency and more complex pattern detection.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: The sources do support the general textbook idea of confirmation by structure: rejection at support/resistance, neckline breaks/retests, and triangle close-outs. But they are generic chart-pattern rules, not evidence that this improves a 5-minute ORB on liquid US stocks after your stated costs.
review.exact_rule_change: If you insist on an objective proxy, change the entry trigger to: after 10:00, take the first ORB only if the signal bar is a 5-minute close beyond the OR high/low and beyond the high/low of the prior 24 regular-session 5-minute bars; do not enter on wick-only breaks. One new parameter: lookback = 24 bars.
review.mechanism: In theory this should cut some August-style fakeouts by requiring the breakout to clear a broader local structure, so fewer trades should stop out immediately and a few more may reach target. The cost is later entries, lower trade count, and possibly missing the best initial impulse, which is dangerous on a small book with fixed per-share slippage.
review.data_missing: We can build a crude OHLCV proxy from the 5-minute bars we already have, but true neckline/triangle detection is subjective on this data. Lower-timeframe bars, premarket levels, or manual labels would help if you want real chart-pattern classification.
review.already_tried_note: The core mechanism is the same as the already rejected 'two consecutive closes beyond the range' test: add more confirmation before entry. This version is just a more elaborate, more subjective confirmation filter.
review.overfit_note: There are many degrees of freedom hidden inside 'classic structure'—lookback length, what counts as a touch, which patterns qualify, and whether to use close vs retest. With only 67 sessions and ~53 trades, this is very easy to fit to noise.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer false breakouts and a slightly higher target-hit rate. More likely: fewer trades, later entries, and no net improvement after costs because the bot already has an entry-confirmation layer and this filter just removes sample.
review.test_protocol: Replay all 67 archived sessions with the baseline vs the variant, using the fixed 24-bar proxy before looking at results. Compare net PnL after costs, stop rate, target rate, and total trades, and split the archive into Jul-Aug vs Sep-Oct. Only count it as interesting if it improves in both halves and still produces roughly 30+ variant trades; if the lift comes from one month or from a collapsed trade count, discard it. If it clears archive, forward-test on the next 20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: This is textbook chart-lore with weak empirical support, and the closest prior experiment was already a more direct version of the same idea and got worse. On our data, it is subjective, high-variance, and likely to starve an already modest trade count more than it fixes failed breakouts.

name: Higher-timeframe market regime gate
one_line: Only take longs when the broad market is in an up regime and shorts when it is in a down regime.
parameter_choices: Use SPY above its open, prior close, or 20-day average for longs; below those for shorts; optionally require the market to be above or below a short-term trend line before allowing entries.
disagreement: Sources agree that the market regime matters, but differ on how much weight to put on SPY versus the traded name itself; keep the market gate separate from any stock-level trend filter.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: One source item explicitly proposes the near-identical rule: only take longs when SPY is above its 20-day average and shorts when below. The other items support the broader trend/regime idea, but the support is still practitioner guidance, not evidence that this helps Midas specifically.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a daily SPY regime gate: at 10:00 New York, allow long ORB entries only if SPY's most recent completed daily close is above its 20-day simple moving average; allow short ORB entries only if SPY's most recent completed daily close is below its 20-day simple moving average. New parameter: regime lookback = 20 sessions. Leave all other Midas rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is mainly a bad-day filter. In weak broader tape, breakouts are more likely to fail, and shorts are more likely to get squeezed; in strong tape, the reverse is true. So the gate could reduce stop-outs and max drawdown, and maybe lift win rate, but it will probably also cut some of the few target days. It will not materially lower per-trade costs; any benefit comes from skipping low-quality regimes.
review.data_missing: None for this version. You already have daily SPY closes, so the 20-day SMA gate can be computed from existing data. If you wanted a true trend line instead, you'd need to define it, but not more data.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule. However, the bot already has an intraday SPY confirmation ('beats SPY's open-to-now return in that direction'), so this is only an added higher-timeframe overlay, not a completely new market filter.
review.overfit_note: Only one fixed knob if you commit to the 20-day SMA, but the family of plausible regime gates is large (open, prior close, 20-day, slope, trendline). With 67 sessions, it is easy to pick the one that flatters the archive unless you freeze the rule before looking.
review.expected_effect: If it works, expect fewer losing days and fewer failed-breakout stops, with a possible bump in win rate and drawdown control. The likely trade-off is fewer trades and a real chance of cutting some of the rare target days, so net P&L may improve only slightly or not at all.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule exactly as written (SPY most recent completed daily close vs 20-day SMA) and replay it side-by-side with the frozen baseline on all 67 archived sessions. Use paired day-level comparison and report: net P&L after costs per session, profit factor, win rate, trade count, and max drawdown. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just one lucky stretch. If the gate cuts trade count by more than about 30% without improving day-level expectancy and drawdown, kill it. If the archive test passes, forward-test on the next ~20 unseen trading days with no further parameter changes.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap to replay, no new data needed, and it targets the exact failure mode we care about: bad market regimes. The edge may be small and the gate may starve the bot, but this is simple enough to test without wasting live days, provided you do not tune the threshold after seeing the archive.

name: Stock-level trend confirmation
one_line: Only take breakouts when the stock itself is already trending in the breakout direction.
parameter_choices: Use one stock trend proxy at a time: 10-day EMA, 20-day SMA, positive 20-day momentum, 5 closes above SMA20, HH/HL or LL/LH structure, RSI above or below 50, or positive APO-style confirmation.
disagreement: The books mostly agree on trend-following, but they disagree on which proxy is best and how much lookback to use; test one definition at a time rather than stacking them all.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: B7-c002-11 explicitly says prices above a 10-day EMA are buy conditions and below it are sell conditions, which is very close to this filter. B2-c009-04, B2-c011-01, B4-c004-07, and B4-c005-02 all reinforce the same general 'trade with the prevailing trend' idea. The only adaptation is applying that trend gate to Midas' ORB entries rather than using it as a standalone direction rule.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00 NY, only allow a long ORB if yesterday's daily close is above the stock's 10-day EMA, and only allow a short ORB if yesterday's daily close is below the stock's 10-day EMA. Compute the EMA on daily closes through yesterday only. No other trend proxy is used in this test.
review.mechanism: This should remove a chunk of the weakest breakouts: longs in names that are still drifting down and shorts in names that are still drifting up. Those are the trades most likely to break, reverse, and either hit the stop or go nowhere into the close. If it works, the gain will come from fewer stop-outs, fewer dead-flat exits, and lower commission/slippage from skipping marginal setups.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: We have rejected a market-level trend overlay on SPY/QQQ, but not a stock-level daily EMA gate on the ORB universe. This is similar in spirit, but not the same test.
review.overfit_note: The filter itself is simple, but the broader idea family has many interchangeable proxies (EMA, SMA, RSI, momentum, HH/HL). That makes it easy to data-mine if we start shopping among them. Fix 10-day EMA now and do not compare alternatives on the same archive.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, fewer failed-breakout stops, slightly lower costs, and a better win rate on trend days. The main risk is missing some valid news-driven reversals or early trend changes.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the 10-day EMA rule before looking at results. Replay baseline vs. filter on all 67 archived sessions, then score the first half and second half of the archive separately. Use net P&L after costs as the primary metric, with expectancy per trade, win rate, stop rate, target rate, and flat-at-close rate as diagnostics. Only promote it if both halves improve or at least do not deteriorate materially, and if the filtered set still has enough trades to be meaningful (roughly 25+ archive trades; below that, treat the result as underpowered). If it passes the archive, run it unchanged on the next 20 unseen sessions with no retuning.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with the data we have, cheap to replay, and directly targets the bot's main failure mode: countertrend breakouts that stop out or drift flat. The evidence is not strong enough to trust blindly, but it is strong enough to justify one clean test.

name: Skip extreme volatility regimes
one_line: Stand aside or cut size when realized volatility is clearly in a bad regime for ORB.
parameter_choices: Threshold on 20-day rolling standard deviation, 60-day rolling vol, one-step GARCH forecast, annualized realized vol, or a simple SPY decline/high-vol label; trade only in a middle band.
disagreement: Some sources favor skipping volatile regimes outright, while others prefer scaling aggressiveness by volatility; this idea is the skip/size-down version.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general premise that volatility clusters, is nonstationary, and can be measured with rolling realized vol / 20-day std / 60-day horizons. None of them directly show that an ORB on US equities should be skipped specifically in extreme-volatility regimes, so the exact filter is our adaptation, not a quoted rule.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00 New York, compute SPY’s 20-session annualized realized volatility from daily close-to-close returns. Compare it to the prior 60 sessions of the same volatility series; take the existing ORB only if today’s value is between the 25th and 75th percentile of that 60-session history. Otherwise skip the day entirely. No other ORB rules change.
review.mechanism: This is meant to avoid the days where the whole market is whipping around enough to turn breakouts into stop-outs and late reversals. On this bot, that should mainly reduce failed-breakout losses and worst-day drawdown, and maybe trim some execution noise. The tradeoff is fewer trades and the risk of skipping some of the best trend days.
review.data_missing: none for the proposed SPY-based filter; daily closes are enough to compute the regime signal, and the 5-minute bars remain available for the ORB itself.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly. The rejected ideas were different filters/overlays (single-name ORB, SPY/QQQ intraday overlay, universe pruning, confirmation closes, morning fade), but not a volatility-regime skip rule.
review.overfit_note: There are many ways to define "extreme volatility" (lookback, asset, threshold, percentile band). With only 67 sessions and few trades, this can be tuned into noise unless the parameters are fixed before any inspection and left untouched.
review.expected_effect: Most likely fewer stop-outs and fewer ugly days, with lower drawdown and possibly slightly better after-cost expectancy. Also likely fewer trades and a real chance of throwing away some of the winning trend days that drive most of the edge.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule exactly as written before looking at results. Replay it on all 67 archived sessions side by side with the baseline. Primary metric: after-cost net PnL per session. Secondary metrics: max drawdown, stop-out rate, target rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both chronological halves of the sample, not just overall. If archived replay looks better, run the same fixed rule on the next 20 unseen sessions and only keep it if the forward sample does not revert the gain and does not cut trade count so much that expectancy becomes unstable.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our data, cheap to replay, and the hypothesis is at least directionally supported by volatility-clustering literature. The support is only partial and the overfit risk is high, but this is still concrete enough to test without new data or a new strategy.

name: Volatility-scaled breakout threshold
one_line: Make the ORB trigger harder to hit on noisy days and easier on quiet days.
parameter_choices: Use a larger buffer beyond the opening range when first-hour or rolling volatility is high; shorten lookbacks in high vol and lengthen them in low vol; set the entry multiplier from 5-minute or first-hour realized volatility.
disagreement: A worked example says dynamic thresholds degraded performance, so this should be treated as a falsifiable variant rather than a presumed improvement.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the broad idea that volatility regimes should change trading aggressiveness, and that volatility-based signals can become less aggressive in noisy periods. But none of them states a first-hour-volatility-scaled ORB trigger. The closest source is also cautionary: it says dynamic thresholds degraded performance in a worked example, without statistics.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the existing ORB, but at 10:00 compute σ30 = the standard deviation of the six 5-minute close-to-close returns from 9:30–10:00 (expressed as a decimal return). Set buffer_pct = 0.5 × σ30. Then go long only if a 5-minute close is > OR high × (1 + buffer_pct), and go short only if a close is < OR low × (1 - buffer_pct). Leave stops, target, sizing, and flat time unchanged.
review.mechanism: On choppy mornings, the first break of the opening range is often just a wick-and-revert. A volatility buffer should filter some of those marginal breaks, which could cut stop-outs and dead-end flats. On quieter mornings the buffer stays smaller, so we still get some early continuations. The downside is fewer trades and a real chance of missing the few big winners, which matters because this bot’s edge is already thin and costs are meaningful.
review.data_missing: None; the needed opening-session volatility estimate can be computed from the existing 5-minute OHLCV bars.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact formula, but it is the same family as the rejected 'two consecutive closes beyond the range' idea: make the entry harder to reduce failed breakouts. So the mechanism has already been explored in spirit and did not help.
review.overfit_note: There is at least one free multiplier to tune, and only 67 archived sessions with 53 trades. The six-bar volatility estimate is noisy, so it would be easy to fit a threshold that only looks good on this sample.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer false-breakout stops, but also fewer entries and more missed winners. Net effect after costs is uncertain and could easily be slightly negative on this low-sample system.
review.test_protocol: If you insist on checking it, fix buffer_pct = 0.5 × σ30 before looking at results. Replay on all archived days versus the frozen baseline. Compare after-cost P&L per session, profit factor, max drawdown, and trade count, and require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just overall. Also require trade count not to drop by more than 25%. If it fails either half, or the improvement is only from cutting trades, do not forward-test. Only if it passes should it be paper-traded on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: This is just a volatility-tuned version of a stricter-entry filter, and that family is already adjacent to a change we tried and rejected. The source support is weak, the only near-match warns that dynamic thresholds can hurt, and our sample is too small to justify another knob that is likely to reduce fills and miss the few large winners that currently carry the edge.

name: News and scheduled-event blackout
one_line: Do not trade ORBs on obvious event days that are prone to gap or headline noise.
parameter_choices: Manual no-trade on earnings day and 1-2 sessions around earnings; exclude major macro-release mornings; optionally exclude profit-warning or major headline names.
disagreement: No direct disagreement; the main constraint is that this will need a manual calendar at first.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: Multiple sources advise keeping a calendar of earnings/macro/news events and avoiding trading through major news because it can create unpredictable volatility. That supports the general idea of an event filter, but none of the excerpts gives a measured ORB edge or a tested blackout window. This is our adaptation, not a directly documented rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a hard event-blackout layer before the current 10:00 NY in-play screen: (1) do not trade any symbol with scheduled earnings within a ±1-session window of the trade date; (2) do not take any new ORB entries on major pre-open macro-release days, using a full-day blackout on those dates. Keep all other ORB rules unchanged; if fewer than 2 names remain, sit out as usual.
review.mechanism: This could cut the worst ORB failures on headline days, where the opening range is dominated by earnings or macro shocks and the breakout often reverses or gaps through the stop. The likely benefit is fewer stopouts and lower drawdown, especially on ugly days. The likely cost is fewer trades and possibly fewer of the big 2.5R winners, because our current universe already overweights catalyst names.
review.data_missing: We do not have a timestamped earnings calendar or a macro-release calendar in the current archive. Regular-session 5-minute OHLCV and daily closes cannot tell us whether an earnings release was before open, after close, or whether a given day was an event day at all.
review.already_tried_note: We have not explicitly tested an event blackout. The current RVOL screen already leans toward eventful names, but that is not the same thing as excluding event days.
review.overfit_note: This is a small, hand-curated filter on a tiny sample. It is easy to tune the blackout window after seeing results, and event days are rare enough that one or two outliers can fake a win. If the calendar and windows are not fixed before replay, it is very easy to overfit.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer failed-breakout stopouts and a cleaner equity curve. More likely: lower trade count, lower variance, and only a modest improvement in stop rate, with a real chance of lower total P&L if the filter removes the days that generate the big winners.
review.test_protocol: Do not judge this on intuition. First, pre-register the calendar source and blackout windows. Then replay all 67 archived sessions side by side with baseline and compare: trade count, net P&L after costs, expectancy per trade, profit factor, stop rate, max drawdown, and number of sit-out days. Split the archive into first 34 and last 33 sessions and require the filtered version to improve in both halves, not just in aggregate. Also check that the removed event days were actually worse than non-event days. Because event days are sparse, require at least about 10 event sessions in the archive or about 20 filtered trades; otherwise call it inconclusive. If it passes archive testing, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions before deployment.
review.verdict_reason: Plausible as a filter, but we cannot test it from the current data because the archive lacks the event calendar and announcement timestamps. Also, our bot already trades high-RVOL catalyst names, so a blanket blackout could easily remove the best opportunities. Build the calendar first; until then, do not spend replay cycles on it.

name: Extreme-momentum plus relative-volume in-play gate
one_line: Only promote names that are already making a large directional move and have strong relative volume.
parameter_choices: Require a large day-over-day return extreme such as +10% or -10% versus the prior close, or a 30-day return z-score beyond +/-2; keep relative volume as a hard qualifier and rank only the most extreme movers.
disagreement: High-volume continuation is supported by some sources, but others warn that high-volume moves can reverse; treat this as a momentum-extreme test rather than assuming volume alone means continuation.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)

review.source_support_note: No source states this exact gate. The closest support is a trader anecdote that his best trades were in stocks up more than 10% vs prior close with high relative volume, plus research summaries that extreme volume / winner-plus-high-volume conditions can be followed by same-direction excess returns. But there is also cited literature warning that high-volume price changes can reverse, so this is an adapted idea, not a direct rule.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00 ET, keep the existing in-play screen, but only allow longs if the stock’s move from yesterday’s close to the 10:00 close is >= +10.0%, and only allow shorts if that move is <= -10.0%. Among names passing that hard momentum gate, keep the existing top-8 ranking by 9:30–10:00 relative volume and leave the ORB entry/stop/target/flat rules unchanged. Do not use the 30-day z-score variant in this test.
review.mechanism: This is a stronger quality filter on the existing ORB. It should cut out the lukewarm names that drift, flatten, and cost us money, and concentrate the bot on the most attention-grabbing movers where continuation is more plausible. Best case: fewer failed-breakout stops and fewer flat-at-close trades, with a higher hit rate on the 2.5R target. Worst case: it throws away too many of our already-scarce trades and leaves us chasing late-stage exhaustion moves.
review.data_missing: None; the 10:00 move vs prior close and relative-volume gate can be computed from regular-session 5-minute OHLCV plus daily closes.
review.already_tried_note: Not tried as a hard +10%/-10% momentum gate. But the live bot already uses relative volume for selection and already has a weaker gap filter (>+2% skip longs, <-2% skip shorts), so this is a stricter version of an existing selection idea, not a totally new axis.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob (the 10% threshold) and it is borrowed from anecdote, while the 30-day z-score alternative would add another knob if we let it in. Extreme movers are rare in a 55-name universe, so the archive may end up with very few qualifying trades and any result will be easy to cherry-pick.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, lower cost drag, and possibly a higher breakout continuation rate on true catalyst days. It may also reduce the flat exits that are currently eating the edge. The main risk is that it filters us into late, exhausted moves and starves the bot of enough opportunities to matter on a $1,000 book.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the threshold at +10.0%/-10.0% before looking at results. Replay the full archived sample side by side with baseline, keeping all other rules identical. Compare net P&L after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, win rate, and trade count, with a required check that the filter helps in both chronological halves of the archive. Also require that it still produces a meaningful sample: if the archived run yields fewer than about 15 trades total, treat the test as too sparse and reject it. If the archive looks better, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions and require it to stay ahead of baseline without materially worse drawdown.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible and cheap to replay, but the source support is mostly anecdotal/adapted and the 10% extreme-momentum gate is likely to be too sparse and too close to an exhaustion-chase filter given our regular-session-only data and no catalyst/news context. This is exactly the kind of idea that can look clever on a tiny sample and then die from starvation or late entries.

name: Breakout-bar volume confirmation
one_line: Keep the in-play name, but only enter if the actual breakout bar itself has above-baseline volume.
parameter_choices: Use breakout-bar volume above the recent intraday average, above the 9:30-10:00 baseline, or a combined volume-and-range score; the filter should act on the entry bar, not just the morning selection window.
disagreement: Some literature warns that high-volume price moves can reverse, so use this as a confirmation filter rather than a blanket preference for high-volume days.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The books support the general principle that volume can confirm breakouts/continuations and that volume and volatility tend to rise together. They do not specify Midas's exact rule of a same-time-slot, 10-session baseline or a 1.5× threshold, so that part is our adaptation rather than a direct source rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current ORB setup, but only take the first breakout trade of the day if the trigger bar’s volume is at least 1.5× the average volume of that same 5-minute clock slot over the prior 10 regular sessions for that symbol. If the first close beyond the opening range fails this volume test, skip it and wait for the first later volume-qualified breakout (up to 15:15); otherwise no trade that day.
review.mechanism: This should filter out low-conviction breakouts that barely push through the opening range and then fall back into it, which is a known failure mode in this bot. In best case it reduces stop-outs and dead-flat closes, and may improve the share of trades that keep going to target. Trade count will probably drop a bit, but the trades that remain should be more purposeful.
review.data_missing: none; the existing 5-minute regular-session OHLCV is enough to compute same-slot historical volume baselines.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the rejected list. It is related to the existing morning relative-volume screen, but this is a distinct entry-bar confirmation filter and not one of the prior tests.
review.overfit_note: Only one real threshold, but it is easy to tune to 67 days if we let ourselves. The rule is simple enough to freeze ex ante and validate on both halves of the archive before touching live days.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer false breakouts and fewer stop-outs, with a possible small improvement in target hits. Costs may improve indirectly from better trade selection, but the main benefit is avoiding the weak breakout days that currently bleed the bot.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the 1.5× threshold before looking. Replay the change on all 67 archived sessions side-by-side against the frozen baseline. Primary readout: post-cost expectancy per session and max drawdown; secondary readouts: trade count, win rate, PF, and how many trades still reach 2.5R. Require the change to improve both halves of the archive (first 33 vs last 34 sessions) rather than only the full sample. Reject if trade count drops by more than 25% or if the improvement is driven by one outlier day. If archived replay is better, paper-run on the next ~20 unseen sessions and keep it only if the after-cost edge still beats baseline without worse drawdown.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully data-feasible, and directly targets the bot’s main weakness: failed breakouts. The evidence is only moderate and the trade-count risk is real, but that is exactly why it should be tested with a fixed threshold rather than argued abstractly.

name: Intraday volume-profile forecast filter
one_line: Trade only when the morning’s realized volume and volatility are not running hotter than the expected intraday profile.
parameter_choices: Forecast the day with a 30-session seasonal volume profile, EWMA smoothing constant 0.25-0.35, and 30-minute buckets; allow entries only if cumulative actual volume and realized volatility stay below forecast.
disagreement: This intentionally conflicts with the usual high-volume-is-good heuristic, so it should be tested as a separate low-noise regime rather than mixed with the high-volume filters.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Day Trade (sample)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: B1-c023-05 directly proposes forecasting intraday volume with a 30-day seasonal average and EWMA smoothing, then only entering when cumulative actual volume and realized volatility are below the forecast. That is essentially this filter; the ORB-specific application is our adaptation, not the source's.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a pre-entry regime gate to the existing ORB rule: after a name qualifies as in-play, and before any long/short entry, compute the symbol’s cumulative regular-session volume and realized 5-minute return volatility from 9:30 up to the current bar, using the prior 30 sessions as a 30-minute seasonal profile smoothed with EWMA alpha = 0.30; take the ORB trade only if both are below their same-time forecast, otherwise skip it. Start testing only after a 30-session warm-up.
review.mechanism: This tries to avoid the hottest, most overextended mornings where breakouts are already running too fast and then fail back into the stop. If it works, it should cut stop-outs and bad days more than it cuts target days, and also reduce churn on a small account. The obvious risk is that it may also filter out the rare strong trend days that actually pay us, especially because our current universe already prefers high-volume names.
review.data_missing: None required beyond the existing 5-minute regular-session OHLCV and daily closes; no premarket, L2, news, float, or spread data needed.
review.already_tried_note: No prior test of a volume/volatility profile gate. The rejected ideas were different: single-stock ORB, SPY/QQQ timing overlay, tighter universe caps, double-close confirmation, and morning fade.
review.overfit_note: This has at least two tunable choices (lookback length and EWMA alpha) and it can be made to fit the last 67 sessions very easily, especially if it just suppresses a handful of bad breakout days. A regime filter like this is exactly the kind of thing that can look good in-sample by starving the sample.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, fewer failed-breakout stops, and possibly lower max drawdown. But it may also remove some of our best momentum winners, so the net effect is genuinely ambiguous; if the filter is too strict, it will just starve the strategy.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule at 30 sessions and EWMA alpha 0.30 before looking at results. Replay baseline vs filtered bot on all 67 archived sessions, after excluding the first 30 sessions as warm-up for the profile. Compare net $ after costs per session, profit factor, stop rate, target rate, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive (first half vs second half) and no collapse in activity (at least about 60% of baseline trades); if it only looks better by skipping most trades, reject it. If it survives the archive, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions without retuning.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, feasible with our existing OHLCV, and directly targets our main weakness of failed breakouts. The source support is only opinion-level and the idea may starve the strategy, but that is exactly why it deserves one clean pre-registered replay test rather than more speculation.

name: Support/resistance zone filter
one_line: Avoid ORB trades that are too close to obvious higher-timeframe support or resistance, and prefer repeated-test zones over single-line levels.
parameter_choices: Build pivots with windows of 3, 5, or 7 bars; merge nearby levels within 0.5% to 10%; treat levels as zones with a 20% of range tolerance; require three touches before a level counts.
disagreement: Books disagree on exact line-versus-zone treatment and on how many confirmations are enough; use the conservative version with zones and multiple touches.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the ingredients, not this exact ORB filter: pivot highs/lows (windowed fractals), merging nearby levels into zones, requiring multiple touches, and the general claim that higher-timeframe support/resistance is more reliable. But none of the items gives a tested result for "skip ORB trades near higher-timeframe S/R zones" on stocks-in-play ORB, so the exact application is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Before any 10:00 ORB entry, build support/resistance zones from the prior 20 regular sessions of 5-minute bars using a 3-bar pivot rule; merge pivot levels within 0.5% and keep only zones with at least 3 touches. Then skip a long if the breakout close is within 20% of the opening-range width below the nearest resistance zone above OR high; mirror for shorts around support below OR low. Keep every other Midas rule unchanged.
review.mechanism: This should filter out breakouts that are running straight into obvious overhead supply or floor support, which is where our bot has been getting failed breakouts, stop-outs, and same-day drifts back to the close. If it works, the win rate and target-hit rate should improve, the flat-at-close bucket should get cleaner, and we should pay fewer commissions/slippage dollars because we take fewer marginal trades.
review.data_missing: We can approximate this from the 5-minute regular-session OHLCV we already have by deriving pivots/zone clusters from prior sessions. But we do not have pre-market levels, order book/L2, or full higher-timeframe daily OHLC history beyond the intraday archive, so this is only a proxy for true multi-week support/resistance.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. We have tried other filters and entry tweaks, but not a higher-timeframe support/resistance zone filter.
review.overfit_note: There are many arbitrary choices hiding inside this idea: pivot window, lookback length, merge threshold, touch count, and proximity buffer. With only 67 sessions and 53 trades, it would be very easy to tune a zone rule to the past and starve the sample.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, fewer immediate reversals into stop-losses, and a modest rise in win rate if the filter is real. The downside is missed breakouts and possible sample starvation; if the filter is too strict, total expectancy could get worse even if the raw win rate rises.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule now. Replay baseline vs. filtered Midas causally on all archived days, building zones only from prior data. Compare net $/session after costs as the primary metric, plus stop-out rate, target-hit rate, flat-at-close rate, and trade count. Require the filter to improve in both halves of the archive (first vs. second 33 sessions, or Jul-Sep vs. Oct) and to keep roughly at least 70% of baseline trades; if it drops much below that, call it too sparse. If it passes the archived test, paper-trade the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting it.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with current data, cheap to replay, and directly attacks our main failure mode (failed breakouts). The rule needs to be kept very narrow and fixed up front, but it is worth a controlled test now rather than a broad discretionary S/R experiment.

name: Lengthen the opening range
one_line: Wait for 45 minutes of price discovery before allowing the first breakout.
parameter_choices: Use a 45-minute opening range instead of 30 minutes; optionally stand down on days where the first 45 minutes are clearly hesitant.
disagreement: No direct disagreement; this is a pure tradeoff between later entry and fewer false breakouts.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: Both sources support the general intuition of waiting through the noisy post-open/hesitant period before committing risk, but neither source recommends a 45-minute opening range specifically. This is an extrapolation from the books' qualitative advice, not a direct rule from them.
review.exact_rule_change: Parameter change only: keep the current in-play scan at 10:00 unchanged, but replace the 9:30–10:00 opening range with a 9:30–10:15 opening range. Do not allow any ORB entry until 10:15. After 10:15, keep all other Midas rules unchanged: first 5-minute close beyond the 45-minute OR high/low that also beats SPY in the same direction, next-bar-open fill, same gap filters, same stop, target, flat time, and day-loss halt.
review.mechanism: Waiting an extra 15 minutes should filter some early auction noise and weak first-hour fakeouts, so fewer trades should immediately reverse into the stop. The wider opening range also widens the stop, which shrinks position size under fixed 1% risk and can slightly reduce dollar slippage/commission. The tradeoff is later entry, less time to reach 2.5R, and likely fewer target hits.
review.data_missing: None for the base test; 5-minute regular-session OHLCV and SPY are enough.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is a timing tweak to the current ORB, not the rejected two-close filter, pet-stock test, or SPY first-half/last-half overlay.
review.overfit_note: Only one new knob, but there are many plausible OR lengths (35/40/45/60), so it is easy to mine a short sample if we start tuning after looking at results. Fix 45 minutes once and do not search.
review.expected_effect: If it helps, expect fewer stop-outs and fewer bad breakout days, with a smaller trade count and possibly more flat-at-close exits because entries are later. Net P&L only improves if the cleaner breakout quality more than offsets the lost intraday runway.
review.test_protocol: Replay the baseline 30-minute ORB and the fixed 45-minute ORB on all archived days side by side, with no other changes. Compare cost-adjusted net P&L per session, profit factor, stop rate, target rate, average trade, and max drawdown; do not judge it on win rate or PF alone if trade count collapses. Require the effect to be directionally positive in both halves of the archived sample, not just in the full-sample aggregate. If 45 minutes wins on archived data, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with existing data, cheap to replay, and it targets the bot's main failure mode. The evidence is weak and the tradeoff is real, but this is a legitimate parameter test rather than a new strategy or a data-dependent idea.

name: CUSUM change-point halt
one_line: Suspend new entries after a persistent shift in short-term returns is detected.
parameter_choices: Run CUSUM on 5-minute returns or SPY-relative returns with k=delta/2 and a user-set threshold h; the adaptive version updates the shift estimate with EWMA lambda.
disagreement: Fixed and adaptive CUSUM are alternatives, not additions; test one detector at a time.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book excerpts do support CUSUM as a change-point detector and give the k = δ/2 / user-threshold framing. But they do not show that halting an ORB after a CUSUM trigger is profitable; that trading application is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a fixed day-gate, not a new strategy: run two-sided CUSUM on SPY 5-minute close-to-close returns. Use k = 0.02% (so δ = 0.04%) and h = 0.10%. If either cumulative sum trips before the day’s ORB entry fills, cancel that day’s entry and allow no new entries for the rest of the session. Do not test the adaptive EWMA version in this pass.
review.mechanism: This is meant to keep us out of late-morning regime flips where an opening breakout is more likely to get chopped up or reverse into a stop. Best-case bucket: fewer failed-breakout stops and fewer bad days. Secondary benefit: a bit less cost from avoiding marginal trades. Main risk: it may also block some good trend days.
review.data_missing: None needed; 5-minute regular-session bars for SPY and the traded names are enough.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact detector. The closest thing already tried was the first-half-hour SPY/QQQ timing overlay, which is a related market-timing filter and it cut profit, so this family of idea is not new.
review.overfit_note: Threshold choice is arbitrary, and with only 67 sessions it is easy to tune the gate to explain away August after the fact. If we search k/h/series type, this will overfit fast.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer stop-outs and fewer ugly days, but also fewer trades and possibly fewer target winners. Net effect is probably modest because the bot already has an SPY-relative entry filter and a -3% day stop.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule before looking at outcomes. Replay it on all archived days side by side with baseline. Judge on daily net P&L after costs, max drawdown, and losing-day count, not just win rate. Require the improvement to show in both halves of the archive, and do not accept a version that mainly wins by starving trades; keep trade count within about 80% of baseline. If the replay is clearly better, confirm unchanged on the next ~20 unseen trading days. If it only helps the August cluster and hurts the rest, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our existing bars, cheap to replay, and directly targets the failed-breakout cluster. The evidence is only textbook-level and the overfit risk is high, but that is still good enough for one frozen backtest before we spend any forward days.

name: Special-day calendar filter
one_line: Treat month-end, quarter-end, expiry, and triple-witching sessions as their own regime.
parameter_choices: Flag month-end, quarter-end, expiry, and triple-witching dates; compare them separately from normal days.
disagreement: Special-day effects are widely acknowledged, but their strength should still be checked on Midas before hard-coding them.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly says to model normal days first and then model special days separately, and it names month-end, quarter-end, expiry and triple-witching as days with distinct intraday volume patterns. That supports calendar tagging/regime splitting, but it does not claim ORB should be skipped on those days or that any specific profit edge exists.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a binary calendar filter: if the session is the last trading day of the month, the last trading day of a quarter, or an options-expiry Friday (which covers triple-witching in Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec), set `special_day = true` and take no ORB trades that session. Keep all other Midas rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: These sessions can have abnormal liquidity, positioning, and end-of-period flow, so the current RVOL + opening-range breakout logic may be less reliable and may suffer worse fills or more false breakouts. The best-case benefit is fewer bad days and lower drawdown; the downside is skipping some good trend days.
review.data_missing: None for the test. The calendar flag can be derived from the trading-date list we already have; no pre-market, L2, news, float, or other extra data is needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. The closest prior overlay was the SPY/QQQ first-half-hour regime idea, which is a different type of intraday overlay rather than a fixed calendar filter.
review.overfit_note: The rule itself is deterministic, but the special-day subset is tiny in a 67-session sample, so one lucky or unlucky month-end/expiry can dominate the result. It is also easy to cherry-pick which calendar days 'count' after looking at the replay.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small effect either way. Best case: fewer ugly breakout failures and a bit less drawdown on weird calendar days. More likely: lower trade count with only modest PnL change, because these days are rare and the bot already normalizes via RVOL.
review.test_protocol: Pre-fix the calendar rule before looking at results, then replay all 67 archived days side-by-side with the frozen baseline, holding every other rule constant. Primary metrics: net after-cost PnL per session and max drawdown; secondary: profit factor, win rate, and trade count. Keep the change only if it improves net PnL and does not worsen drawdown, with the same sign of effect in both halves of the archive. If it passes that replay check, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions without changing the rule. Do not tune which special days count after seeing the results.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully computable from our existing date data, and at least plausibly targets a weak spot: regime days where the bot's normal breakout logic may be less stable. The expected edge is probably small, but this is worth one clean replay before spending time elsewhere.

name: Corporate-action and bad-bar hygiene
one_line: Clean the data before testing so the ORB statistics are not polluted by split days, halts, or malformed candles.
parameter_choices: Adjust previous close for splits and dividends; drop zero-volume bars and High==Low bars; exclude halts, suspensions, and other discontinuities from calibration and evaluation.
disagreement: No real disagreement; the main risk is forgetting that different data vendors can still disagree on OHLC.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The quoted items directly support the hygiene pieces of this idea: adjust for splits/dividends and keep previous close consistent for gap logic (B1-c004-03/05), track suspensions/limit-style interruptions (B1-c004-04), and remove zero-volume and High==Low bars before analysis (B2-c004-01/02/05). The only adaptation is that our feed may not expose explicit corporate-action or halt flags, so we have to operationalize them from the bar series.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a hard data-QA gate before any ORB replay: require a complete regular-session bar set (all 78 five-minute bars, no missing timestamps); drop any 5-minute bar with Volume=0 or High==Low; and, if the vendor supplies an adjusted previous close, use it for the overnight-gap filter, otherwise leave the existing gap rule unchanged and do not invent split math.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha; it removes malformed candles and discontinuous sessions that can fake an opening-range high/low, trigger phantom breakouts, misplace stops/targets, or misclassify the overnight gap filter. The likely benefit is fewer bad days and cleaner stats, with only a small chance of any PnL lift on already-clean liquid names.
review.data_missing: We can do the zero-volume, zero-range, and missing-timestamp checks from our 5-minute OHLCV. We do not have explicit halt/suspension metadata, split/dividend-adjusted daily closes, or corporate-action flags, so true corporate-action handling is only partial unless the vendor already provides adjusted closes.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the rejected list. The bot has not previously had a separate replay with explicit bad-bar/corporate-action hygiene.
review.overfit_note: There are essentially no tunable knobs if we hard-code the cleaning rules. The only way to overfit this would be to invent a discontinuity threshold and then tune it to the 67-day archive.
review.expected_effect: Small at best. On clean liquid-stock data the effect is likely near zero; on days with vendor glitches, missing bars, or unadjusted corporate-action discontinuities it could remove a few false entries and impossible fills. This is mostly a backtest integrity fix, not a trading edge.
review.test_protocol: Replay the full 67 archived sessions twice, baseline vs cleaned, with all trade logic frozen. Compare trade count, net after-cost PnL, profit factor, max drawdown, and the number of changed trades/days. Split the archive into first 33 and last 34 sessions and require the direction of effect to be consistent in both halves. Minimum informative sample: at least 5 affected symbol-days or 3 changed trades; if fewer, treat the result as QA only and keep the cleaner pipeline only if every changed trade is clearly attributable to a bad bar or incomplete session. Then confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: This is feasible with our current bar data in partial form and costs almost nothing to replay, so it is worth one archive run. But it is not an alpha hypothesis. The bar-cleaning subset can only remove garbage, and the corporate-action part is only partly testable without adjusted closes or action flags. Expect little or no PnL lift, but adopt it as standard preprocessing if it removes clearly bad sessions.

name: Regime-split walk-forward validation
one_line: Test any new filter separately in different market regimes instead of trusting the full-sample average.
parameter_choices: Split by high-vol vs low-vol, bull vs bear SPY, pre/post breakpoint dates, and normal vs special days; keep parameter selection walk-forward and non-overlapping.
disagreement: Some sources prefer simple averaging when regime estimates are unstable, so do not overcomplicate the split; start with a few coarse buckets.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
