review.source_support_note: The sources support regime-aware testing and walk-forward thinking in general, but none state this exact pre-registered regime-split validation protocol for an intraday ORB bot. They argue that relationships can appear only in certain regimes, and that strategy parameters/relationships can decay across regimes; one source also warns that unstable regime weighting can be worse than a simple average, so the split should stay coarse.
review.exact_rule_change: No live trading rule change. Pre-register one regime split for all future candidate filters: SPY 20-day realized volatility above vs below its trailing 60-session median. Any new filter must be evaluated out-of-sample separately in those two buckets using walk-forward selection on prior data only, and only promoted if it improves both buckets versus the unchanged baseline.
review.mechanism: This does not create edge by itself; it reduces false positives. On Midas, that matters because the current edge is small, sample-starved, and probably regime-sensitive. A regime split can reveal whether a proposed filter actually reduces failed breakouts in both market states or only looks good because one month dominates the backtest. The main gain is avoiding wasted tests and overfit filters, not lower costs directly.
review.data_missing: none for the proposed split; SPY daily closes and the existing 5-minute bars are enough to compute the regime label and replay trades.
review.already_tried_note: They have tried strategy tweaks and SPY overlays, but not a pre-registered regime-split walk-forward validation protocol.
review.overfit_note: As proposed, there are many possible regime definitions (high/low vol, bull/bear, breakpoints, special days), which makes p-hacking easy on 67 sessions. The safe version is one fixed split only; do not branch into multiple regime taxonomies at once.
review.expected_effect: Lower false discovery and fewer wasted live tests; little or no direct PnL impact unless this protocol leads to a genuinely regime-specific live gate.
review.test_protocol: Pick one candidate filter before looking at results. Replay all 67 archived sessions with the baseline ORB unchanged, and score the candidate separately in the pre-registered SPY high-vol and low-vol buckets. Compare post-cost expectancy per trade, profit factor, and max drawdown versus baseline within each bucket and in aggregate. Minimum bar: at least 20 archived sessions per bucket or 20 trades per bucket if available. Reject any filter that only helps one bucket, hurts the other, or only looks good on the full sample. If it survives the archive, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions with the split frozen.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and useful as a pre-registration rule, but only if we keep it to one coarse split. It will not generate edge on its own, so it should be used as a research wrapper rather than a live trading change. The main danger is turning this into multiple regime buckets and p-hacking the small sample.

name: Seasonality validation before codifying a calendar rule
one_line: Measure weekday and month effects on Midas first, because the books disagree on which calendar windows are strong or weak.
parameter_choices: Compare weekdays and month buckets separately; check April, May-July, August, September, and December; only hard-code a seasonality rule if the effect is stable out of sample.
disagreement: The sources conflict on month effects, especially April and the summer period, so seasonality should be empirically verified on our own data.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books support the general claim that seasonality exists and that weekday/month effects can matter, but they do not support this exact validation-first workflow or any specific Midas rule. The month claims are mostly opinion-level and even conflict (e.g. April/seasonal strength is described differently across excerpts).
review.exact_rule_change: No live trading rule yet: add logging tags for each Midas signal/trade (`weekday`, `month`) and keep the bot unchanged until one bucket shows stable out-of-sample weakness. If a calendar filter later survives testing, the first simple candidate from the sources is: skip new ORB entries in September.
review.mechanism: If there is real calendar drift, this lets us detect it before hard-coding a noisy filter. A genuine weak weekday or weak month could reduce failed-breakout stops and flat closes by keeping the bot out of bad windows, while avoiding unnecessary trade starvation.
review.data_missing: We can compute weekday effects from the 67-session 5-minute archive, but not robust month-of-year seasonality for April, May-July, August, September, and December. We only have 5-minute intraday data from Jul 24 2026 onward, so the key month claims in the sources cannot be properly checked yet; daily closes are not enough for this intraday strategy.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. They have not already tested a weekday/month calendar filter on Midas.
review.overfit_note: This is classic small-sample bucket mining: weekday × month gives many degrees of freedom, but we only have ~53 trades total. It would be easy to 'discover' a calendar rule that fits the current 67 days and dies immediately out of sample.
review.expected_effect: At best, a modest reduction in bad days if one calendar bucket is truly weak. I would not expect a large uplift unless the effect is very clean, because calendar seasonality is indirect and likely smaller than the bot's breakout/stop mechanics and costs.
review.test_protocol: Do not scan many buckets and pick the best one. Replay all archived days with the baseline, and bucket after-cost expectancy, win rate, target rate, stop rate, and drawdown by weekday and by month. Split the archive once into early vs late halves; a bucket only counts if it is weak in both halves and has at least 8 trades per half. Because the intraday archive does not include April/December, do not codify any month filter yet unless the sample grows to at least 20 trades in the candidate bucket or we have another full year of 5-minute history. If a bucket survives, forward-test that single frozen filter on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: The idea is cheap to analyze, but the current 5-minute archive is too short for meaningful month-of-year validation, and the sample is too small for broad weekday/month mining without severe overfit risk. Use it as a diagnostic/logging step now; do not spend a live test on a calendar rule yet.

name: Low-beta market-sensitivity screen
one_line: Skip very low-beta names when the breakout thesis is supposed to ride the market tape.
parameter_choices: Use 20-day beta-to-SPY, with a threshold around the universe median or roughly 0.8; compare against a 60-day beta variant.
disagreement: Some names are too unresponsive to the market to follow through, while others may still break out cleanly despite low beta.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books mention beta as a standard derived statistic and one excerpt explicitly suggests a 20-day beta-to-SPY filter as a test idea, but neither source gives direct ORB evidence. The low-beta comment in the other book is about minimum-variance portfolios, not breakout follow-through, so the support is mostly extrapolation and partly mixed.
review.exact_rule_change: Before step 2, compute each candidate's beta to SPY from the prior 20 daily close-to-close returns; exclude any name with beta < 0.8 from the in-play list, then keep the top 8 by relative volume from the remaining names. Leave the rest of the ORB rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: ORB breakouts need the market tape to keep pushing. Very low-beta names often do not amplify SPY direction, so they can print a breakout level and then stall, drift flat, or reverse. Filtering them should mainly reduce failed-breakout stops and especially the many flat-at-close exits, with a possible side benefit of fewer trades and less cost drag. It may also remove some catalyst-driven winners, so the effect is likely modest rather than transformative.
review.data_missing: None for this filter. We can compute a 20-session beta from the daily closes we already have, using SPY as the benchmark; no premarket, L2, news, or floats are needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly. The closest rejected item was the SPY/QQQ intraday overlay, which is a different market filter and failed because it cut profit. No prior test specifically screened ORB candidates by beta.
review.overfit_note: Only one cutoff, but the beta estimate itself is noisy on 20 sessions and the threshold can be tuned to 67 historical days very easily. If you start comparing multiple cutoffs and lookbacks, this becomes high-risk fast.
review.expected_effect: Best-case: slightly fewer entries, fewer dead-money flats, a higher target-hit rate, and a small reduction in failed breakouts. Worst-case: you throw away good catalyst names and starve the strategy. I would expect any edge to be small.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the cutoff at beta < 0.8 before looking. Replay all 67 archived sessions side by side with baseline, using only information available by 10:00 on each day. Primary metric: after-cost net PnL per session and per trade. Secondary metrics: win rate, target rate, stop rate, flat-at-close rate, average R, and trade count. Require the filter to improve performance in both halves of the archive, and do not accept a version that cuts trade count by more than about 20% unless the PnL gain is clearly better. If the replay leaves fewer than about 25 historical trades, treat it as too sparse to trust. If it clears the archive, paper trade the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully computable from the data we already have, and it targets a real failure mode rather than adding a new strategy. The evidence is weak and the beta estimate is noisy, but this is still worth one controlled replay because the downside is only time, not capital.

name: Short-horizon, differenced inputs only
one_line: Build any auxiliary signal from short lagged returns or differences, not raw price levels.
parameter_choices: Use 1-bar or 2-bar returns, short 5-bar lag windows, and first differences for daily features; avoid level-based predictors.
disagreement: Raw levels often create spurious signal, but differenced inputs may also throw away useful slow trends.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the modeling hygiene behind the idea: stock prices are often treated as nonstationary / random-walk-like, and first differences or short-horizon returns are the standard stationary transform. But none of the excerpts show that this improves ORB trading P&L; that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: No standalone live rule change. If we add an auxiliary filter/model, hard-code its inputs to short-horizon differences only: 1-bar return, 2-bar return, and 5-bar return on 5-minute bars; for daily regime features use first differences of daily closes. Default lookback window: 5 bars. Do not use raw price levels as predictors.
review.mechanism: This could only help indirectly by making any added filter less likely to key off arbitrary price levels and more likely to generalize across symbols/regimes. For Midas, the best-case effect is a slightly better pre-entry filter that avoids some failed-breakout stops or bad days. It does not directly improve execution, costs, or the opening-range logic itself, so the expected lift is small.
review.data_missing: None; all required features are derivable from the existing 5-minute OHLCV bars and daily closes.
review.already_tried_note: We already rejected a close cousin: Gao-style short-horizon return overlays on SPY/QQQ. That was a return-based predictor family and it hurt. This idea is broader, but it lives in the same short-memory / differenced-input camp.
review.overfit_note: Very easy to fit noise if we start searching over return windows, transforms, and thresholds. With only 67 sessions and ~53 trades, a few lucky days can make a weak feature look good. If you want to test it, the feature set must be frozen before looking at results.
review.expected_effect: If anything helps, it will show up as slightly better generalization for a future filter and maybe fewer false-positive entries. I would not expect a direct jump in win rate or profit factor from this alone, and it is unlikely to meaningfully change costs.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend unseen days on this as a generic principle. If you insist on testing, first define one fixed auxiliary filter in advance, such as a 5-bar momentum gate built only from 1/2/5-bar returns, and compare that fixed version against the same bot with no added filter on all archived days. Judge it on net P&L after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, and trade count (do not allow a big trade-starvation effect). It must improve both halves of the archive, then it can be confirmed on the next ~20 unseen sessions. No window searching.
review.verdict_reason: As stated, this is a feature-engineering convention, not a trading edge. We already know short-horizon return ideas are fragile here, and the current bot does not use a predictive model where this would naturally plug in. The data are available, but the idea is too generic to justify a fresh test unless you first define a specific auxiliary filter to evaluate.

name: ACF-based nonstationarity regime filter
one_line: Skip or cut size when recent return sequences look too persistent or too slowly mean-reverting.
parameter_choices: Compute the autocorrelation of the last 10-20 bars of opening-range failure or post-entry returns; veto when lag-1 to lag-3 autocorrelation stays too high.
disagreement: Slow ACF decay suggests the tape is drifting or mean-reverting in a way that can hurt continuation trades.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book item is not just adjacent theory; its own suggested test idea is almost the same as this proposal: use slowly decaying ACF as a regime check and skip/reduce size when it is high. What it does not provide is a validated edge on our ORB bot or a costed backtest.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00 New York, compute SPY's rolling sample autocorrelation on the most recent 12 completed regular-session 5-minute close-to-close returns. Average lag-1, lag-2 and lag-3 autocorrelations. If that average is > +0.25, cut the day's ORB risk from 1.0% of equity to 0.5%; otherwise leave the bot unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is a day-level tape filter. If the market is already in a very persistent or slowly mean-reverting state, our breakout entry is more likely to arrive in a sloppy, late, low-follow-through regime and end up as a stop or a flat close. Cutting size should reduce the damage on those bad days, though it may also trim the strongest trend days.
review.data_missing: We can compute this from the 5-minute bars we have, but not literally from today's post-entry return path before the entry decision. By 10:00 we only have 6 bars from the open, so a 10-20 bar ACF has to spill into prior regular-session bars (or the prior session). That makes this a pre-entry proxy, not the exact sequence described in the idea.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact statistic, but we already tested a similar intraday sequence/regime overlay on SPY/QQQ ('first half hour predicts last half hour') and it cut profit. That is a real warning sign for this whole family of filters.
review.overfit_note: The estimate is noisy on short 5-minute windows, the cutoff is arbitrary, and with only 67 sessions it would be easy to pick a window/threshold that flatters the archive. Because it is a day-level filter, a couple of lucky or unlucky days can swing the result.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer stopouts and fewer bad flat days on chop/persistent-drift regimes, with lower drawdown. More likely: it also cuts some of the few real trend days that pay for the system, so the net lift after costs is small or negative.
review.test_protocol: Fix the parameters before looking: 12-bar window, +0.25 threshold, size multiplier 0.5. Replay all archived sessions side by side with the frozen baseline. Judge on daily net P&L after costs, max drawdown, stop rate, target rate and trade count, and require the effect to hold in both chronological halves. Only if the archive is clearly better should we confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions with no retuning.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap to replay with the data we already have, so it is worth an archive screen now. But I would not spend live unseen days on it unless the replay shows a clear after-cost lift; the underlying signal is weak and likely to be noisy.

name: Cross-sectional co-movement regime filter
one_line: Trade ORB only in the cross-sectional correlation regime that has historically produced better follow-through.
parameter_choices: Use a rolling 20-day average pairwise correlation or a simple PCA score across the basket and SPY; define high- and low-co-movement states.
disagreement: Some days the market acts as one block, and other days names move independently; ORB may prefer only one of those states.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book supports looking for regime changes and co-movement shifts, but it does not specifically argue for gating an ORB by cross-sectional correlation. The ORB application is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a pre-open regime gate: compute the prior-20-session average pairwise correlation of 1-day returns across the 55-stock universe (daily closes only). Take the existing ORB only when that score is below 0.30; otherwise skip the day.
review.mechanism: When the basket is highly correlated, the day is mostly beta/noise and individual breakouts tend to whip back with the tape. Low co-movement should make a stock-specific breakout cleaner, reducing failed-break stops and some flat-at-close trades, though it will also cut the number of trades.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tried. We already have a separate SPY direction confirmation and previously rejected a different SPY/QQQ intraday overlay, so this is adjacent in spirit but not the same test.
review.overfit_note: One binary gate on only 67 archived sessions is easy to fit by luck, and the 20-day correlation estimate is noisy. The threshold direction (below vs above) is another implicit choice, so this can become a regime-mining exercise fast.
review.expected_effect: Could lower stop-outs and some dead-flat exits on choppy, high-beta days, but likely at the cost of fewer trades and potentially missing some good breakout days.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule now. Replay all 67 archived sessions side-by-side vs baseline. Primary metric: net $ after costs per session; secondary: PF, win rate, stop rate, flat-exit rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just the full sample. If the filter leaves fewer than about 25 trades or only helps one half, treat it as noise. If it passes archive, run unchanged for the next 20 unseen sessions and compare to baseline.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with existing daily closes and cheap to replay, and it is not already rejected. The source only weakly supports it, so don't expect much, but it is simple enough to pre-register and sanity-check without spending live days.

name: Low-rank feature compression for candidate scoring
one_line: Compress several stock and market features into a few factors before deciding which names are worth trading.
parameter_choices: Fit 1-3 components from a small feature set such as momentum, relative volume, beta, volatility, and gap size; score names on the compressed factors.
disagreement: A low-rank summary may denoise the inputs, but it can also hide useful nonlinear structure.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book directly supports reduced-rank / canonical-correlation style compression and even suggests using a few cross-sectional factors to rank names, but it is only a modeling recommendation, not evidence that the filter improves this ORB bot after costs.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00, replace the current top-8-by-relative-volume ranking with a 1-component rolling PCA score built from standardized {9:30–10:00 relative volume, overnight gap %, 5-day close-to-close return, 20-day realized volatility, 20-day beta vs SPY}; fit the PCA on the trailing 60 sessions only, then trade the top 8 names by PC1 score. Keep all other ORB rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: If the factor really captures a 'tradable breakout' latent style, it could remove redundant/noisy qualifiers and weed out names whose high volume is just churn, which might cut failed breakouts and a few stop-outs. The likely benefit is modest: maybe a slightly better win rate and fewer bad days, but probably also fewer trades.
review.data_missing: No extra data needed; all inputs can be derived from our existing 5-minute bars and daily closes.
review.already_tried_note: We have already tried universe pruning / candidate-selection changes (top-5 only, price caps), but not factor-ranked selection. This is still the same family of upstream filters, so it could fail in the same 'starve the book' way.
review.overfit_note: There are several implicit degrees of freedom (feature set, normalization, component count, and fit window) relative to only 67 sessions / 53 trades. PCA loadings on 55 names can move around a lot, so it is easy to fit noise and mistake it for edge.
review.expected_effect: At best a small improvement in candidate quality and stop rate; more likely a slight trade-count drop with no reliable after-cost gain.
review.test_protocol: Run a walk-forward replay on every archived day: each day fit the 1-component PCA only on prior sessions (no lookahead), rank the current candidates, and keep the top 8. Compare to the frozen baseline on after-cost net PnL per session, expectancy per trade, win rate, stop rate, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just the full sample, and require no collapse in trade count (e.g. keep at least ~75% of baseline trades). If it still looks better, paper trade the next 20 unseen sessions before deciding.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, but the sample is tiny for a model-based ranking rule and the likely edge is small. We should not trust a fitted low-rank score on 67 sessions unless it beats the baseline cleanly in walk-forward replay and in both halves of the archive.

name: Basket-relative deviation overlay
one_line: Only take ORB trades when the stock is already far away from a simple basket or market-neutral reference.
parameter_choices: Use a basket of SPY plus a few liquid names, compute a residual z-score over a 20-day window, and trade only when the deviation is extreme.
disagreement: A relative-value dislocation may add conviction, or it may just add mean-reversion drag to the breakout.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book excerpt supports the general cointegration/pairs-trading idea that linear combinations of names can carry signal, but it does not say to gate opening-range breakouts on a basket-relative z-score. The ORB overlay is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00, compute each candidate's 9:30-10:00 return minus an equal-weight basket return of SPY plus the 3 most liquid other names in our universe (ranked by trailing-20-session average dollar volume, excluding the candidate). Standardize that residual with a 20-session rolling mean and stdev from prior sessions only. Keep the existing ORB only if z >= +1.0 for longs or z <= -1.0 for shorts; otherwise skip.
review.mechanism: Use the basket filter as a conviction screen. If the stock is already decoupling from the market/peer basket in the first half hour, the breakout is more likely stock-specific rather than just beta noise, which could cut failed-breakout stops and some flat-at-close scratches. Main downside: it will likely shrink trade count, so the edge must come from higher quality, not more frequency.
review.data_missing: None for this version. The basket can be built from our 5-minute regular-session OHLCV and prior volume. We do not need premarket, L2, news, sector labels, or float.
review.already_tried_note: Adjacently similar to the rejected SPY/QQQ first-half-hour overlay, because both are market-relative filters. But this is cross-sectional relative strength versus a basket, not a time-series predictor of the rest of the day, so it is not the same test.
review.overfit_note: Only one real threshold, but the basket choice and z-cut can easily be tuned to the 67-day archive. Because ORB already has a market filter, this overlay may just repackage the same signal and look good only in-sample.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer stopouts and a slightly cleaner equity curve, with modestly better hit rate on the remaining trades. Most likely: lower trade count and a small or no change in expectancy unless the basket z-score is genuinely capturing stock-specific momentum. It is unlikely to fix costs by itself.
review.test_protocol: Freeze basket_size=3 and z_thresh=1.0 before looking. Replay the full archived sample side by side with baseline. Evaluate after-cost net P&L per session, PF, max DD, stop/target/flat counts, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive (Jul-Sep and Oct) and at least about 20 filtered trades total, with at least about 8 in each half; if the filtered version cannot clear that, reject as underpowered. Do not sweep thresholds. If it passes, paper trade unchanged for the next 20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible from the data we already have, cheap to replay, and it is a real selection overlay rather than a whole new strategy. The main risk is that it just cuts trades and overfits the archive, which the frozen replay/holdout protocol should reveal quickly.

name: Time-based trade management
one_line: Use minimum-hold and no-progress time exits to avoid instant stop-outs and stale trades.
parameter_choices: Require 1-3 bars before the stop is active, and exit after 2-4 bars if price has not moved meaningfully in the breakout direction.
disagreement: A little patience can reduce noise, but too much can turn a failed breakout into a larger loss.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: B1-c022-04 explicitly supports the general idea of a minimum holding duration and separate entry/exit thresholds to reduce noise-driven churn. B1-c006-07 gives the broad momentum-then-mean-reversion rationale for cutting stale trades. Neither source states this exact ORB rule with specific bar counts, so this is an adaptation, not a direct citation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current OR breakout entry. After a fill, do not allow the original OR stop to trigger until 1 full 5-minute bar has completed. If, by the close of the 3rd full 5-minute bar after entry, the trade has not closed beyond the entry price in the breakout direction, flatten at the next bar open. No other changes.
review.mechanism: This could help only if a meaningful share of the bot's bad trades are early noise followed by drift back into the range. The time stop may turn some long, dead holds into earlier scratches and reduce the number of trades that sit around until the close. But the minimum-hold also makes immediate fakeouts more expensive, so it is more likely to improve the stale/flat bucket than the true fast-fail bucket.
review.data_missing: None for a first-pass replay. Five-minute OHLCV is enough to simulate the delayed stop and the 3-bar time exit. Tick data would only be needed if we wanted exact intra-bar sequencing, which we do not have.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule. The closest prior test was requiring two consecutive closes beyond the range before entry, which is a related 'wait longer' idea but changes entry timing rather than post-entry management. The morning-fade overlay is also different. Still, the prior result is a caution that more waiting can easily hurt this setup.
review.overfit_note: Only two discrete knobs, but intraday exit timing is very sample-sensitive. If we sweep 1/2/3/4 bars on the same 67 sessions and pick the best, that will be overfit. Fix the parameters before looking and require both halves of the archive to improve.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer stale holds and some earlier scratches, with a modest reduction in end-of-day flat exits. Worst case: bigger losses on immediate reversals and fewer of the rare breakout runners surviving long enough to pay for the losers. Net effect is likely small and uncertain.
review.test_protocol: Fix the rule at 1-bar minimum hold and a 3-bar no-progress time exit before looking at results. Replay the full 67 archived sessions side by side with the frozen baseline using the same fills and cost model. Primary metric: net P&L per session after costs. Secondary guards: max drawdown, loser-size distribution, and whether the rare target hits disappear. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just overall. If it passes the archive check, forward-test unchanged on the next ~20 unseen sessions before considering adoption.
review.verdict_reason: This is feasible with the data we already have, cheap to replay, and it targets a real weakness of the bot without becoming a new strategy. The effect may be small or negative, but that is exactly why it should be tested on the archive now rather than guessed.

name: Late-stage trend exhaustion filter
one_line: Avoid breakouts in names that already look extended.
parameter_choices: Measure days since the last 20-day high, or the run-up over the last 5/10/20 days, and skip the most extended names.
disagreement: Some trends persist, but late-stage breakouts can be exhaustion traps.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source says momentum can persist for about a year and then reverse, which is loosely related to the idea of avoiding very extended names. But it does not directly justify a 5/10/20-day exhaustion screen or an ORB-specific entry filter, so this is our adaptation rather than a stated rule.
review.exact_rule_change: After the existing 10:00 in-play selection, add one pre-entry filter: compute each candidate’s 20-session close-to-close return using daily closes. Skip long ORB entries if that return is > +15%; skip short ORB entries if that return is < -15%. Leave all other ORB rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could reduce failed breakouts in names that are already stretched and more likely to snap back, so the likely benefit is fewer stopouts and fewer late-day drifts back inside the range. The downside is that it may also remove some of the strongest continuation names, so trade count and the rare target hits may fall.
review.data_missing: No additional data beyond the daily closes we already have.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact filter, but it is in the same family as the already-rejected universe-pruning ideas (top-5 only, price caps). The starvation risk is similar, even if the metric is different.
review.overfit_note: One threshold looks simple, but the best cutoff is likely unstable on only 67 sessions and 53 trades. It would be easy to fit recent losers and accidentally exclude the few strong breakout winners.
review.expected_effect: If it helps, the gain will probably come from a modest drop in stopouts and flat-to-fail trades, not from more targets. I would expect a smaller trade count and an uncertain net effect on P&L after costs.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the +15% cutoff before looking at results. Replay the filter side-by-side against the current baseline on all 67 archived sessions. Judge it on net P&L after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, stop rate, and trade count. Require at least about 35 archived trades after filtering, and no more than a 20% drop in trade count. Only keep it if both halves of the archive improve or at least do not degrade, then confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions without retuning.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our data and cheap to replay, but the source only gives broad momentum-persistence evidence, not direct support for this intraday exhaustion screen. With our small sample, the cutoff is easy to overfit, and it could just as easily kill the few strong continuation winners as remove bad breakouts.

name: Cost-aware in-play ranking
one_line: Prefer names with better historical execution cost when choosing among otherwise similar candidates.
parameter_choices: Rank the top candidates by estimated slippage/fee burden, or drop the worst 20-30% cost names from the final list.
disagreement: A name can have good gross edge but still be poor net edge after costs.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general principle that cheaper names/cost awareness matter and that trading less can improve results, but none of them prescribe ranking an ORB watchlist by historical execution cost or dropping the worst cost names. That specific implementation is our extrapolation from their liquidity/cost heuristics.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00, keep the existing in-play filter and top-8 by relative volume, then rank those 8 by a 20-session average liquidity/cost proxy using only our 5-minute bars: average session dollar volume. Exclude the worst 2 names (25%) and only allow entries from the remaining 6. Not a new strategy; just a pre-trade ranking filter.
review.mechanism: Should lower slippage/impact and commissions by avoiding the weakest-liquidity names, which could improve net expectancy and slightly reduce ugly fills. The trade-off is that we may throw away some of the most volatile names, so any gain is likely small and comes mostly from lower costs, not better breakout quality.
review.data_missing: We can compute a rough liquidity proxy from the 5-minute bars, but not true historical execution cost. Missing: symbol-level fill/slippage logs or bid-ask spreads/L2 to measure actual cost dispersion.
review.already_tried_note: We already tried narrower selection (top-5 only) and price caps, which starved the universe or cherry-picked it. This is not the same rule, but it is the same family of 'trade fewer names' filters, so the failure mode may repeat.
review.overfit_note: Only 8 names are in the final pool and we have 53 trades total. A cost-ranking rule adds tuning choices and will mostly fit noise unless the cost spread across symbols is huge, which is unlikely in this already-liquid universe.
review.expected_effect: Maybe a small reduction in average cost per trade and a slightly better net PnL/day, but probably fewer trades and possibly fewer of the biggest breakout winners. I would expect the effect size to be modest at best.
review.test_protocol: Replay baseline vs this filter on all 67 archived sessions with the rule frozen before looking. Compare net PnL/session, average cost/trade, max drawdown, and trade count; require improvement in both chronological halves, not just overall. If the archive gain is smaller than the daily noise or trade count drops by more than 20%, do not spend unseen days on it.
review.verdict_reason: Without real spread/fill data, this is only a liquidity proxy; in our already-liquid 55-name universe the incremental cost spread is probably too small to matter, while the pruning can easily remove the volatile names that generate the few full targets. Given the tiny sample and the prior failure of narrower selection rules, this is not a good use of scarce live days.

name: Volume-growth acceleration filter
one_line: Prefer breakouts when volume is accelerating, not just already high.
parameter_choices: Use raw day-over-day volume growth if shares outstanding are unavailable; if available, use share-adjusted growth and bucket it into low/medium/high bins.
disagreement: Volume acceleration may distinguish real participation from a one-off noisy burst.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports volume-growth binning and asymmetric cutoffs, but it is not direct evidence for an ORB breakout filter on our bot. The share-adjusted version is also not available to us, so we have to adapt it to raw day-over-day 30-minute volume growth.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current in-play screen and ORB logic unchanged, but add one pre-entry filter: compute raw 9:30–10:00 volume growth versus yesterday’s same window, bucket it as low (<15%), medium (15% to 50%), or high (>50%), and only allow a breakout entry if the name is in the high bucket (>50%).
review.mechanism: This tries to separate true participation from a one-day volume burst. If volume is still accelerating versus the prior session, breakouts may be more likely to keep going instead of snapping back into the stop. That should reduce failed-break stops and may lift target hits, though it will probably reduce trade count and lower fees only a bit.
review.data_missing: Shares outstanding are unavailable, so we cannot do the share-adjusted version; use raw day-over-day 30-minute volume growth instead.
review.already_tried_note: We already require high same-day relative volume to get into the in-play list, but we have not tested a separate acceleration filter versus yesterday’s same 9:30–10:00 volume.
review.overfit_note: Only one real decision threshold, but it is close to the existing relative-volume screen and could be tuned to the 67-day archive. Freeze the 15%/50% bins before looking at results and do not re-optimize them.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer marginal trades, fewer fake breakouts, and a somewhat higher target-hit rate if the effect exists. Costs should fall slightly from fewer trades, but the main gain would have to come from better entry quality.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule ex ante. Replay baseline vs filter on all 67 archived sessions with identical fills/costs. Primary metric: after-cost PnL per session and profit factor; secondary: stop rate, target-hit rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive (first 34 vs last 33 sessions) and at least about 25 trades total; if the filter starves the sample below that, reject it. If it survives the archive test, paper it on the next ~20 unseen sessions side by side with baseline.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our existing OHLCV data, cheap to replay, and it targets a real failure mode. The main risk is redundancy with the current relative-volume screen, so the archive replay will quickly show whether it adds anything or just cuts trade count.

name: High-participation / high-volatility name filter
one_line: Bias toward the more energetic names and away from quiet tape when testing ORB.
parameter_choices: Require realized volatility above the median or 60th percentile and relative volume above 1.5x to 2x; compare the play batch versus mega caps.
disagreement: One view says ORB needs active, volatile names; the opposite view says quieter names break out more cleanly.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book excerpts support the general premise that high-volatility / high-attention names are where predictive effects tend to be stronger, and that volume and volatility are linked. They do not specifically say an ORB should be filtered by realized volatility, nor do they justify the exact median/60th-percentile cutoff. That part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00 New York, after the existing 1.5x 9:30–10:00 relative-volume screen, compute each candidate’s 9:30–10:00 realized volatility as the standard deviation of 5-minute log returns. Keep only candidates whose realized volatility is at or above the median realized volatility of today’s qualifying names, then apply the existing top-8-by-relative-volume selection and original ORB entry rules. If fewer than 2 names remain, stand down.
review.mechanism: This is meant to remove the 'busy but dead' mornings: names that trade a lot but do not expand enough to reach 2.5R. If the bot’s losses are coming from failed breakouts and end-of-day drifts, a higher-volatility filter could raise the share of days where the first breakout actually travels, increasing target hits and reducing flat-at-close exits. The tradeoff is fewer trades and a possible loss of some quieter, cleaner breakouts.
review.data_missing: none for this version; 5-minute regular-session OHLCV is enough to compute realized volatility and relative volume at 10:00.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact filter. The bot already biases toward active names via the relative-volume screen and the play-batch universe, and top-5/price-cap experiments were rejected, but no explicit realized-volatility filter has been tested.
review.overfit_note: Only one new threshold, but it is easy to snoop if we start comparing median vs 60th vs 70th percentile and if we slice by play-batch vs mega-cap. With only 67 archived sessions, the danger is not the idea itself but tuning it after the fact.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer low-velocity breakouts, fewer stop/flat losers, slightly higher target rate, and a better chance of surviving costs. Worst case: it just cuts trade count and throws away some good quieter breakouts without improving expectancy.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the filter exactly as median realized volatility and do not optimize it. Replay all archived sessions side-by-side against baseline. Primary metric: paired net P&L per session after costs; secondary metrics: target-hit rate, flat-at-close rate, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in both chronological halves of the archive, not just in aggregate, and do not keep it if total replay trades fall below about 30. If it passes the archive, paper trade the next 20 unseen sessions and require the same direction of effect before promoting.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with the data we already have, cheap to replay, and it targets a real weakness of the current bot: too many breakouts that move enough to trigger, but not enough to pay. The edge is not proven and could easily be small or negative, but it is a reasonable one-change test rather than a waste of time.

name: News-day continuation filter
one_line: Treat news days as a positive momentum regime rather than only a blackout regime.
parameter_choices: Use a manual or feed-based news flag, then compare high-volume news days against other days; optionally require the news-day return to align with the ORB direction.
disagreement: News can create gap risk and noise, but it can also create continuation and follow-through.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The cited book excerpt supports the general claim that news days—especially high-volume news days—can have positive post-news continuation. It does not propose an ORB filter, so applying it to our intraday breakout bot is an extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a binary pre-open catalyst flag: only allow the existing ORB trade if the symbol has a same-day stock-specific news/catalyst item before 10:00 ET (earnings, guidance, M&A, FDA, analyst action); otherwise skip that symbol for the day. Keep all other ORB rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: If true catalyst days trend more than non-news chop, this should raise target hits and reduce the August-style failed-breakout stops by keeping us out of low-information days. It may also improve the fraction of trades that finish as winners instead of 15:45 flats. The tradeoff is fewer trades and potentially worse slippage on headline days, which our fixed cost model may understate.
review.data_missing: We cannot identify news days from the current archive. Missing inputs: a pre-10:00 ET news/headline or earnings calendar tag per symbol. OHLCV alone can proxy 'high volume' but not 'news.'
review.already_tried_note: Not as an explicit filter, but the current 'stocks in play' + relative-volume universe already captures many event-driven names, so the incremental effect may be small and the trade-count loss real.
review.overfit_note: One binary label looks simple, but the label itself is easy to define post hoc and the true event sample will be tiny. With 67 sessions, it is easy to fit a few memorable winners and call it 'news edge.'
review.expected_effect: Best case: higher profit factor from more full-target days and fewer dead-on-arrival breakouts on true catalyst days. More likely: modestly better target rate but too few trades to move equity much, because the current rel-volume screen already catches many newsy names.
review.test_protocol: Do not test until news tags are frozen ex ante. Build a binary catalyst label for each symbol/session from a fixed external news/earnings calendar or headline feed, then replay the full 67-day archive side by side with baseline. Compare net PnL/day, PF, win rate, average R/trade, target-hit rate, stop rate, and trade count on tagged vs untagged days. Require the filter to improve both halves of the archive, not just the full sample. Minimum bar: at least 15 tagged trades in the archive and no collapse in trade count; otherwise treat it as noise. If it survives the archive, confirm on the next 20 unseen trading days or until 10 tagged trades occur.
review.verdict_reason: Useful only if we add a real pre-open news/catalyst feed. With the current archive we cannot label news days, and the existing rel-volume 'stocks in play' screen already overlaps heavily with news-driven names, so this is not worth spending a live test slot on yet.

name: Liquidity-tier-specific ORB rules
one_line: Give thin names and mega caps different opening-range rules instead of using one universal gate.
parameter_choices: Split the universe into mega caps and the $20-$80 play batch, then use a longer opening range or a higher dollar-volume gate for the thinner tier.
disagreement: A single rule may be too loose for thin names and too strict for liquid ones.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The books support the general premise that liquidity matters: low-liquidity names are more slippage-prone, and less-liquid stocks behave differently at the open. But neither source actually recommends a tier-specific 45-minute ORB rule. The specific split between mega caps and the play batch is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current 9:30-10:00 ORB for the mega-cap tier. For the $20-$80 play batch only, change the opening range to 9:30-10:15 and forbid entries before 10:15; all other rules (SPY confirmation, stop, target, sizing, flat time) stay unchanged.
review.mechanism: Thin names are where opening noise and false breakouts are most likely. Giving them an extra 15 minutes should let the first impulse settle before we commit, which could cut stop-outs and bad days in that tier. The trade-off is fewer and later entries, so the main expected gain is quality, not frequency.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: We already have a rough liquidity split in the universe (mega caps vs the play batch), and we have tried narrower universe filters, but not a tier-specific OR window like this.
review.overfit_note: This is only one knob, but it only affects a subset of trades and it is easy to fit to the last 67 sessions. A 45-minute OR could look good simply because a recent losing cluster happened before 10:15. Lock it ex ante and demand it work in both halves of the archive.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer play-batch trades, fewer failed-breakout stops, and a slightly better win rate in thin names. It may also miss some early runners and reduce overall opportunity, so the net effect could be small unless thin-name noise is the real problem.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the 45-minute play-batch OR before looking at results. Replay baseline vs variant on all 67 archived sessions. Primary metric: cost-adjusted net PnL per session; secondary: max drawdown, stop rate, and total trade count. Only judge the idea if the archive produces at least 15 play-batch trades; otherwise wait for more data. Pass only if the variant improves net PnL and drawdown in both halves of the archive and does not cut trade count below 75% of baseline without a clear expectancy gain. If it passes, paper-trade the next 20 unseen sessions with no retuning.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully computable from the data we already have, and it targets a real weakness in the bot: thin-name failed breakouts. The source support is only partial, so this should be an archive-first test, not a live bet, but it is plausible enough to spend one replay on.

name: High-confidence channel/triangle structure filter
one_line: Only use channel/triangle context when the fit is strong, well-populated, and geometrically clean.
parameter_choices: Use a larger fractal pivot window (e.g. 5 or 7 instead of 3); require at least 3 pivots per side or ~5 extrema in the window; accept only when channel fit R² is high (e.g. >0.9); test backcandles of 20/40/60; use a tight slope threshold for triangles (e.g. 0.01).
disagreement: Stricter geometry should reduce false positives, but it may also cut trade count sharply; open question is whether channels and triangles should be one shared filter or separate filters.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The source directly supports the detector ingredients: larger fractal windows, minimum pivot/extrema counts, high R², and trying 20/40/60-bar lookbacks for channels/triangles. It does not show that using those structures as an ORB gate improves P&L, so the trading application is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add one shared pre-entry geometry filter to Midas: only take the first ORB trigger of the day if the prior 20 regular-session 5-minute bars classify as a clean channel/triangle under a strict fractal detector (pivot window = 5, at least 3 pivot highs and 3 pivot lows, and fitted channel/triangle R² > 0.90). If the detector fails, skip trading that day. Do not sweep 20/40/60 or split into separate channel-vs-triangle rules in the same test.
review.mechanism: This is meant to keep us out of messy open-driven chop and only trade breakouts when the tape is already orderly and compressed. If it works, the main win should be fewer failed-breakout stops and fewer bad days, with a possible lift in win rate. The obvious cost is fewer trades and a real chance of missing some good early breakouts.
review.data_missing: None for the proposed rule; 5-minute regular-session OHLCV is enough. Caveat: the filter cannot be evaluated until enough bars have accumulated, so it will naturally exclude the earliest morning opportunities.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is a new pre-entry geometry filter, not the consecutive-close rule, the SPY overlay, or the morning-fade idea.
review.overfit_note: This hides a lot of degrees of freedom: lookback, fractal window, min pivots/extrema, R² cutoff, slope threshold, and whether channel/triangle are pooled or separate. With only 67 sessions, it is easy to tune a detector that looks good in-sample and then dies.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer chop-day stop-outs and fewer August-style failed breakouts. More likely: materially fewer trades, with only a modest improvement in win rate if any. After costs, this may end up flat unless the filter is very selective and robust.
review.test_protocol: Freeze one variant before looking: shared clean-geometry gate on the last 20 bars, pivot window 5, R² > 0.90, and the 3-pivot-per-side minimum. Replay all 67 archived sessions side by side with the current baseline. Compare after-cost net P&L/day, expectancy per trade, profit factor, max drawdown, stop rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, and at least about 25 trades total; if the filter only wins by shrinking activity to a trickle, kill it. If it survives the archive, paper trade the next ~20 unseen sessions without retuning.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible from the data we already have and cheap to replay. The source only supports the detector logic, not the trading edge, so this is high-overfit and must be frozen to one variant; but it is still worth a controlled archive replay because it could plausibly cut the failed-breakout problem without extra data.

name: Minimum reward-to-risk gate
one_line: Skip ORB entries whose target-to-stop geometry is too poor after fees and slippage.
parameter_choices: Set a minimum pre-entry reward-to-risk ratio, starting at 1.5R and testing 1.5R to 2.0R; compute it after gap rules and opening-range distance are known.
disagreement: Whether to enforce the raw geometric R or a more conservative post-cost R is the main choice.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The book quote is a generic trade-selection heuristic: if the take-profit / stop-loss ratio is below 1.5, reconsider the trade. That supports the *idea of screening on R:R*, but it does not specifically support an ORB-specific post-cost filter, and it does not address the fact that Midas already uses a fixed 2.5R target.
review.exact_rule_change: After the 10:00 entry signal is known, compute the projected net reward-to-risk using the actual entry price, the OR stop, the fixed 2.5R target, and the assumed round-trip costs (0.05% commission + $0.02/share slippage each side). Take the trade only if projected net RR >= 1.5R. Default parameter: min_net_rr = 1.5.
review.mechanism: This would only remove the worst economics: very tight-stop / low-dollar-risk setups where commission and slippage eat too much of the expected gain. It does not improve breakout quality or target selection; at best it trims a few high-cost trades and slightly lowers cost drag.
review.data_missing: None for the rule as stated. 5-minute OHLCV plus the existing cost model is enough to approximate entry, stop, target, and post-cost RR. True bid/ask spread data would be nicer, but it is not required for this test.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list, and not a duplicate of the two-close filter or the morning fade. It is a new screen, though very close to a generic 'skip bad geometry' rule.
review.overfit_note: Only one threshold, so not a giant knob farm. But the proposed 1.5-2.0 sweep is still easy to tune to 67 sessions, and any apparent lift is likely to come from a handful of trades. The bigger issue is not overfit, it's that the filter is probably almost inert.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small reduction in trade count and a small drop in cost drag, if any. Unlikely to change the failed-breakout rate or the many flat exits. If it helps, it will be by excluding the tightest, most cost-sensitive entries.
review.test_protocol: Freeze min_net_rr at 1.5 before looking. Replay all 67 archived sessions side by side with baseline. Compare net PnL after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, trade count, and the fraction of candidate trades filtered. Advance only if it improves net PnL and drawdown in both halves of the archive and removes a meaningful share of trades; if it filters only a few trades, treat it as a no-op and stop. If the archive result is genuinely better, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: As framed, this is mostly redundant. Midas already fixes the target at 2.5R, so a raw reward-to-risk gate is effectively constant; the only meaningful version is a post-cost proxy that mainly screens out a few tight-stop, cash-cap trades. That does not address the actual failure mode here (failed breakouts / fade-back days), and the expected effect is too small to justify burning live sample on it.

name: Macro surprise alignment on event days
one_line: On scheduled macro release days, only trade if the surprise direction supports the breakout direction.
parameter_choices: Use a manually maintained macro calendar; trade only if the release surprise is directionally aligned with the ORB (positive surprise for longs, negative surprise for shorts); optionally require a minimum surprise magnitude.
disagreement: Open question is whether to blackout all major event days or allow only directionally aligned trades.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general premise that macro-surprise sign and size move prices, but it does not specifically justify a 10:00 ET ORB filter, nor the choice between blackout vs aligned-only. The step from "economic surprise moves markets" to "gate our breakout entries by surprise direction" is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: On any day with a pre-10:00 ET U.S. high-impact macro release from a fixed pre-registered list (CPI, PPI, NFP, GDP, retail sales, ISM, weekly initial claims), keep the existing ORB rules unchanged except: if the release surprise is positive (actual > consensus), allow only longs; if negative (actual < consensus), allow only shorts. If there is no qualifying release, trade as usual. Do not add a surprise-magnitude threshold.
review.mechanism: Macro prints can set the day’s broad risk tone before our 10:00 entry window. Filtering to surprise-aligned direction should cut the worst failed-breakout days, especially the stop-out/reversal cases, and may also improve follow-through on aligned days. It is a day-level quality filter, so it should not raise costs much, but it will reduce trade count on event days.
review.data_missing: We do not have the macro-release calendar or the actual-vs-consensus values needed to compute surprise sign. The current archive only has 5-minute OHLCV and daily closes.
review.already_tried_note: This specific macro-surprise filter is not on the rejected list. We have not previously tested a scheduled-event-day gate.
review.overfit_note: The event list itself is a tuning knob, and the true sample of qualifying release days in 67 sessions is small. It would be easy to cherry-pick which releases count or to infer a threshold from a handful of outlier days.
review.expected_effect: If it works, expect fewer stopouts and fewer bad days on macro mornings, with a modest lift in win rate and expectancy on those days. Trade count will drop on release days, so the main gain should be better quality rather than more activity.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the event list before looking at results. Manually add the pre-10:00 ET release calendar and consensus/actual surprise signs for all archived days, then replay baseline vs filtered ORB side by side on the 67 sessions. Judge on net P&L after costs, profit factor, stop rate, and expectancy specifically on qualifying event days; require the effect to appear in both halves of the archive. Do not add a surprise-magnitude threshold unless it was pre-specified. If fewer than about 12 qualifying archived event days exist, treat the result as inconclusive and wait for more data. If it passes archive testing, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions, counting only qualifying macro days.
review.verdict_reason: The idea is plausible, but it cannot be evaluated from the current data archive because the necessary macro calendar and consensus/actual surprise data are missing. The qualifying-day sample will also be sparse, so it should only be tested after the event list is frozen and the external data are added.

name: Session-specific confirmation strength
one_line: Tighten market-confirmation rules in the intraday session where Midas historically lags.
parameter_choices: Split the day into morning, midday, and afternoon buckets; require stronger SPY confirmation in the weaker bucket; test different thresholds by session.
disagreement: Need to learn which session is actually weaker, and whether SPY, QQQ, or both should provide the confirmation.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general premise that lead-lag relationships can change by session, but it does not specifically argue for tightening SPY confirmation, choosing a weaker intraday bucket, or using a 0.10% threshold. The SPY-only version is our adaptation; the SPY/QQQ/both choice is not supported by the cited text and we do not have QQQ data anyway.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current ORB entry rules unchanged, but add one pre-registered midday gate: if the signal bar is between 11:00 and 14:00 New York time, only allow a long when SPY’s return from the 9:30 open to that bar is at least +0.10%, and only allow a short when SPY’s return is at most -0.10%. Outside 11:00-14:00, keep the existing SPY confirmation rule exactly as-is. Do not add QQQ or a multi-index confirmation test in this run.
review.mechanism: Midday is usually the weakest, choppiest part of the day. Requiring the broad market to already be moving decisively in the trade direction should filter out some low-energy fake breakouts, which could reduce stop-outs and some late-day drifts to flat. The downside is fewer entries and possibly missing stock-specific breakouts that do not need broad-market help.
review.data_missing: The SPY-only version is computable from our 5-minute regular-session bars. We cannot test the QQQ-or-both branch because QQQ data is not in the archive.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. Existing SPY/QQQ timing overlays were different ideas and do not cover this session-specific SPY confirmation filter.
review.overfit_note: This can turn into a session-by-session, threshold-by-threshold search on only 67 sessions / 53 trades, which is fragile. Only a single pre-registered bucket and threshold should be tested; no grid search.
review.expected_effect: If it helps, expect fewer midday trades, a lower stop-out rate, and a modest lift in win rate/PF. Net PnL improvement is likely small unless midday is truly the main source of failed breakouts. It may also reduce total opportunity too much for a 1k book.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one fixed variant: midday only (11:00-14:00) with a 0.10% SPY confirmation threshold. Replay all 67 archived sessions side by side with baseline using identical fills/costs. Compare after-cost net PnL per session, profit factor, win rate, stop rate, flat-exit rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive (Jul-Aug and Sep-Oct), and treat results as inconclusive if the modified rule produces fewer than ~15 trades on the archive or cuts trade count by more than ~30%. If it passes the archive check, run the same fixed rule on the next ~20 unseen sessions; reject if the live-like holdout does not also improve after costs.
review.verdict_reason: The source only gives weak/partial support, but the SPY-only midday filter is fully testable with our existing bars and costs. It is narrow enough to pre-register, cheap to replay, and targets a real failure mode (midday fake breakouts). The broader bucket/benchmark search would be overfit, but this one fixed hypothesis is worth a replay now.

name: Sector-strength overlay for longs
one_line: Favor long breakouts in sectors that are already outperforming the broad market.
parameter_choices: Measure sector relative strength versus SPY over a short and medium lookback (for example 5 and 20 days); allow longs only when sector strength is positive or above a set threshold.
disagreement: Unclear whether the edge comes from a short lookback, a slower lookback, or only applying the filter to longs.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: Burns makes the broad claim that stocks in sectors already trending up are preferable. That supports the general direction of the idea, but not the specific implementation: relative strength vs SPY, the 5-day/20-day lookbacks, or a longs-only breakout filter are our own extrapolations.
review.exact_rule_change: For long ORB signals only, add a sector-momentum filter: using a fixed stock-to-sector ETF map (e.g. XLK/XLF/XLE/etc.), compute the sector ETF's close-to-close return minus SPY's return over the last 5 trading days and the last 20 trading days; take the long only if both values are > 0.0%. Shorts stay unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is meant to screen out long breakouts in weak sectors, where failed breakouts and same-day reversals are more common. If it works, it should raise the long-side win/target rate, reduce stopouts and dead-flat closes, and slightly improve the quality of the few runners that drive most of the P&L. It will not directly fix shorts or execution costs, and it may reduce trade count.
review.data_missing: We need a frozen stock->sector mapping for the 55-name universe and daily closes for the sector ETF proxies. No pre-market, news, float, or L2 is required, but sector labels are not in the current feed.
review.already_tried_note: None of the rejected overlays were a sector-strength filter on long breakouts. The prior tests were different: SPY/QQQ timing, top-5/price-cap universe cuts, two-close confirmation, and morning fade.
review.overfit_note: There are hidden choices in sector classification, proxy choice, lookback length, and threshold. With only 67 sessions and a small long sample, it would be easy to fit a regime that does not repeat.
review.expected_effect: If anything, this should modestly improve long-side expectancy and target rate, while cutting some long stopouts and flat, low-quality entries. The likely downside is fewer longs and potentially lower total trade count; the effect on the full strategy may be small unless the current losers are concentrated in weak sectors.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the stock->sector map and the rule before looking at results. Replay the full 67-day archive side-by-side with the baseline. Primary metric: net P&L after costs per session and expectancy per long trade. Secondary metrics: long win rate, target rate, stop rate, trade count, and max drawdown. Require improvement in both halves of the archived sample, not just the total. Reject if long trade count falls by more than 30% or if max drawdown does not improve. If it passes, forward-test on the next 20 unseen sessions, or until it produces at least 8 long trades, with no parameter changes.
review.verdict_reason: The idea is plausible, but it is only loosely supported by the source, needs a frozen sector map that is not in the current feed, and has high overfit risk on a tiny sample. It is worth a replay only after the sector labels/proxies are added; I would not make it a live test right now.

name: Prior-day selloff blocker for longs
one_line: Do not take long breakouts after a sharp prior-day selloff.
parameter_choices: Block longs when the prior day close-to-close return is below a threshold such as -3% or -5%; optionally relax the rule for especially volatile names.
disagreement: Question is whether this should be a hard block or just a size reduction after large down days.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The book’s rule-of-thumb is directly in the same direction: avoid buying after significant drops and prefer upward trends. But it does not specify a numeric threshold, and it is not specifically about opening-range breakout longs, so the exact filter and threshold are our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a hard long-only filter: if a candidate stock’s prior session close-to-close return is <= -5.0%, skip all long ORB entries in that stock for the next session. Do not change short entries or any other rule.
review.mechanism: This should mainly cut failed long breakouts and immediate stop-outs in names that are still under distribution after a bad day. On this bot, the likely benefit is fewer long-side losers and slightly fewer low-quality flats; it may also trim costs a bit by reducing trades. The main risk is that it will also block some strong rebound days that would have worked.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the reject list. It is different from the failed-breakout fade test, and different from the existing overnight gap filter.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob if we fix the threshold up front, but with 67 days it would be easy to over-tune the cutoff if we started searching -3% vs -5% vs other values. The interaction with the existing ORB filter also means the sample of long trades may get small fast.
review.expected_effect: Modest chance of improving long-side selectivity by avoiding weak trend days. Best-case: fewer long stop-outs and a slightly better PF; worst-case: fewer trades and missed rebound winners with little net gain.
review.test_protocol: Fix the threshold before looking at results; I would use -5.0% as the default. Replay the full archived history side by side against the frozen baseline, keeping every other rule identical. Compare: after-cost net PnL, profit factor, max drawdown, long-trade stop rate, and average expectancy per long trade. Require the improvement to show up in both halves of the archived sample (or rolling windows) so we are not just fitting one bad patch. If the archive looks better, forward-test unchanged on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully testable with the data we already have, and plausibly targets one of the bot’s known failure modes (bad long breakouts after weak prior days). The source is weak, but the cost of testing is low and the rule is simple enough to evaluate without over-committing.

name: Indicator-stack hygiene
one_line: If indicators are added, cap them at one per role so the filter stack stays non-redundant.
parameter_choices: Use at most one momentum indicator, one trend indicator, and one volatility indicator; avoid stacking near-duplicates.
disagreement: The main debate is which indicator family deserves each role for Midas.
books: Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: The quoted source directly recommends using one indicator from each group to avoid redundant signals. That is essentially the same hygiene rule, just generalized into a broader research constraint. It is still opinion, not performance evidence.
review.exact_rule_change: No live trading-rule change to Midas today; this is only a research constraint. If we add indicator filters later, cap the stack at at most 3 indicators total: one momentum, one trend, and one volatility indicator, and never include two indicators from the same role in the same entry filter.
review.mechanism: This could only help by preventing us from building a bloated, redundant indicator stack that looks more convincing than it is. In theory that reduces overfitting and keeps the decision rule cleaner. It does not directly attack Midas's real problems: failed breakouts, flat exits, and costs. On the current bot it is effectively a no-op.
review.data_missing: We can compute common indicators from the 5-minute OHLCV we already have, but the idea does not specify which momentum, trend, or volatility indicators to use, so there is no concrete signal to test yet.
review.already_tried_note: Nothing in the rejected list is an indicator-stack experiment, and the live bot currently does not use a multi-indicator filter stack.
review.overfit_note: The rule is too generic to validate directly, and any actual test would first require choosing indicator families and lookbacks, which adds many degrees of freedom on only 67 sessions of history.
review.expected_effect: Near zero on the current bot. At best it prevents future redundant indicator experiments from fooling us; it is unlikely to improve breakout quality, hit rate, or costs by itself.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend live/unseen days on this as-is. If we want to study the principle, first freeze a specific indicator stack, then compare a one-per-role version against a deliberately redundant version on all archived days only, with costs included. Require improvement in net expectancy in both halves of the archive and no material trade-count collapse before considering any 20-day unseen confirmation.
review.verdict_reason: This is a research hygiene rule, not an alpha source. Midas currently has no indicator stack to simplify, and the idea is too generic to turn into a specific, precommitted trade rule without first inventing a new indicator-based strategy. That would be a separate model-selection project with high overfit risk and no clear path to helping the current ORB bot.

name: Immediate trailing stop from entry
one_line: Replace the opening-range stop with a trailing stop that starts immediately and only ratchets in the trade's favor.
parameter_choices: Trail can be a fixed percent or dollar amount; book examples include 2% of the last close, 3% from the previous close, or a $0.15 trail. Only ratchet upward for longs and downward for shorts.
disagreement: The sources agree on the mechanism, but one worked example with a 2% trail reported much worse win rate and drawdown than a static stop/target setup, so the trail may be too tight.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books support trailing stops in general, and one source gives a concrete 2% trailing-stop example with stats. But none of the sources explicitly support an immediate-from-entry trailing stop on an opening-range breakout system, and the only quantified example in the set is negative.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current opening-range stop with an immediate 2% trailing stop from entry: for a long, initial stop = entry price x 0.98; after each completed 5-minute bar, ratchet the stop up to max(previous stop, highest 5-minute close since entry x 0.98). For a short, initial stop = entry price x 1.02; after each completed 5-minute bar, ratchet down to min(previous stop, lowest 5-minute close since entry x 1.02). Keep the existing 15:45 flat.
review.mechanism: This would mostly tighten exits, not fix entries. Best case, it cuts a few ugly round-trips and keeps some trend-day winners from giving back too much. More likely on 5-minute ORB, it gets clipped by normal noise before the move develops, turning a marginal system into more small losses/scratches and fewer 2.5R winners. It does not reduce costs; it mainly changes the distribution of exits.
review.data_missing: No tick/quote or intrabar sequence data, so trailing-stop fills have to be approximated from 5-minute OHLC bars. Exact intra-bar stop/ratchet ordering is not observable.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is related to the existing fixed-stop recipe, but a true immediate trailing stop has not been tested yet.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob (trail distance), but the result is very sensitive to that knob and easy to cherry-pick on 67 days. If we scan multiple trail distances, overfit risk jumps fast.
review.expected_effect: Likely neutral to worse. It may reduce a few full givebacks, but on this bot it is more likely to raise stop-outs, lower win rate, and cut the already-scarce full targets. The 2% trailing-stop example in the source set already showed materially worse win rate and drawdown than a static stop/target setup.
review.test_protocol: Only if we insist on checking it: replay the exact rule with the 2% default on all 67 archived days side by side with the frozen baseline, using the same entries and conservative bar-based stop fills. Primary metric: after-cost net P&L per day and max drawdown. Secondary: win rate, profit factor, and share of trades exiting before 15:45. Require improvement in both halves of the archived sample, not just the full sample, and no meaningful drop in trade count. Then confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions before considering it real.
review.verdict_reason: This is just a tighter stop with a trailing wrapper. The only quantified source example in the set shows worse win rate and drawdown, and on our 5-minute ORB the most likely effect is getting chopped out by ordinary noise before trend days develop. That is not the problem this bot is trying to solve, and with our tiny edge and high per-trade costs, the expected value looks poor. If we ever test trailing exits, the better candidate is a trail that starts only after the trade is already profitable, not immediate-from-entry.

name: Delay trailing until the trade is up
one_line: Keep the OR stop at first, then switch to a trailing exit once the breakout is already in profit.
parameter_choices: Activate the trail at 1R or 1.5R; trail behind recent 5-minute swing structure or by a fixed percent/dollar amount.
disagreement: No direct quantitative conflict in the excerpts; this is simply the less aggressive trailing variant.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books broadly support trailing stops and the idea of letting winners run, but they do not directly prove the specific Midas rule 'wait until +1R, then trail.' This is a reasonable adaptation of generic advice, not a directly sourced tested rule.
review.exact_rule_change: For every current ORB trade, keep the original opening-range stop until the position first reaches +1.0R unrealized. At that point, cancel the fixed 2.5R profit target and switch to a trailing stop based on the last completed 5-minute bar: long = stop trails up to that bar’s low only; short = stop trails down to that bar’s high only. Keep the existing 15:45 flat rule unchanged.
review.mechanism: This only changes winner management. It could preserve the rare breakout that actually trends, reduce giveback on moves that would otherwise be flattened at 15:45, and convert some of the current flat exits into positive exits. It does not fix failed breakouts at entry; it mainly tries to improve the payoff tail on the trades that already prove themselves.
review.data_missing: None for the rule itself. 5-minute regular-session OHLCV is enough if we update the trail only on completed bars and assume fills at the next bar open when the stop is breached.
review.already_tried_note: The rejected ideas were different entry filters and a fade overlay. A delayed trailing exit has not been tested yet.
review.overfit_note: If we let the activation threshold and trail distance float, this can be tuned to a 67-day sample very easily. Locking the rule to one setting (+1R, prior completed 5-minute bar) keeps it testable, but the sample is still small and the number of true trend winners is tiny.
review.expected_effect: Best case: a few strong winners run beyond 2.5R instead of being capped, improving average winner size and maybe turning some flat exits into gains.
