More likely: a modest change, with some smaller winners scratched out earlier and no effect on failed breakouts. This is a payoff-shape test, not a cure for the entry edge.
review.test_protocol: Fix the rule before looking at results: activation at +1.0R, trail to the last completed 5-minute bar. Replay the exact same entries, sizing, costs, and 15:45 flat on all 67 archived sessions. Primary metric: post-cost net P&L per session and per trade. Secondary: profit factor, max drawdown, average winner size, and how many trades that were flat under baseline become positive or vice versa. Require the variant to improve in both halves of the archive (Jul–Aug and Sep–Oct) and not worsen max drawdown or cut trade count by more than 10%. If it passes the archive replay, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting it.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with current data, cheap to replay, and it targets a real weakness of the bot: too many exits are flat and the best trades are being capped. The source support is only generic, so this is not a strong conviction bet, but it is a sensible one-change test worth spending before more elaborate exit ideas.

name: Scale out partial profits and move the runner to breakeven
one_line: Take partial profits instead of exiting all at once, and reduce risk on the remainder.
parameter_choices: Most concrete version is 50% off at 1R with the stop on the rest moved to breakeven; variants include a 3-way split with a trailing last third or a topslice after repeated rejection at the same level.
disagreement: Books differ between partial-taking and letting winners run; no head-to-head intraday test appears in the excerpts.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: B2-c013-02 is essentially the same rule: take partial profits once price has moved by a fixed fraction of the take-profit distance and move the stop on the remainder to breakeven. B2-c011-11 and the Naked Trader excerpts support the broader partial-exit / let-the-runner-run idea. The only extrapolation is applying it to our ORB bot and keeping the existing 2.5R target on the runner.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current all-or-nothing exit with: when a trade first reaches +1R from entry, sell 50% of the position, then move the stop on the remaining 50% to the entry price (breakeven). Keep the existing 2.5R final target and 15:45 flat for the runner; no other exit changes.
review.mechanism: This could help by banking something on days that push in our favor and then fade, so more trades end as partial winners instead of flat or full losers on the runner. The breakeven stop also cuts back the giveback on the remaining size. The downside is obvious: it adds another commission/slippage event and cuts the payoff on the few big winners that currently carry most of the edge.
review.data_missing: We can do the replay with 5-minute OHLCV, but we do not have tick-level intrabar sequencing. The only missing piece is exact ordering when the same 5-minute bar could touch +1R and then the breakeven stop; we need a fixed OHLC convention for that.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tried. The rejected ideas were about entry filters and a failed-breakout fade, not a simple scale-out + breakeven exit on the existing ORB.
review.overfit_note: Only two fixed knobs, but the sample is tiny and the effect will depend on a sparse subset of trades that actually reach +1R. It is very easy to fool ourselves by tuning the scale-out fraction, trigger distance, or runner stop on just 67 sessions.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer full givebacks and more breakeven/partial-win days, but smaller average winners and higher costs. Net expectancy is uncertain and could easily be flat to slightly negative unless a meaningful share of trades reaches +1R and then reverses.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule exactly as written and replay it on all 67 archived sessions side by side with the current baseline. Keep entries, universe selection, and the 2.5R/15:45 backbone unchanged. Primary metric: net PnL after all costs; secondary: max drawdown and profit factor. Also report the conditional effect on trades that first touch +1R, because that is the only place this rule can help. Require improvement in both halves of the archive (roughly first 33 sessions vs last 34) before any live use. If it wins the archive test, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions with no further tuning.
review.verdict_reason: This is cheap, fully deterministic to replay, and directly supported by the cited material. It may well fail after costs, but it is feasible with our current data and worth a frozen backtest before we dismiss it.

name: Exit on VWAP or momentum failure
one_line: Flatten a breakout when it loses VWAP or the momentum proxy turns back toward neutral, instead of waiting only for the target or close.
parameter_choices: Long exits can trigger on a close back below VWAP, a cross below a short rolling mean, or a momentum/APO flip back toward neutral; mirror the logic for shorts.
disagreement: No measured consensus in the excerpts; this is a stricter failure exit than the current time-based flat.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: No source states this exact ORB rule. The VWAP source only says VWAP is a useful daily value/execution reference, and the APO examples show generic exit-on-reversion templates. So the idea is a reasonable extrapolation, but the VWAP leg in particular is not directly evidenced as an exit rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Add one early-exit overlay to the existing ORB recipe: compute session VWAP from the regular-session 5-minute bars (cumulative typical price × volume / cumulative volume). After entry, if a long position gets a completed 5-minute close below session VWAP, flatten at the next bar's open; if a short gets a completed close above session VWAP, flatten at the next bar's open. Keep the current stop, 2.5R target, and 15:45 flat. Do not test the momentum-proxy variant in this run.
review.mechanism: This is meant to cut the common breakout-fail pattern sooner: the trade loses the days value reference, then either stops out later or bleeds into the close. Exiting on VWAP failure should reduce average loss and max drawdown, and may turn some stopouts into smaller scratches. The tradeoff is that some true runners will be cut early, so average win size could fall.
review.data_missing: None for the VWAP-only version. If you want the momentum leg, you must define the exact proxy first; our 5-minute OHLCV is enough to compute a rolling mean or APO, but the current idea is too vague to bundle in this test.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is only loosely related to the failed-breakout fade, but that was a different, opposite-direction strategy, not an exit overlay.
review.overfit_note: There are almost no tunable knobs if we lock to session VWAP, but the concept is still easy to over-interpret on 67 sessions because the winners are sparse and concentrated. The main overfit danger is choosing among multiple plausible trigger variants after looking at the replay.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer late-day give-backs and smaller losses on failed breakouts, with some improvement in win rate and drawdown. The likely cost is fewer full runners and a lower average win, so total P&L may improve only modestly or even worsen if the few big winners get cut too often.
review.test_protocol: Replay the frozen baseline and the VWAP-exit variant on all 67 archived sessions with every other rule unchanged. Do not tune anything after seeing the result. Compare primary net P&L after costs and max drawdown, plus secondary metrics: profit factor, average loss size, and how often the new exit replaces a stop or 15:45 flat. Because the trade sample is small, require the variant to beat the baseline in both halves of the archive, not just overall. If it does, paper it on the next ~20 unseen sessions before deciding.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully computable from our existing data, and directly targets the bots known failed-breakout/give-back problem. The evidence is only indirect and the risk is cutting the few runners, but this is exactly the kind of rule that can be falsified quickly in replay and then on the next 20 live days.

name: ATR/support-based initial stop
one_line: Use a volatility- or structure-based initial stop instead of the opposite side of the opening range.
parameter_choices: Candidate stops include ATR(14) × 2.5, or a stop just beyond the nearest intraday support/resistance pivot; keep the current target unless tested separately.
disagreement: Evidence is thin and mostly illustrative; the ATR example looked strong but used only a handful of trades, so this is promising rather than proven.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: One source directly backs an ATR(14) stop with atr_f=2.5, but it is a tiny 7-trade case study on a different strategy and it pairs the stop with an ATR-based target. The support/resistance guidance is generic opinion only, so the link to a stop-only change in Midas is related but not direct.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current "stop at the opposite side of the opening range" with a fixed ATR stop: compute ATR(14) from regular-session daily bars built from the 5-minute OHLC data; for a long set stop = entry - 2.5×ATR(14), for a short set stop = entry + 2.5×ATR(14). Keep the existing 2.5R profit target and all other ORB rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This makes the stop scale to the stock's normal volatility instead of treating the opening range as the only invalidation level. On choppy, high-vol names it may avoid getting clipped by routine noise just beyond the OR, which could convert a few current stop-outs into target hits. The tradeoff is smaller size and/or longer holds, so it only helps if the added breathing room beats the lower share count and unchanged target.
review.data_missing: No extra market data is required, but the ATR must be approximated from our regular-session 5-minute bars (session ATR, not full 24h ATR). If you want the support-pivot variant, you also need a fixed pivot definition.
review.already_tried_note: We have rejected entry-side ideas (two-close confirmation, failed-breakout fade, SPY overlay, single-name focus), but not a stop-placement change like this. No prior ATR-stop test is listed.
review.overfit_note: Only one main knob if we lock ATR at 2.5, but the sample is tiny and stop placement can be tuned to fit a few ugly days. The support-pivot version is especially discretionary.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer premature stop-outs on volatile breakout names and a few more runners hitting target. More likely: little change in the many trades that already go flat, while wider stops reduce size and can make the 2.5R target harder to reach.
review.test_protocol: Freeze ATR(14)=2.5 before looking. Replay the candidate on every archived day side-by-side with the frozen baseline. Score net PnL after all costs, profit factor, max drawdown, average R per trade, stop frequency, and % of trades flat at 15:45. Require improvement in both the first and second halves of the archive, not just the full sample. If it beats baseline after costs on the archive, paper it on the next ~20 unseen sessions without retuning.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and at least plausibly targets the small cluster of failed-break losses. I would not bother with the vague support-pivot version yet, but the fixed ATR stop is worth a replay test because it needs no new data and no live capital.

name: Target-multiple sweep / randomization
one_line: Treat the 2.5R target as an assumption and see whether performance depends on that exact exit point.
parameter_choices: Sweep fixed targets from 1R to 4R, or randomize around 2.5R.
disagreement: Not a strategy disagreement; this is a robustness check.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: B2-c014-08 directly supports the robustness check idea: randomizing take-profit values to see whether performance depends on one exit point. B2-c010-05 supports the current 2.5R baseline as a plausible reward/risk choice. Neither source justifies the exact 1R–4R sweep as a rule; that range is our extrapolation. B6-c008-13 is only a generic profit-target opinion and is weakly relevant to intraday ORB.
review.exact_rule_change: Validation-only change: keep the current entry, stop, sizing, and 15:45 flat rule unchanged, and vary only the profit-target multiple. Replay the bot with target_R set one at a time to 1.0R, 1.5R, 2.0R, 2.5R, 3.0R, and 4.0R (baseline/current default remains 2.5R). Optional stress test: draw target_R from Uniform(2.0R, 3.0R) with a fixed seed.
review.mechanism: This is mainly a robustness check, not a new alpha source. If the P&L is highly sensitive to the exact 2.5R target, the current edge is fragile and we should not trust it. If a slightly lower target converts some of the many flat-at-close trades into realized wins, it could reduce time-in-trade and make the edge easier to monetize after costs. But if the few winners are the only thing paying for the stops and slippage, a lower target will likely hurt expectancy by clipping the right tail.
review.data_missing: None for the sweep itself. 5-minute OHLCV is enough to simulate stop/target hits, with the usual conservative same-bar fill convention if both stop and target are touched in one bar.
review.already_tried_note: The bot already uses a fixed 2.5R target, so the baseline exit is not new. What has not been tried is a proper target sweep or randomized target sensitivity test.
review.overfit_note: One nominal parameter, but many candidate values means an easy multiple-comparisons trap on only 53 trades / 67 sessions. It would be very easy to pick the best-looking target by noise, especially because only 3 trades have hit the current target so far.
review.expected_effect: As a diagnostic, useful. As a live improvement, uncertain. A lower target may raise hit rate and reduce flat exits, but it may also destroy the current edge if the rare big winners are doing most of the work. I would expect a broad plateau if the exit is not critical; a sharp optimum would be a warning sign rather than a win.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the candidate set before looking at results. Replay all archived days with identical entry/stop/sizing and target_R values of 1.0R, 1.5R, 2.0R, 2.5R, 3.0R, and 4.0R. Use the same conservative intrabar assumption for stop/target collisions across all runs. Primary metric: net $ after costs per trade and per session. Secondary metrics: profit factor, max drawdown, and share of trades closed before 15:45. Require any promoted target to beat the baseline 2.5R in both halves of the archive on net expectancy and not worsen drawdown materially (e.g. >20%). Then confirm only one preselected candidate on the next ~20 unseen sessions/trades; do not re-optimize after seeing those results.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, fully data-feasible, and directly relevant to whether the current 2.5R exit is too tight or too loose. It is not a new strategy, but it is a worthwhile robustness test before we change the live target. The main caution is overfitting: we should treat the sweep as validation, not as an excuse to cherry-pick the best number from 67 days.

name: Real stop-order fill modeling
one_line: Backtest exits as actual stop orders with gap-through handling rather than as perfect synthetic fills.
parameter_choices: If price trades through a stop, fill at the stop price when possible and otherwise at the next bar open or worse; include slippage and commission.
disagreement: Not a strategy disagreement; this is execution realism only.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The excerpt supports using stop orders as exits and defines them as inactive until the stop price trades. It does not specify our fill model, so the gap-through/next-open handling is our conservative adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Backtest stop-loss exits as stop-market orders: on the first 5-minute bar whose high/low trades through the stop, fill at the stop price; if that bar opens beyond the stop, fill at that bar's open (gap-through = worse open price). Keep the existing 0.05% round-trip commission and $0.02/share slippage on entry and exit. No live strategy logic changes.
review.mechanism: This does not add alpha; it makes the stop leg realistic. It should remove any overly optimistic stop fills from the backtest, especially on fast reversals and gap-throughs, so we learn whether the current edge survives real execution. If the strategy only works with perfect fills, this will expose that.
review.data_missing: We only have 5-minute OHLCV, so we cannot know the exact intrabar path or whether a stop was hit and recovered within the same bar; tick/L2 data and bid-ask quotes are missing. We can still approximate trigger vs gap-through conservatively.
review.already_tried_note: Stops are already part of the live recipe, but this specific fill model has not been separately tested. It is a backtest/execution assumption change, not a new signal.
review.overfit_note: No tunable alpha parameters if fixed as a rule. The main risk is not overfitting but making the simulator arbitrarily pessimistic or optimistic; keep the rule conservative and fixed before looking at results.
review.expected_effect: Likely lowers reported PnL a bit and may increase measured drawdown versus a perfect-fill backtest; improves realism and decision quality more than live performance.
review.test_protocol: Run a side-by-side replay on all 67 archived sessions: baseline stop fills vs stop-market/gap-through fills, with all else frozen. Compare net PnL after costs, PF, win rate, average stop loss, max drawdown, and the day-by-day sign of returns. Require improvement or at least no material degradation in both halves of the archive before confirming on the next ~20 unseen sessions. No parameter tuning after seeing results.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with the data we have, essentially zero extra complexity, and important because stop exits are a meaningful part of the current P&L. It won't create alpha, but it is the right backtest correction before spending scarce live days on new ideas.

name: Reversion-window test for time exits
one_line: Measure how quickly breakout trades mean-revert after entry and use that decay window to set a time stop or earlier exit.
parameter_choices: Track 15/30/60/90-minute post-entry reversion; if adverse/favorable excursion usually decays by a given window, use that as the max hold or tighten the stop.
disagreement: Quick reversion may just be noise on some days, so a time stop can cut real trends if set too aggressively.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general microstructure claim that temporary impact reverts after execution stops and that the decay window matters. It does not specifically justify using that fact as a breakout-trade exit rule; that step is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a hard 60-minute max hold from fill: any ORB position still open 60 minutes after entry is exited at the next 5-minute bar open, regardless of P&L; keep the existing stop, 2.5R target, and 15:45 flat otherwise unchanged.
review.mechanism: This only helps if failed breakouts on Midas usually lose momentum quickly and then spend hours chopping back toward entry. A 60-minute time stop could cut those dead trades before the late-day drift, reducing some flat exits and a few late reversals into bigger losers. The trade-off is obvious: it may also cut the small number of true trend days that become the only large winners.
review.data_missing: No additional data is required. We can estimate it from 5-minute OHLCV and entry timestamps, though intrabar sequencing will still be bar-resolution only.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly. The bot already has a same-day flat at 15:45, but we have not tested an entry-relative 15/30/60/90-minute decay stop.
review.overfit_note: If we let the archive choose among 15/30/60/90-minute windows after the fact, this will overfit fast on 53 trades. Only one precommitted window should be tested.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer dead-flat holds, less late-day giveback, and slightly lower drawdown. Likely downside: some truncated winners and a smaller average win. I would expect a modest effect, not a structural change in edge.
review.test_protocol: Precommit to one candidate only: 60-minute max hold from fill. Replay baseline vs candidate on every archived day with identical entries, sizing, stops, targets, and costs. Judge on after-cost net P&L/day, max drawdown, profit factor, win rate, and the share of exits triggered by the time stop. Split the archive chronologically and require improvement in both halves, not just in aggregate. If it survives replay, paper it on the next ~20 unseen sessions unchanged. Do not scan 15/30/90-minute alternatives after looking at results.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible from the data we have, cheap to replay, and it targets a real weakness of this bot. The source is only partial, so keep the test strict and precommitted; if it doesn't help in both replay halves, kill it.

name: Structure-anchored stop and target
one_line: Anchor exits to the impulse structure (swing/FVG/OR extension) instead of the fixed OR stop and 2.5R target.
parameter_choices: Stop below/above the most recent swing extreme, the FVG candle, or the impulse candle; target the midpoint, 4R, or the next structure extension.
disagreement: Structure can reduce random stop-outs, but it may also miss many trades or leave the reward/risk too thin.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the *general* idea of structural exits: one uses swing/Fib levels, and the other explicitly talks about a stop under the candle that creates an FVG plus a 4R or midpoint target. Neither source is an ORB study, so applying this to our opening-range breakout is an extrapolation, not a direct replication.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current ORB entry rules unchanged. For the first valid breakout trade of the day, replace the stop at the opposite side of the opening range with a stop 1 tick beyond the low/high of the breakout signal candle (the 5-minute bar that first closes outside the OR). Replace the fixed 2.5R target with a 4R target. No other exit rules change.
review.mechanism: This ties risk to the candle that actually proves the breakout instead of to the whole opening range. If the OR stop is too blunt, the candle-based stop should cut failed fakeouts sooner and shrink losses; the 4R target gives the rare trend days more room to pay for the many flat exits. The tradeoff is fewer hits if 4R is too ambitious.
review.data_missing: None essential for this concrete version; 5-minute OHLCV is enough to identify the signal candle extreme and measure 4R. Tick/L2 would only matter if we wanted a more exact microstructure/FVG implementation.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejection list. The closest prior rejection was a different entry filter (two closes beyond the range), not a structural stop/target change.
review.overfit_note: 'Structure' can mean swing low/high, FVG, impulse candle, or OR extension, and each can be tuned multiple ways. With only 67 archived sessions, we should freeze one candle-based stop and one target before looking at results, or this will just fit noise.
review.expected_effect: Could reduce the August-style fakeout losses and improve the payout on the rare strong trend day, but it may also lower win rate if the candle stop is too tight and 4R is too far. The only way this helps is if the structural stop materially improves loss size without killing the few real runners.
review.test_protocol: Freeze exactly one variant: stop = 1 tick beyond the breakout candle extreme; target = 4R; keep all other rules unchanged. Replay all 67 archived sessions side by side with the current baseline. Compare post-cost expectancy per trade, net PnL per day, profit factor, win rate, max drawdown, and the number of flat-at-close exits. Require the variant to beat baseline in both chronological halves of the archive and not worsen drawdown. If it passes, confirm on the next 20 unseen live sessions with no further tuning.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully replayable with our current bars, cheap to test, and directly targets the fakeout-loss bucket. The source support is only partial and the overfit risk is high, so we should test one frozen structural version only—not a menu of swing/FVG options—but it is worth a controlled backtest now.

name: Fixed percentage stop with 2R target
one_line: Use a fixed percent-of-entry stop and a 2R take-profit as a simple baseline exit rule.
parameter_choices: Stop distance 5%, 10%, or 15% from entry; take-profit at 2R.
disagreement: Percent stops are crude across a $20-$300 universe and may be too loose on high-priced names or too tight on low-priced ones.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The source does support the general pattern of a percentage stop-loss with a 2R take-profit, but it is a daily/close-based case study, not an intraday 5-minute opening-range breakout system. The match is directional, not direct, and the 5%/10%/15% choices are our adaptation, not the book's evidence.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current opening-range stop with a fixed 10% stop from entry and a 2R take-profit; for longs, stop 10% below entry and target 20% above, and for shorts, stop 10% above entry and target 20% below. Keep the rest of the Midas recipe unchanged.
review.mechanism: Only plausible benefit: the wider fixed stop could reduce stop-outs on noisy breakouts and shrink share count, which lowers commissions/slippage. The problem is that a 10% stop makes the 2R target a 20% intraday move, so on a same-day ORB with a 15:45 flat it will almost never hit; most trades become dead-money flats with smaller notional, not better edge.
review.data_missing: We can simulate it from 5-minute OHLCV, but we do not know the exact intrabar sequence inside a bar, so same-bar stop/target collisions are ambiguous unless we adopt a conservative fill rule.
review.already_tried_note: Not on this bot. The rejected tests so far were different overlays and filters, not a fixed-percent stop with a 2R exit.
review.overfit_note: There are only three stop-width candidates and only 67 archived days. Because 2R targets will be rare, one or two lucky hits can dominate the comparison, so it is very easy to tune this to noise if we let the backtest choose among 5/10/15% after the fact.
review.expected_effect: Most likely flat to worse. You may get fewer stop-outs and lower costs from smaller size, but the profit target is so far away that target hits will likely vanish and the strategy will drift toward low-signal end-of-day flats.
review.test_protocol: Do not allocate live unseen days to this idea unless an archived replay already beats the baseline clearly. If you insist on a sanity check, pre-register 10% only, replay it on all 67 archived sessions with a fixed conservative rule for same-bar stop/target collisions, and compare net P&L, profit factor, max drawdown, stop rate, and target-hit rate versus the current OR stop. It must improve in both halves of the archived sample and not collapse target hits before it gets any live test.
review.verdict_reason: Reject. The source only supports the generic concept, not this intraday application. On Midas, a 5/10/15% fixed stop implies a 10/20/30% same-day target, which is too far for a system that must flatten by 15:45 and trades a mixed $20-$300 universe with no leverage. It will under-size or exclude higher-priced names, likely drive target hits toward zero, and is a worse volatility proxy than the existing opening-range stop.

name: Asymmetric short-side exits
one_line: Give short trades smaller targets or shorter time stops than longs.
parameter_choices: Short target 1.5R-2R versus 2.5R on longs, or a short max-hold 15-30 minutes shorter than the long-side rule.
disagreement: Some shorts trend harder than longs, so asymmetric exits could clip the rare big short winner too early.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The book supports the general idea that shorts should be shorter-term and that profits on shorts should be taken quickly. It does not specify an asymmetric target versus longs or any numeric R-multiple, so the 1.5R short target is our adaptation, not a direct quoted rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the existing 2.5R target for long trades, but for short trades only set the profit target to 1.5R (all other rules unchanged: same stop, same entry logic, same 15:45 flat).
review.mechanism: This could help if Midas shorts tend to make an early move and then give it back into the close or on a squeeze. A smaller short target should turn more of those brief moves into realized wins and reduce short flat-at-close exits. It will not fix bad entries, and it may clip the rare big short trend.
review.data_missing: None; the existing 5-minute regular-session OHLCV is enough to simulate this under the same bar-based fill assumptions as the baseline.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. We have tried a different exit overlay and a morning fade, but not a short-only asymmetric target or hold rule.
review.overfit_note: Only one knob, but the short-side sample is probably small and a few outlier shorts can dominate results. Do not sweep 1.5R/2R/2.5R after the fact.
review.expected_effect: Best case: slightly higher short-side win rate and fewer short flat exits. Worst case: lower average short winner size and no net gain. I would expect only a small effect either way.
review.test_protocol: Freeze 1.5R before looking. Replay all 67 archived sessions side-by-side with the baseline. Judge by after-cost net P&L, short-only expectancy, win rate, and max drawdown, and require improvement in both archive halves (Jul-Aug and Sep-Oct), not just one lucky patch. If the archive looks positive, paper trade the next ~20 unseen sessions; do not bless it unless the live shorts also beat baseline by the end of that window. If there are fewer than ~10 short trades in the archive, treat the result as provisional only.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with the data we have, cheap to replay, and not already tried. The source support is weak and the upside is likely small, but this is a legitimate one-parameter test rather than a new strategy.

name: Performance-based exposure throttle
one_line: Adjust the per-trade risk budget up or down based on recent win/loss or monthly performance instead of keeping it fixed.
parameter_choices: Kelly-style fraction from recent win/loss counts and payoff ratio (f*=p−q/(W/L)); or discrete monthly step changes like ±2 shares with min 1 and max 50 shares; slow exposure increases after good performance and decreases after bad months.
disagreement: The books disagree on mechanism: Kelly is continuous/formula-based, while Donadio/Ghosh use discrete stepwise exposure changes. They also differ on how aggressively to react.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: B1 supports a Kelly-style bet-size update from estimated win/loss rate and payoff ratio; B4 gives a concrete example of increasing/decreasing trade size after good/bad months. Both are directly about adaptive sizing, but neither proves this is a good fit for a tiny ORB bot with only 53 trades and a weak edge.
review.exact_rule_change: No new strategy; add a performance throttle on top of the existing 1% risk-per-trade rule. Start with exposure multiplier = 1.0. Every 20 completed sessions, compute net PnL over that trailing window. If it is positive, increase the multiplier by 0.25; if negative, decrease it by 0.25. Clamp the multiplier to 0.75x–1.25x. Effective risk per trade = 1% of equity × multiplier, still subject to the existing cash cap and stop distance.
review.mechanism: This only changes how much capital you put on after the bot has been working or not working. Best case, it trims position size during bad stretches so drawdowns are smaller and dollar costs are lower, and lets size recover during good stretches. But it does not improve breakout quality, target rate, or exit quality; it mostly just amplifies or suppresses whatever edge you already have.
review.data_missing: None beyond your own trade/equity history. The 20-session PnL throttle can be computed from the existing replayable trade log and daily equity curve.
review.already_tried_note: Not specifically tried. The current bot uses fixed risk-to-stop sizing plus a cash cap, but there is no rule that changes exposure based on recent performance.
review.overfit_note: The sizing signal is your own recent PnL, and with only 53 trades it will be very noisy. A Kelly-style estimate is especially unstable here; the rule can easily chase random streaks rather than a real change in edge.
review.expected_effect: Most likely outcome is slightly smoother equity and smaller bad months, with little or no improvement in raw expectancy. It may also reduce the dollar impact of the few bad streaks, but it will not fix the failed-breakout problem and could easily suppress the already tiny upside.
review.test_protocol: Precommit the rule and replay it on all 67 archived sessions using walk-forward sizing only (each day’s size can use only prior days). Compare baseline vs throttle on net PnL after costs, max drawdown, and average dollar risk per trade. Require it to improve both halves of the archive, not just the full sample, and to do so after at least two 20-session update cycles. If it fails that archive replay, do not spend live unseen days on it. Only if it clearly improves the archive should you confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible and cheap, but the sizing input is too noisy at this sample size. This is mostly a risk-smoothing overlay, not an edge source, and it does nothing to address the bot’s main problems: failed breakouts, flat exits, and costs. I would not prioritize live testing this before a larger trade history or a one-way drawdown brake instead of a symmetric up/down throttle.

name: Rolling drawdown halt
one_line: Pause new entries or cut size when trailing 5-session or 20-session PnL breaches a loss threshold.
parameter_choices: Weekly loss from pnls[-1]-pnls[-6] (5 sessions); monthly loss from pnls[-1]-pnls[-21] (20 sessions); example bands in the books include roughly -$4K weekly / -$6K monthly in one example and -$6K / -$15K in another.
disagreement: The sources agree on rolling PnL-based loss gates, but the exact bands differ across examples and seem strategy-specific rather than universal.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly uses the same class of control: rolling 5-session and 20-session PnL loss gates (e.g. weekly_loss = pnls[-1] - pnls[-6], monthly_loss = pnls[-1] - pnls[-21]). This is a near-identical risk-management rule, though the dollar bands are strategy-specific and must be adapted to Midas.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a two-stage rolling PnL circuit breaker checked before the 10:00 entry scan: if the trailing 5 completed sessions of net PnL are <= -$6, skip all new entries for that session; if the trailing 20 completed sessions are <= -$15, trade all new signals at 50% of normal size until the 20-session PnL recovers above 0.
review.mechanism: This is a drawdown governor, not alpha. It could help if failed breakouts cluster into a bad regime: after a losing patch, it stops us from continuing to pay commission and slippage into the same weak tape, which should reduce multi-day bleed and max drawdown. It will not fix the breakout edge itself and may simply suppress some profitable rebounds.
review.data_missing: None; we can compute the rolling session PnL from our own fills and existing 5-minute bars (or from daily realized PnL if we stay flat overnight). No L2, news, premarket, or other external data is needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule, but it overlaps with the existing fixed -3% intraday day-loss halt. This is a multi-session version of the same kind of capital-preservation control.
review.overfit_note: Two arbitrary thresholds on only 67 sessions is very easy to tune to the August drawdown. On a $1,000 book, the source's dollar bands are not portable; any normalized thresholds are still likely to be regime-specific and could over-fire on normal noise.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer bad days and lower max drawdown, with maybe slightly lower costs from skipped trades in bad regimes. More likely: little change in expectancy, and possibly lower total PnL because the few profitable bursts may be cut off too.
review.test_protocol: Fix the thresholds before looking at the replay. Backtest baseline vs. gate on all archived days, but score only after a 20-session warm-up because the monthly window needs history. Compare net PnL, max drawdown, profit factor, and trade count in the first and second halves of the post-warm-up sample. A pass needs a material DD reduction (say >=20%) with no more than a small PnL drag (say <=10%) and the effect should show up in both halves, not just the August losing patch. If it passes offline, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions with the same settings.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible and cheap to simulate, but this is a risk overlay, not a fix for the bot's weak breakout edge. The source supports the general idea, but the exact loss bands are strategy-specific and poorly transferable to a $1,000 book. With only 67 sessions, the result is likely to be driven by one bad streak, so I would not spend a live test slot on it until an offline replay shows a clear drawdown benefit without a meaningful PnL hit.

name: Volatility / tail-risk stop and size scaling
one_line: Use a range-based volatility estimate to widen stops and automatically shrink size on volatile or heavy-tailed sessions.
parameter_choices: OHLC-based estimator with optimal a=0.17; serial-correlation-adjusted realized volatility; wider stop distance and smaller size when vol is high; half-size on heavy-tail / high-kurtosis days.
disagreement: Sources disagree on the estimator (close-to-close, serial-correlation-adjusted, or OHLC range-based) and on whether the response should be larger stops, smaller size, or both.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the ingredients, not the exact ORB rule. One book explicitly recommends OHLC-based volatility estimators and even gives a=0.17; others say volatility should affect risk behavior, stops that are too tight can fail in volatile markets, and returns are heavy-tailed. None of them directly say 'widen the OR stop and shrink ORB size,' so this is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: For each candidate trade, compute the symbol's prior-20-session daily volatility from OHLC bars using the composite estimator with a=0.17. Convert it to a price stop buffer d_vol = 1.0 × close_{t-1} × sigma_hat20. Set the stop distance to max(current opening-range stop distance, d_vol); then keep the existing 1% equity risk sizing to that stop. No other entry/exit changes.
review.mechanism: On days when the name is genuinely more volatile than the opening range suggests, the current OR stop is likely too tight and the trade gets chopped out. A volatility floor should keep some breakout trades alive long enough to work, while the automatic sizing shrink reduces dollar exposure on those noisy days. Best case: fewer failed-breakout stopouts and smaller tail losses. Downside: more flat exits and smaller winners if the floor is too conservative.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. The bot already sizes to its stop, but it has not tried a separate OHLC-based volatility floor on the stop distance.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob if we freeze the estimator form: the 1.0× volatility floor. But with only 67 sessions it is still easy to tune the lookback or multiplier to the sample if we are not disciplined.
review.expected_effect: Likely a modest reduction in drawdown and stop-outs on volatile breakout days, with smaller position sizes and slightly lower cost dollars on those days. I would not expect a big lift in raw expectancy unless failed-breakout days are the main source of losses.
review.test_protocol: Replay baseline vs. this rule on all 67 archived sessions with the multiplier fixed before looking. Compare after-cost net PnL, profit factor, max drawdown, stop-out rate, and average R. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just overall. Because this is mainly a risk overlay, it only passes if it improves or at least holds net PnL while clearly improving drawdown; if it only lowers DD by shrinking size but cuts PnL materially, reject. If it wins on replay, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with the data we have, cheap to replay, and it targets a real failure mode: tight stops on volatile names. The expected edge is probably small, but this is a legitimate low-cost risk overlay rather than a whole new strategy, so it is worth a controlled test.

name: Liquidity-aware notional cap
one_line: Cap each order by a liquidity-normalized exposure limit so thin names cannot consume too much of the book.
parameter_choices: Normalize by ADV; use a 20-day ADV baseline or the common 30-day mean/median daily volume; 66-day window if you want an earnings-cycle view; combine with a hard per-symbol notional ceiling.
disagreement: The books differ mainly on the liquidity lookback window: 20-day, 30-day, or 66-day. They also mix relative ADV normalization with absolute per-asset caps.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The excerpts support the ingredients, not this exact rule: one book recommends ADV-normalized sizing and notes 30-day mean/median volume as the common baseline, another says smaller orders fill better, and a third describes hard per-asset caps. But none of them state this specific "liquidity-aware notional cap" as a trading rule; that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: After the existing stop-based size is computed, cap entry notional at the lesser of that size and 0.1% of the symbol's 30-session median daily dollar volume (computed from regular-session OHLCV). Keep the existing no-leverage cash cap, stop, target, and one-trade-per-day rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: In theory this could prevent the rare thin-name trade from being oversized relative to recent liquidity, which could lower impact and make exits easier to fill. In Midas, though, order sizes are already tiny and the universe is liquid, so this is unlikely to move the needle. If it helps at all, it would be on execution/costs and maybe a tiny drawdown reduction, not on the failed-breakout problem.
review.data_missing: No extra data is needed to compute the cap; 30-session daily dollar volume can be derived from the existing 5-minute OHLCV. What we do not have is spread/L2/tick data, so any real fill-quality benefit would only be a proxy in backtest, not directly observed.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tried. The closest prior filters were universe-thinning ideas (top-5 only, price caps), but those were about selection starvation/cherry-picking, not liquidity-normalized sizing.
review.overfit_note: If we freeze the 30-session window, there is only one real knob (the cap fraction). But the expected effect is so small that any apparent improvement over 67 days is likely noise, and if we start shopping 20/30/66-day windows or several cap levels it becomes obvious data-mining.
review.expected_effect: Probably near-zero. At best, a tiny reduction in slippage/impact on the rare low-liquidity name; more likely no measurable change in PF or drawdown. If the cap is tightened enough to matter, it will mostly just shrink the few good winners.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend unseen days on this unless the cap actually binds. First replay all 67 archived sessions with the fixed 30-session / 0.1% rule and record: (1) fraction of trades whose size changes, (2) average size reduction on those trades, and (3) net P&L, PF, and max DD in both halves of the archive. If fewer than ~10% of trades are affected, stop and reject. Only if it materially binds and improves both halves should you even consider the next ~20 unseen days.
review.verdict_reason: On a $1,000 book trading already-liquid names with roughly $500 positions, any sensible ADV-based cap will almost never bind. That means it cannot materially improve fills or risk, and our current bar-based backtest cannot measure the tiny microstructure effect anyway. If you tighten the cap enough to matter, you are just cutting size on the few trades that might pay. This is execution hygiene for a much larger book, not an edge for Midas.

name: Downside-risk candidate filter
one_line: Prefer breakout candidates with better recent downside behavior instead of ranking only by relative volume.
parameter_choices: Lower-quartile returns and lower partial moment (LPM) as the downside-risk score; apply the score as a penalty or exclusion filter before the breakout trade is chosen.
disagreement: No direct disagreement; the source defines the downside-risk measure but does not specify a cutoff, so the threshold must be chosen empirically.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book supports downside-risk measures (lower-quartile returns, LPM) as a way to rank risk, but it does not claim that using them to select opening-range breakout candidates adds edge. Applying the measure to Midas is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the existing universe and 10:00 top-8 relative-volume screen. For each of the 8 names, compute a 20-session downside-risk score from daily closes: (1) the mean of the worst 25% of daily close-to-close returns and (2) the 20-session LPM2 of negative daily returns. Rank both measures across the 8 names, average those two ranks into a downside-risk rank, then add that rank to the existing relative-volume rank. Trade only the name with the lowest combined rank; no other rules change.
review.mechanism: This tries to avoid names that have been leaking lower or printing ugly downside tails, which are the names most likely to turn an OR breakout into a stopout or a dead-flat close. If it helps, the gain should come mostly from fewer failed-breakout stops and some fewer bad flat exits. Main risk: it may also filter out the high-beta names that actually produce the few big winners.
review.data_missing: None; the filter can be built from the daily closes we already have.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tried, but it is the same broad class of universe/ranking tweak as the top-5 and price-cap experiments that already failed. New metric, same selection-pipeline bucket.
review.overfit_note: One lookback is already a tuning knob, and the score itself is a flexible rank construction. With only 67 archived days, it is easy to fit noise and end up selecting the wrong kind of volatility.
review.expected_effect: Best case: a modest drop in stopouts and worst-day losses, with a small lift in net PnL. More likely: little change, or worse, because the filter may just throw away the volatile names that generate our targets.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the lookback at 20 sessions before looking at results. Replay baseline vs this filter on all 67 archived days side by side with identical fills/costs. Primary metric: after-cost net PnL and max drawdown on the full archive and separately on the first 33 vs last 34 days. Secondary: stopout count, target count, and trade count. Only keep it if it improves both halves, not just one regime, and does not cut trade count by more than about 15%. If it passes replay, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions before considering live use.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible and cheap, but the causal link is thin: downside-risk over prior daily closes is a weak proxy for intraday breakout quality, and this filter could easily discard the names that actually pay for costs. Good backlog test, not a priority live test.

name: Extreme-signal de-risking
one_line: When the opening move is unusually extended or relative volume is extreme, trade smaller rather than larger.
parameter_choices: Cut size in half on unusually extended first 30 minutes or unusually high relative volume; treat this as a conservative override to the base size rule.
disagreement: No direct disagreement; this is a rule-of-thumb response to extreme signals rather than a measured threshold.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the generic principle that extreme signals should be handled conservatively with smaller risk. It does not specifically recommend opening-range breakout size cuts, relative-volume thresholds, or a 50% multiplier. Applying that principle to our high-RVOL ORB trades is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the base ORB unchanged. Add one sizing override: if the symbol’s 9:30-10:00 relative volume is >= 2.0x its trailing 10-session average at 10:00, set position size to 0.5x the normal size for that trade; otherwise leave size at 1.0x.
review.mechanism: This is a drawdown-control overlay. On unusually active days our breakouts are more violent, so the same failed-breakout pattern can cost more dollars. Cutting size on those days should reduce stop-loss damage, slippage dollars, and commission dollars, and may lower max drawdown. The trade-off is obvious: the rare big winners on those same days also get smaller, so this is not a new alpha source.
review.data_missing: None for the chosen rule; the existing 5-minute regular-session bars are enough to compute the trigger.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly. We already use relative volume to decide which names are in play, but we have not tested a position-size override tied to extreme RVOL. This is adjacent, not the same test.
review.overfit_note: Only one cutoff and one multiplier, so the knob count is low. But the trigger subset will be small, and it would be easy to tune the 2.0x threshold to the 67 days if we let it. Do not add the 'extended first 30 minutes' version in the same test.
review.expected_effect: Most likely: lower absolute PnL, lower volatility, and possibly lower max drawdown; maybe slightly lower cost dollars on the worst whipsaw days. Best case is that it trims bad days without hurting expectancy much. I would not expect it to raise the win rate or create new edge.
review.test_protocol: Precommit to the 2.0x RVOL cutoff before looking. Replay baseline vs overlay on all 67 archived sessions side by side. Evaluate actual dollar equity curve, after-cost net PnL, and max drawdown; also inspect the subset of triggered trades separately. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just the full sample. If the override fires on fewer than ~12 archived trades, treat the result as too sparse to trust. If it passes archived replay, paper it on the next ~20 unseen sessions with the same fixed cutoff and no retuning.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully computable from existing data, cheap to test, and genuinely different from the prior rejected ideas. The caveat is that this is more of a risk overlay than an alpha idea, so the bar should be high: if it does not improve archived after-cost PnL and drawdown in both halves, kill it quickly.

name: Soft stop before hard stop
one_line: Exit on the first adverse 5-minute close before the opening-range stop is actually touched.
parameter_choices: One 5-minute close against the position; keep the existing hard OR stop as backup if the soft exit does not trigger or gaps through occur.
disagreement: No direct disagreement; the source is giving general risk advice rather than competing parameterizations.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The source quote is almost the same risk idea: if the trade starts going against you, get out before the stop is hit. But it is generic opinion, not a tested ORB rule, so the 5-minute close-based version is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a soft exit to every ORB trade: after the entry has filled, if the first completed 5-minute bar closes back inside the opening range against the position (long: close < OR high; short: close > OR low), flatten at the next 5-minute bar open. Keep the existing opposite-side OR stop as a hard backstop and for any stop-through cases. No other exit changes.
review.mechanism: This could cut the exact failure mode we have seen: breakout, then quick reversal and drift toward the hard stop. On those days it should reduce average loss size and possibly max drawdown. The tradeoff is that it will also kick us out of normal pullbacks and may turn some trades that would have been flat or even won into small losses, so the net effect is uncertain.
review.data_missing: None for a bar-close implementation; 5-minute OHLCV is enough. We cannot know true intrabar sequence, so the backtest must use a fixed OHLC rule: hard stop if the stop is touched, otherwise soft exit on the close signal.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly. The rejected morning-fade idea was an opposite-side entry strategy, not an early-exit risk rule.
review.overfit_note: Only one obvious knob in the written rule, but many hidden choices in how 'adverse close' is defined. With just 53 trades and lots of plausible variants, this can still be tuned to noise.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer full-stop losers and a bit less drawdown on failed-breakout days, but probably more small losses and fewer trades that have time to recover. Net uplift is plausible but probably modest.
review.test_protocol: Fix the rule now; do not tune it after seeing results. Replay it side by side with the frozen baseline on all archived days. Use one deterministic precedence rule: if a 5-minute bar can contain both the hard stop and the soft exit, assume the hard stop fills first; otherwise soft-exit at the next bar open after the first adverse close. Compare primary outcome = net P&L after costs; secondary = max drawdown, average trade, win rate, and average loss size. Require improvement in both halves of the archive (Jul-Aug vs Sep-Oct), not just in the full sample. If it clears that, forward test on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with the data we already have, cheap to replay, and directly aimed at our failed-breakout loss pattern. The source is only opinion and the rule may just convert some flats into small losses, but it is plausible enough to earn one fixed-parameter test rather than being rejected outright.

name: Method: realistic stop-slippage and gap testing
one_line: Validate any stop or sizing change with slippage-aware backtests that treat stop-losses as market orders and include gap-through behavior.
parameter_choices: Model stops with extra slippage on fast moves and gaps; compare live paper vs backtest on worst-day loss, stop frequency, and time-in-trade; stress-test fills, gaps, and risk limits before deployment.
disagreement: No direct disagreement; these are validation recommendations, not competing live rules.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources do support the core premise: one explicitly says a stop-loss becomes a market order and can slip, and another says risk systems need accurate backtests plus stress testing. That supports conservative stop-fill modeling. The exact gap-through handling is our extrapolation, not stated verbatim.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not change live trading yet. For all stop/sizing backtests, model stop exits as market orders: if a 5-minute bar trades through the stop, fill at the worse of the stop price and that bar’s open, then apply $0.02/share adverse slippage.
review.mechanism: This makes the backtest honest about the main failure mode for Midas: breakout entries that reverse hard and hit the stop. It should reduce fake edge, prevent oversizing on a fragile setup, and stop us approving stop/sizing tweaks that only work with optimistic fills.
review.data_missing: Exact intrabar path and true fill depth inside the 5-minute bar; bid/ask or tick data would be needed for real stop slippage. We can approximate with OHLCV and the bar open, but not measure it exactly.
review.already_tried_note: We already account for commissions and a fixed slippage charge in the live recipe, but we have not clearly been running a separate stop-as-market / gap-through stress model as a gate for stop or sizing changes.
review.overfit_note: Few knobs if the stress fill is fixed upfront, but it is easy to tune the penalty until a candidate looks good or bad. Keep the rule fixed before looking at results.
review.expected_effect: No direct PnL boost from the method itself. The payoff is better risk estimates, smaller chance of over-sizing, and fewer live surprises on stop-heavy days. If a change only works under fantasy fills, this should expose it.
review.test_protocol: Replay the current bot and any candidate stop/sizing change on all 67 archived sessions using two fill models: baseline and stressed stop fills. Compare net PnL, profit factor, max drawdown, worst-day loss, stop count, and average loss per stopped trade. Require the stressed model to preserve the edge in both halves of the archive, not just the full sample. Then paper-trade the unchanged bot for the next ~20 unseen sessions and check whether live worst-day loss and average stop loss stay within about 20% of the stressed backtest. Do not trust any stop/slippage estimate until you have at least ~10 stop events across archive + new data.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible, and directly relevant to the bot’s main weakness: failed breakouts and stop losses under small-book costs. It is not a new alpha idea, but it is a worthwhile validation gate before we test any stop or sizing change.

name: Method: size-sensitivity stress test
one_line: Randomize position size around the base rule in backtest to see whether the strategy is fragile to sizing noise.
parameter_choices: Apply small random up/down multipliers around the baseline size; compare equity curvature, drawdown, and profit factor to the unjittered version.
disagreement: No direct disagreement; this is a diagnostic test rather than a live trading rule.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: B2 explicitly recommends varying trade size to assess how position sizing changes risk and return; B4 separately warns that profitability is not linear in risk. That supports a sizing-stress-test diagnostic, but not a live alpha rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not change entries or exits. In replay only, multiply each trade’s base share size by an independent jitter factor m ~ Uniform(0.90, 1.10) (±10%, mean 1.0) with a fixed seed, and compare the result to the unjittered baseline.
review.mechanism: No direct alpha. This only checks whether the bot’s PnL is fragile to modest sizing noise, rounding, or the cash cap. If PF/DD swing a lot under ±10% size jitter, the strategy is too close to the cost floor or too dependent on sizing quirks; if it barely moves, sizing is not the bottleneck. It does not reduce failed breakouts, improve targets, or lower costs by itself.
review.data_missing: None for the replay itself. A more realistic market-impact model for size scaling would need spreads, L2, or tick data, which we do not have.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tried. The live bot already uses a fixed 1% risk-to-stop formula, but the random jitter sensitivity check itself has not been run.
review.overfit_note: Only one knob if the jitter band is fixed ex ante. The Monte Carlo seeds should not be tuned. The main risk is over-interpreting a robustness toy on only 53 trades, not parameter fitting.
review.expected_effect: Neutral on mean expectancy; it should mostly rescale the equity curve mechanically. The only useful outcome is a robustness readout, not a better live edge.
review.test_protocol: Run the existing ORB replay on all 67 archived sessions as baseline, then rerun 500 Monte Carlo variants with the ±10% size jitter fixed before looking at results. Compare net PnL, profit factor, max drawdown, and per-trade return distribution to baseline, and also split the archive into first 33 vs last 34 sessions to see whether the sensitivity is consistent. A useful diagnostic is: median PF within 10% of baseline and median max DD within 20% of baseline; otherwise size sensitivity is material. This is QA only; do not use it as a deploy rule. If you later convert the finding into a real sizing change, confirm on the next ~20 unseen trades.
review.verdict_reason: This is a diagnostic, not a trading improvement. On this small book with near-linear costs, modest random size jitter will mostly just rescale PnL and is unlikely to teach us anything actionable about the edge. It does not address the known weaknesses of failed breakouts, flat exits, or cost drag. If we want a useful sizing test, compare explicit notional caps or a liquidity-aware sizing rule instead.

name: Short-side eligibility filter
one_line: Skip shorts in names that are likely to face short-sale execution constraints or uncertain borrow, and compare short-side results only on eligible names.
parameter_choices: Start with a conservative no-short list for names with known short-sale frictions; if borrow data is unavailable, proxy with a strict operational filter and keep long/short stats separate.
disagreement: This may reduce rejected or unfillable shorts even if it does not create alpha, so the main gain is more realistic short-side testing.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source correctly warns that short-sale execution constraints exist and can affect liquidity, but it does not propose a borrow/eligibility filter or any rule tied to our universe. The proposed blacklist is our extrapolation, not a near-identical rule from the book.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a hard short-side blacklist: do not take any short breakout in the $20–$80 "play" batch; longs unchanged. Parameter: `no_short_symbols = {all names in the play batch}` (fixed, predeclared list).
review.mechanism: This could reduce live short entries that are hard to borrow, rejected, or awkward to execute, and it may also remove some squeeze-prone names. That would improve execution realism and maybe cut a few ugly short-side losses, but it is not an alpha source and will likely just reduce short trade count.
review.data_missing: True borrow/locate availability and short-sale constraint flags are not in our 5-minute OHLCV or daily-close data. A static blacklist is implementable as an ops choice, but it is not a signal we can infer from the current dataset.
review.already_tried_note: We have not separately filtered shorts by borrow/eligibility. The closest existing safeguard is the overnight-gap short skip, which is unrelated.
review.overfit_note: Any proxy blacklist would be arbitrary, easy to tune to the 67-day sample, and especially dangerous because the short sample is already small. You would be fitting to an unobserved variable with no ground truth in the archive.
review.expected_effect: Mostly cleaner live execution and fewer unfillable/rejected shorts; likely fewer short trades and no demonstrated uplift in net PnL. This is a realism safeguard, not a return enhancer.
review.test_protocol: Do not allocate a live test without an external borrow/locate feed or a fixed, predeclared short blacklist. If you add one, replay the full 67-day archive with the blacklist frozen before looking, and compare baseline vs filtered on short-side fillability/rejection count, short-side PnL, and total PnL. Require improvement in both halves of the archive and at least ~20 short trades remaining; then confirm on the next 20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: With our current data, this is not a measurable alpha hypothesis. The real variable is borrow/locate availability, which we do not have; any proxy blacklist would be arbitrary and easy to overfit while shrinking an already small short sample. Treat it as a live-ops safeguard only after adding borrow data.

name: Tighter hard notional cap
one_line: Reject trades whose entry notional exceeds a fixed fraction of equity, even if the cash limit would allow them.
parameter_choices: Test hard caps at 25%, 33%, and 50% of equity, independent of stop distance; keep the current 1% risk sizing inside that cap.
disagreement: This trades off fewer oversized winners against lower tail exposure and lower sensitivity to execution noise.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book supports generic pre-trade exposure/notional limits, but it does not argue for this specific tighter cap or claim it improves PnL. This is our own extrapolation from risk-control guidance.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a hard entry-notional cap of 33% of current equity: after the existing 1% risk sizing computes shares, reject the trade if intended entry notional > 0.33 × equity; otherwise keep all other rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This would only shrink the largest-position trades, so it can reduce dollar slippage and tail-dollar losses a bit. But because our share PnL scales roughly linearly with size, it mostly rescales both winners and losers. On this bot that means less volatility, not more edge; it is more of a de-leveraging rule than a breakout-quality improvement.
review.overfit_note: If fixed at one pre-committed value, there is only one knob. But the proposed 25%/33%/50% sweep is already three hypotheses, and with only 53 trades it would be easy to choose the best cap by noise.
review.expected_effect: Likely slightly lower drawdown and lower cost dollars, but also lower gross PnL. Net expectancy is probably flat to negative; at best it may smooth equity a bit.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend live unseen days on a cap sweep. If you want a sanity check, replay only one pre-committed cap (33%) against baseline on all 67 archived days, split into two halves, and require improvement in both halves on net return after costs and max drawdown, with trade count not down more than 10%. If it does not clearly beat baseline, stop.
review.verdict_reason: This is basically a de-leveraging knob. With our linear cost model and 1% risk sizing, a notional cap mostly scales the trade down; it does not fix failed breakouts, and it does not remove the cost drag that already eats the edge. On a $1k book, a 33% cap is more likely to shrink the few big winners than to rescue the bad trades, so the expected effect on performance is flat to worse.

name: Support/resistance-based stop placement
one_line: For each breakout, place the stop just beyond the nearest intraday swing point instead of always using the full opening-range opposite side.
parameter_choices: Use the nearest 5-minute swing low/high behind the breakout; test buffers of 1, 2, and 3 ticks or cents.
disagreement: Narrower stops may cut losses faster but can also increase stop-outs on noisy continuation setups.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The book supports the general principle of placing a stop just beyond nearby support/resistance. It does not specifically support an ORB rule that uses the nearest confirmed 5-minute swing point, nor does it compare that stop to the current opening-range opposite-side stop. So this is an adaptation, not direct evidence.
review.exact_rule_change: Leave entry, sizing, target, and time-stop unchanged. Replace only the stop: for a long ORB trade, set stop = highest confirmed 5-minute swing low since 9:30 whose low is below the signal-bar close, minus $0.02; for a short, set stop = lowest confirmed 5-minute swing high since 9:30 whose high is above the signal-bar close, plus $0.02. A swing low/high is a 1-bar fractal (lower/higher than the lows/highs of the bars immediately before and after it), and it must be confirmed by the next bar before it can be used. If no confirmed swing exists, fall back to the original opening-range opposite-side stop.
review.mechanism: If failed breakouts usually reverse at the nearest local pivot, this stop could invalidate the trade earlier and more naturally than waiting for the full opening-range edge to break. That might help the bot avoid some of the long, noisy drifts and late reversals that currently end in flat exits or stop-outs. But because Midas sizes to fixed dollar risk, the direct loss per stop does not shrink; the only real upside is a better invalidation point. The downside is more stop-outs and larger share count, which can raise slippage/commission.
review.data_missing: No extra data is required beyond the existing 5-minute OHLCV. The only caveat is that intrabar touch order is still approximate on 5-minute bars, but that limitation already applies to the current backtest.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the rejected list. It is distinct from the failed-breakout fade overlay and the two-close confirmation rule.
review.overfit_note: There is only one visible knob (the cents buffer), but the pivot definition can be massaged many ways and 67 sessions / 53 trades is a small sample. It would be easy to fit a stop rule that looks good on the archive and then disappears out of sample.
review.expected_effect: Small and uncertain. Best case: a modest improvement if the OR stop is systematically too wide and local pivots are the real invalidation level. More likely: roughly flat or slightly worse after costs because the tighter structural stop increases stop-outs and share count.
review.test_protocol: Fix the rule before looking, using the 2-cent buffer above. Replay all 67 archived sessions side-by-side with the baseline, using identical entries, target, time exit, commission, and slippage assumptions; only the stop changes. Primary metric: net P&L after costs per session. Secondary metrics: profit factor, max drawdown, win rate, and stop-out count. Require the variant to beat baseline on full-archive net P&L and not lose in either archive half (Jul–Aug and Sep–Oct). If it passes, paper it on the next 20 unseen sessions and keep it only if cumulative net P&L stays ahead after costs.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully feasible with the data we already have, cheap to replay, and not redundant with prior tests. The edge is probably small, but the only sensible way to kill or keep it is a paired replay on the archived days before spending any unseen sessions.

name: Historical-max exposure guardrails
one_line: Profile the historical maxima of size, traded volume, and hold-time metrics, then set live risk limits at about 150% of those maxima.
parameter_choices: For each observable metric, set alert / flatten / hard-stop thresholds at 1.0x / 1.25x / 1.5x the worst paper-trading value.
disagreement: A buffer reduces false alarms, but if the historical max was already inflated by a bad regime, the guardrail may still be too loose.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The book source does support the *general* heuristic of setting live risk limits to about 150% of observed maxima. But it is a safety rule from an author example, not evidence that this improves trading edge, and it does not specifically justify a tiered alert/flatten/hard-stop wrapper for Midas.
review.exact_rule_change: Add an exposure guardrail overlay to the existing ORB bot: track the bot’s live gross position size and elapsed holding time each session; if either reaches 1.0× its historical maximum, log an alert; at 1.25×, flatten the open position and block new entries for the rest of the day; at 1.5×, hard-stop trading until manual reset. Use the historical maximum observed in archived replay as the baseline for each metric.
review.mechanism: This is a defensive wrapper, not an alpha change. It could reduce tail damage if the bot mis-sizes, gets stuck in a runaway state, or holds far longer than normal after a logic/execution bug. It does not address the core problem of failed breakouts, and it won’t lower commissions or improve entry quality. On normal days it will mostly do nothing.
review.data_missing: No extra market data is needed for the internal replay metrics. If you meant market venue volume or order-book liquidity, we do not have L2/tick data; but for our own position size and hold-time guardrails, OHLCV replay plus our trade logs are enough.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact wrapper, but the bot already has several similar safety rails: 1% risk-to-stop sizing, cash cap/no leverage, 15:45 flat, no entries after 15:15, and a -3% day-loss halt. This proposal is mostly more monitoring around the same theme, not a new tested edge.
review.overfit_note: There are only a couple of thresholds, but they are anchored to extreme values from just 67 sessions. The historical max is a fragile statistic; one odd day can set the bar too loose or too tight. This is easy to make look sensible in-sample without changing expectancy.
review.expected_effect: Mostly no change in average PnL. Best case: it prevents a rare runaway exposure or bad-state day from becoming a bigger loss. More likely: dormant most days, and if it fires on a normal winning regime it will hurt by cutting off trades early.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend live trading days on this as an edge test. If you insist on a dry run, lock the thresholds from the first ~45 archived sessions, replay the remaining archived sessions side-by-side with the baseline, and score: net PnL after costs, max drawdown, trade count, and number of guardrail-triggered flat days. Advance only if drawdown improves without a meaningful PnL hit (e.g. >5%) and the guardrail actually catches a genuine anomaly. Then shadow the next ~20 unseen sessions before considering any live deployment.
review.verdict_reason: This does not change entry/exit quality or costs, so it is unlikely to improve expectancy on a bot that already has tight sizing and daily loss controls. With our small sample, the historical maxima are too unstable to justify new live complexity, and the guardrail will probably be dormant most of the time. Keep it as a production safety monitor if desired, but it is not worth scarce live test days.

name: Pessimistic execution stress test
one_line: Backtest each candidate with adverse slippage, latency, and fill assumptions instead of clean next-bar fills.
parameter_choices: Test entry/exit with adverse slippage of $0.02/share each side, one-bar delay, occasional partial or missed fills (e.g. 10% fill-ratio stress), and higher exit cost than entry cost.
disagreement: The books agree that live execution is worse than paper fills; they mainly differ on how pessimistic the stress should be.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books strongly agree on the ingredients: slippage must be modeled, latency matters, fees matter, and paper fills can be wildly optimistic; one source even uses a 10% fill-ratio stress example. But none of them gives this exact ORB validation harness for our 5-minute bot, so the specific delay/slippage setup is our operationalization, not a quoted rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Archive-only stress replay: fill entries at the open of the second 5-minute bar after the signal (t+2 open instead of the current next-bar-open fill), and widen slippage to $0.04/share per side on all filled orders; keep commissions unchanged. Do not include partial fills in the base test.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha; it tries to remove fake alpha. If the ORB only looks good with clean fills, this stress will strip out the marginal winners and show us which variants are too execution-sensitive for a $1,000 book. The win is fewer false positives and fewer live days wasted on fragile breakouts.
review.data_missing: We can replay the extra-bar delay and fixed slippage from 5-minute OHLCV, but we cannot estimate true partial/missed fills, queue position, bid-ask spread, or market impact without tick data, L2/quotes, or actual execution logs.
review.already_tried_note: Midas already includes explicit commission and $0.02/share slippage in the live recipe and the reported results are net of costs. What has not been tried is an additional latency stress and a harsher adverse-fill replay; partial fills remain unmodeled.
review.overfit_note: Only two knobs if fixed upfront, but they are still arbitrary stress levels. It would be easy to keep turning pessimism up or down until a candidate looks good or bad, so the settings must be frozen before inspection.
review.expected_effect: Backtest PnL, PF, and win rate should fall; some marginal ORB variants will flip negative. If a variant still survives this stress, it is more believable live. The main effect is stricter screening, not a direct improvement in raw edge.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the stress settings before looking. Replay all 67 archived sessions side-by-side with the baseline, then compare stress-adjusted net PnL, profit factor, max drawdown, and trade count. A candidate passes only if it stays profitable in both halves of the archive and does not depend on a handful of oversized winners. If it passes, log the same comparison on the next ~20 unseen sessions before any live change.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap to run, no new market data required for the implementable part, and directly relevant to our main failure mode: apparent edges that evaporate under worse execution. It will not create alpha by itself, but it is worth adding as a gate before we spend more live days on new variants.

name: Delay entries away from the open
one_line: Push breakout entries later so the first wide-spread minutes of the session can pass before execution.
parameter_choices: Test a 1-bar delay after breakout first, then 2 bars, then a strict no-entry window before 10:30; optionally also stop new entries after 15:00.
disagreement: All sources say the open is expensive, but they do not agree on the best cutoff; too much delay can also kill a speed-sensitive edge.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
