The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books do support the general execution warning that early-session trading is more expensive and that later entries can reduce spread/slippage. One source even suggests a later-entry test with a 10:30 cutoff. But none of the sources provide direct evidence that Midas’ specific opening-range breakout edge survives a 30-minute delay; another source also warns that execution delay can quickly destroy edge.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a time gate to the existing ORB: after the 9:30-10:00 opening range is formed, only allow the first breakout entry if the signal occurs at or after 10:30 New York time. If the first valid breakout happens before 10:30, skip it and stay flat unless a later valid breakout appears after 10:30. Keep all other rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could reduce the worst early-session whipsaws and any hidden wide-spread/slippage period, so it might lower immediate stop-outs and a bit of cost drag. The downside is that Midas is a speed-sensitive momentum setup: waiting until 10:30 may miss the move that pays, make the stop farther from the entry, and shrink position size. So the likely effect is fewer trades, possibly a slightly higher win rate, but also lower average R and possibly worse net P&L.
review.data_missing: No extra data is needed to replay the rule change on our 5-minute bars. However, to validate the stated spread/slippage rationale directly, we would need tick, bid-ask, or L2 data, which we do not have.
review.already_tried_note: Not the exact same rule, but the closest analogue was the rejected 'two consecutive closes beyond the range before entry' confirmation delay. This is the same family of 'wait longer before entering,' just expressed as a clock cutoff instead of bar confirmation.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob if we fix the cutoff at 10:30, but time cutoffs are easy to data-mine on a 67-session sample. If someone starts sweeping 1-bar, 2-bar, 10:30, 15:00, etc., this becomes classic overfit territory fast.
review.expected_effect: Most likely fewer entries and slightly better fills/less early fakeout damage, but also lower capture of the few trades that actually run. Net effect is uncertain and may well be negative once the lost winners are counted.
review.test_protocol: Fix the cutoff at 10:30 before looking at results. Replay baseline vs. the 10:30-filtered version on all archived days. Compare net $/session after costs, avg R/trade, win rate, profit factor, and max drawdown, with a guardrail that trade count should not collapse materially versus baseline (for example, no more than a 25-30% drop). Require the modified rule to improve both halves of the archived sample, not just the full sample. Only if it does, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly not an execution fix for Midas, because the bot already waits until after the open to define the range and enter. A 10:30 cutoff mainly acts as a signal filter and is likely to throw away the few big breakout winners that make the strategy pay. We also do not have spread/tick data to prove the claimed cost benefit, and the closest existing delay/confirmation test already hurt. Too much downside for too little expected gain.

name: Seasonality-adjust the in-play volume filter
one_line: Measure the opening volume burst against each stock’s own intraday profile instead of only against a flat trailing average.
parameter_choices: Replace the 9:30-10:00 relative-volume test with a per-symbol intraday profile from the last 10 sessions, using 5-minute buckets or the first 30 minutes versus the stock’s own average time-of-day curve.
disagreement: No direct disagreement; the only choice is which intraday window to normalize against.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book excerpt supports the general idea of intraday normalization profiles, but it does not state this exact in-play volume screen. The second source only gives indirect support that dense early-session activity changes impact; it is not direct evidence for this filter change.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace step 2’s raw 9:30–10:00 relative-volume gate with a seasonality-adjusted opening-volume ratio: for each symbol, use the prior 10 regular sessions to build the average 5-minute volume profile for the 9:30, 9:35, 9:40, 9:45, 9:50, and 9:55 buckets; define expected opening volume as the sum of those six bucket averages. At 10:00, compute adjusted RV = actual 9:30–10:00 volume / expected opening volume. Keep the existing 1.5 cutoff and top-8 ranking by adjusted RV; leave all other rules unchanged. If a symbol has fewer than 10 prior sessions, it is not eligible until the warm-up is complete.
review.mechanism: This could help by separating genuinely unusual early participation from a stock’s normal opening burst. Right now a name can look ‘in play’ just because it is always active at 9:30. A per-stock time-of-day profile should rank names better, so the bot trades fewer routine openings and more true surprise-volume breakouts. That should mainly reduce failed-breakout stop-outs and some flat exits; it may also trim trade count a bit, with only a small direct effect on costs.
review.data_missing: None for the test itself. We can compute this from the existing 5-minute regular-session OHLCV, using the prior 10 sessions per symbol. No pre-market, L2, news, float, or other external data is required.
review.already_tried_note: The bot already uses an opening relative-volume gate, so this is a refinement of an existing selection rule. However, a seasonality-adjusted intraday profile has not been explicitly tried or rejected in the list.
review.overfit_note: There are not many free knobs if we lock the lookback at 10 sessions and keep the 1.5 cutoff, but the per-symbol profile is still noisy on only 67 days and can be overfit if we start tweaking bucketization or thresholds after seeing results.
review.expected_effect: Most likely a small improvement, if any. Best case: fewer routine high-volume names qualify, the trade list gets cleaner, stop-outs fall a bit, and win rate improves without killing trade count. Worst case: it just filters out good trades and lowers activity. I would not expect a huge edge by itself.
review.test_protocol: Run a deterministic side-by-side replay on all 67 archived sessions with every other rule held fixed and costs unchanged. Do not tune the 1.5 threshold or the 10-session lookback on the archive; lock the rule first. Primary metric: net PnL after costs per session. Secondary metrics: profit factor, stop rate, full-target rate, flat-at-close rate, trade count, and max drawdown. Require the variant to beat baseline in both chronological halves of the archive on net PnL/session, while keeping trade count within 85% to 115% of baseline. If it passes, paper trade it on the next ~20 unseen sessions before adopting it.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with data we already have, cheap to replay, and it is a real change to an existing weak point rather than a new strategy. The support is only partial and the expected lift is probably small, but this is exactly the kind of low-cost filter refinement worth testing before spending time on more complex ideas.

name: Filter out high-spread, low-liquidity names
one_line: Prune the in-play list using spread and liquidity proxies before any breakout logic runs.
parameter_choices: Raise the minimum yesterday dollar volume from $20M to a higher floor, drop the worst OHLC-spread-proxy names, and test a higher price floor for the play batch.
disagreement: Price floor is only a proxy for liquidity; if a spread estimate is available, it should outrank price alone.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books support the general principle that liquidity and spread matter, and one excerpt gives an OHLC-based spread proxy. But none of the sources state this exact pre-ORB filter or these exact thresholds, so the support is related rather than direct.
review.exact_rule_change: Before the 10:00 in-play ranking, tighten the play-batch filter to yesterday close >= $30 and exclude any candidate whose 20-day median Corwin-Schultz OHLC spread proxy is > 5%. Then keep the existing relative-volume ranking and the rest of the ORB rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This should remove names where spread and thin trading are doing more damage than the breakout edge can pay for. On this bot, that mainly means fewer bad fills, fewer immediate stop-outs that were really spread/impact noise, and slightly cleaner breakouts. The trade-off is fewer signals, so the only way this helps is if net expectancy per trade rises enough to offset the lower count.
review.data_missing: True bid-ask spread and Level 2 depth are unavailable, so we can only use an OHLC-based spread proxy. That is enough to test the proposed filter, but it will be noisier than real spread data.
review.already_tried_note: We already tried broader universe pruning via price caps and tighter name selection, and that family of ideas was not good. What has not been tried is this specific OHLC spread-proxy filter, so it is not a duplicate, but it is close enough that I would not expect a huge effect.
review.overfit_note: Only two tunable thresholds here, but with just 53 trades on 67 sessions it is still easy to fit a cutoff to the archive. Fix the thresholds up front and do not optimize them on the backtest.
review.expected_effect: Modest chance of better net expectancy and lower drawdown, mostly from lower slippage and fewer cost-dominated losers. Gross P&L may drop if the filter removes some good momentum names, so this is more of a cost-cleanup than a new alpha source.
review.test_protocol: Fix the rule now and replay all 67 archived sessions side-by-side with the baseline. Compare net P&L after costs, expectancy per trade, profit factor, max drawdown, trade count, and the number of days with fewer than 2 qualified names. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just overall. I would only keep it if net P&L/session improves, max drawdown is no worse, and trade count stays above 80% of baseline. If it passes the archive, paper trade the next ~20 unseen sessions without retuning, which should give roughly 15-20 trades.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, computable from the data we already have, and directly targets the bot's main weakness: costs and thin-name failures. It is not a guaranteed win and could starve the universe, but that is exactly why it is worth one clean test now rather than more discussion.

name: Cap size by Q/ADV and volatility
one_line: Reduce or skip trades when estimated impact from liquidity and volatility is too large.
parameter_choices: Use a square-root cost screen such as TC≈0.33σ√(Q/ADV)+0.5 spread, cap Q/ADV explicitly at small fractions like 0.5%, 1%, and 2%, and size down high-volatility names.
disagreement: The exact cost curve differs across sources, but all agree costs rise nonlinearly with size and volatility.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general principle: transaction costs and market impact rise nonlinearly with relative size (Q/ADV) and volatility, and square-root/power-law cost models are standard. They do not state this exact Midas rule or show that a 0.5%/1%/2% cap improves an ORB on a $1k book.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a pre-trade liquidity cap: compute 20-session ADV from summed regular-session 5-minute volume. If the planned entry notional is >1% of ADV, cut size to 1% of ADV; if it is >2% of ADV, skip the trade. Do not add a separate volatility filter yet; the current stop-based sizing already shrinks size when the range/volatility is wider.
review.mechanism: If it helps at all, it would only be by reducing slippage/impact on the rare thin or very hot names, which could prevent a marginal breakout from becoming a post-cost loser. On this bot, though, the effect is likely tiny because positions are already small, the universe is already liquidity-screened, and volatility is already partly embedded in the stop-based position size. So this mostly targets costs, not the failed-breakout problem.
review.data_missing: We can compute ADV from the 5-minute volume bars and volatility from daily closes, but we do not have bid-ask spreads, level 2, pre-market volume/highs, or true execution data, so the square-root cost estimate cannot be calibrated exactly. The first 20 sessions also need a burn-in for the rolling ADV.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly. The closest prior tests were universe pruning via top-5 only and price caps, which are selection rules, not a post-signal liquidity/impact screen.
review.overfit_note: If we start tuning 0.5% vs 1% vs 2% caps on only 67 sessions, we will mostly fit noise. Worse, the cap is unlikely to bind often enough to give a stable estimate of any real improvement.
review.expected_effect: Likely near zero on trade count and PnL. Best case: a tiny reduction in slippage on rare illiquid prints. More likely: no measurable change because the cap will almost never bind.
review.test_protocol: Do not live-test first. Run a cheap archived-day diagnostic with the fixed 1%/2% ADV cap and count how many trades would be resized or skipped. If fewer than about 5% of trades change, kill the idea. If it does bind, replay all 67 archived sessions side-by-side with baseline and compare net PnL/day after costs, average slippage/share, trade count, and max drawdown in both chronological halves. Only if both halves improve should you forward-test on the next ~20 unseen days.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly a cost-screen idea, not a signal edge, and our orders are far too small relative to ADV for a 1%/2% Q/ADV cap to matter on the current universe. The bot already sizes down when volatility widens via the stop distance, and we lack spread data to calibrate the square-root model properly. So the change is very likely to be redundant and too weak to move the needle.

name: Use marketable limits or IOC fills
one_line: Try limit/IOC execution at the trigger instead of unconditional market fills.
parameter_choices: Test limit orders at the breakout price, marketable limit orders with IOC/FOK behavior, and a rule that cancels the order if it has not filled promptly.
disagreement: Limit orders lower slippage but can miss fills; passive execution is good only when urgency is low, while strong momentum may justify crossing the spread.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books support the general execution principle: limit orders can lower transaction costs but may not fill, and IOC/FOK can avoid partial fills. None of the sources specifically study 5-minute ORB breakout entries on liquid US stocks, so applying this to Midas is an extrapolation, not a directly supported rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Not a new strategy; change only entry execution. On a valid ORB breakout, submit an IOC aggressive limit order instead of a next-bar market fill: long = buy limit at OR high + $0.01, short = sell-short limit at OR low - $0.01. If the order is not fully filled immediately, cancel it and skip the trade.
review.mechanism: This could shave a little entry slippage and avoid paying up on thin opens. But for Midas the main trade-off is worse participation: the strongest breakouts move fast, so a limit/IOC can miss the few winners that drive the PnL while saving only pennies on the many small trades. It does not address failed breakouts or flat exits; it mostly changes cost drag.
review.data_missing: We need at least NBBO/quote or tick data to know whether the aggressive limit would have filled, partially filled, or missed, and at what price. Five-minute OHLCV alone cannot reconstruct queue position, spread, or true IOC behavior.
review.already_tried_note: The frozen bot uses next-bar market-style fills. We have not previously tested limit/IOC entry execution as a separate rule.
review.overfit_note: Only one or two knobs on paper, but with 67 sessions the apparent edge will be dominated by how we assume fills happen. It is easy to pick an optimistic fill model that looks better in-sample without being tradeable.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small reduction in per-share slippage, but also a lower fill rate and fewer trades. On this bot the benefit is probably too small to move the needle unless current fills are much worse than assumed; the missed-breakout cost could easily outweigh the cost savings.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend live days on this with current data. If you still want an offline sanity check, compare baseline next-bar market fills vs the IOC limit variant on all archived sessions, but treat it only as an upper/lower bound because true fill quality is unobservable. Success metric would be net $/signal after costs plus fill rate, with no deterioration in max drawdown. Only revisit as a live test after adding tick/NBBO data, and then require at least ~25 actual forward fills plus the same sign of improvement in both halves of the archive before promoting it.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly an execution-microstructure idea, and we do not have the data to measure it properly. With only 5-minute OHLCV, we cannot know whether an IOC/limit would have filled or missed, so any backtest would be fantasy. The likely dollar savings on ~$500 positions are also too small to justify scarce unseen days, especially because the bot's edge already comes from a few rare winners that a more restrictive entry could miss.

name: Slice larger orders across a few bars
one_line: For bigger fills, execute in a small number of child orders over the next 10-20 minutes instead of all at once.
parameter_choices: Test 2 slices vs 3 vs 4 over the next 10-20 minutes; compare equal TWAP, volume-weighted VWAP, and a front-loaded schedule, and only use this on high-liquidity names or larger notionals.
disagreement: The literature is mixed: equal slices are best under simple linear impact, VWAP works when volume is predictable, front-loaded schedules reduce risk, and some evidence says fewer child orders can cut impact.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general execution family—TWAP, VWAP, front-loaded schedules, and child-order slicing—but they do not directly show that slicing helps Midas. The closest empirical claim even says fewer child orders can reduce impact, so the case for slicing our orders is an extrapolation, not a direct match.
review.exact_rule_change: For any entry or exit with estimated notional > $600, replace the single next-bar-open fill with 3 equal child orders sent at the opens of the next three 5-minute bars (about 15 minutes total). Do not add VWAP or front-loading in the first test.
review.mechanism: Could lower implementation shortfall on the rare larger fills. But Midas's losses are mainly failed breakouts and flat exits, not tape impact, and delaying the full fill by 10–15 minutes is more likely to miss continuation or worsen reversals than save enough slippage to matter.
review.data_missing: We can do a coarse replay from 5-minute bars, but we do not have tick, quote, spread, or book-depth data, so we cannot measure true market impact or validate VWAP/front-loaded variants realistically.
review.already_tried_note: Nothing in the rejected list is a staged-execution experiment.
review.overfit_note: Several knobs are hiding here (threshold, number of slices, schedule shape, entry vs exit). With only 67 sessions and tiny expected savings, it is easy to tune to noise.
review.expected_effect: Likely flat to slightly negative. At best it trims a few cents of slippage on the rare larger order; more likely the extra 10–15 minutes of price risk outweighs the savings.
review.test_protocol: If we insist on testing, precommit before looking: threshold = $600 notional, 3 equal slices, next three 5-minute bar opens only. Replay all archived days against the current one-shot baseline. Score net P&L after all costs, average implementation shortfall per share, and gross expectancy, split between the first and second halves of the archive. Require the sliced version to improve both halves and to do so on at least 20 qualifying orders; otherwise reject and do not spend unseen days.
review.verdict_reason: This is the wrong lever for Midas. Our orders are too small for impact reduction to matter much, we lack quote/tick data to validate the savings, and the extra delay is more likely to hurt breakout capture than help. Use one-shot fills unless order size becomes materially larger.

name: Require expected move to exceed all-in costs
one_line: Skip breakouts unless the implied move is comfortably larger than commissions, spread, and slippage.
parameter_choices: Use a cost-to-edge threshold like expected breakout travel / estimated round-trip cost > 1.5x, 2x, or 3x; optionally add a fixed dollar buffer on top.
disagreement: Whether the gate should be based on a fixed dollar buffer or a volatility-scaled expected-edge ratio.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books support the general premise that spread/commission/slippage and high turnover can destroy small edges. They do not specifically propose an ORB-specific "expected move / cost" gate, so this is our adaptation rather than a directly sourced rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the existing ORB entry logic, but add a pre-entry cost gate after the 9:30–10:00 opening range is set: estimate round-trip friction per share as `0.0005 × signal_price + 0.04` (0.05% round-trip commission plus $0.02/share slippage in and out). Estimate the trade’s available move per share as `2.5 × opening_range_width` (the current target). Only take the breakout if `2.5 × OR_width / (0.0005 × signal_price + 0.04) >= 2.0`; otherwise skip that name for the day.
review.mechanism: This is a cost-hygiene filter. It should remove narrow-range or high-priced breakouts where the full 2.5R target is too small relative to friction, which is where this bot is most likely to waste fills on noise, get flattened, or hand profits back to slippage/commission. Best case: fewer marginal trades, better net expectancy, slightly fewer flat exits and stop-outs. Worst case: we just cut trade count and lose some good but small setups.
review.data_missing: No extra data are required for this proxy version. Literal options-implied move is unavailable, so we are using the opening-range target distance as the move proxy.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly. The closest prior work was universe pruning, price caps, and stricter confirmation rules, but nothing explicitly gating trades by estimated all-in cost versus expected move.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob if you fix the formula, but the threshold can still be tuned to the 67-day archive and may just fit one bad volatility regime. Lock the 2.0x cutoff before looking at results.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small-to-moderate improvement if the cutoff is conservative: fewer cost-dominated trades, slightly better profit factor, and lower drag from flat-at-close exits. I would not expect a huge jump in edge; this is a filter, not new alpha.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the threshold at 2.0x before looking. Replay all archived days side by side against the current bot, using identical entry/exit logic except for this added gate. Compare net PnL after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, average trade return, trade count, and the share of trades that end flat at 15:45. Require improvement in both chronological halves of the archive, not just the full sample. If it clears that bar, paper-trade the next 20 unseen sessions; accept only if cumulative net PnL stays ahead of baseline and drawdown does not worsen materially while trade count does not collapse.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully computable from the data and cost assumptions we already have, cheap to replay, and directly attacks the known cost drag on a weak edge. The expected gain is probably modest, but this is a sensible filter test rather than a speculative new strategy.

name: Volatility-scaled breakout buffer
one_line: Require the breakout to clear the opening range by a volatility-based margin, and optionally probe with half size before committing full size.
parameter_choices: Threshold in ATR or realized intraday volatility units; probe size 25%-50%; add-on only after one confirming 5-minute bar.
disagreement: Whether the buffer should be based on ATR, bar-range percentile, or realized mid-quote volatility.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the *general* ingredients, not this exact ORB rule. B1-c001-08 says intraday returns can be normalized by mid-quote volatility, which loosely supports a volatility-scaled trigger. B1-c028-02 supports no-trade regions and partial scale-in/scale-out under transaction costs. Neither source specifically endorses an opening-range breakout buffer or a half-size probe on this bot.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current raw OR breakout entry with a buffered, two-step entry: after 10:00 NY, a long trigger requires a 5-minute close at least 0.25 × the current opening-range width (OR high minus OR low) above OR high; shorts are symmetric below OR low. Enter 50% of the intended position at the next bar open. If the next 5-minute close is still beyond the same buffered level in the same direction, add the remaining 50% at the following open. Keep the existing stop at the opposite side of the OR, 2.5R target, SPY filter, gap filters, and flat-at-15:45 rule unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is meant to cut the bot’s weakest trades: breakouts that barely poke through the range and immediately snap back. The buffer should filter out noisy breaks, and the half-size probe limits damage if the move is fake. If it works, the gains come from fewer stop-outs and fewer low-quality fills; the trade-off is missing some winners and possibly lowering trade count.
review.data_missing: No extra data are needed for the OR-width version. We can compute the buffer from the existing 5-minute regular-session bars. If you wanted true ATR or mid-quote volatility, that data is not available.
review.already_tried_note: The closest rejected test was requiring two consecutive closes beyond the range before entry. That overlaps with the confirmation leg here, but this proposal is not identical because it enters earlier with half size and adds only after confirmation.
review.overfit_note: Two knobs are enough to overfit 67 sessions if we sweep them: the buffer multiple and the probe fraction. This can easily be tuned to the past noise unless we pre-fix the numbers and keep the search very coarse.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, fewer immediate reversals, and lower cost drag per attempted breakout. Best case: stop-outs fall more than targets do, so net expectancy improves. Worst case: we just miss some of the few big winners and lose edge by being too selective.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the rule exactly as above before looking at results. Replay it on all archived days side-by-side with the baseline. Compare net PnL after costs, profit factor, average trade, stop rate, target rate, max drawdown, and trade count. Require the modified version to improve in both halves of the archive, not just overall, and to avoid a major trade-count collapse (roughly more than 20% is a warning). If it passes on the archive, run it unchanged on the next ~20 unseen sessions and compare against the frozen baseline.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with current data, cheap to replay, and directly aimed at the bot’s main failure mode (failed breakouts and cost drag). The support is only partial and the overfit risk is high, but it is still concrete enough to justify one disciplined test rather than a rejection.

name: Chronological walk-forward holdout
one_line: Freeze a true forward holdout and validate each tweak only on later unseen sessions, ideally with rolling walk-forward blocks.
parameter_choices: 80/20 or 70/30 chronological split; 2 or 3 sets; rolling monthly/yearly walk-forward; keep one final untouched holdout.
disagreement: Books agree on chronological validation, but vary on split ratios and whether to use one holdout or rolling blocks.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: Multiple sources explicitly recommend chronological in-sample/out-of-sample separation, untouched holdouts, and rolling walk-forward validation for trading strategies. The support is direct for the evaluation protocol, though not for any trading alpha rule.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to the trading logic; change only the research gate: for every candidate tweak, fit on the first 70% of archived sessions, validate only on the final 30% chronological holdout (shuffle=False), and require a second check with rolling monthly walk-forward blocks before promotion.
review.mechanism: This does not create edge by itself. It reduces false positives from data snooping, so fewer weak tweaks get promoted and then fail live. The payoff is a more honest estimate of whether a rule actually helps our failed-breakout rate, target capture, and after-cost expectancy.
review.data_missing: None. We can do this with the existing chronological 5-minute archive and daily closes; no pre-market, L2, news, float, or options data are required. The sample is thin, but the protocol is feasible.
review.already_tried_note: We already have time-ordered live paper results, but not a formal frozen holdout plus rolling walk-forward gate for candidate tweaks. So the discipline is partly in place, but the full protocol is not yet being enforced.
review.overfit_note: The method itself has almost no alpha knobs; it is specifically designed to reduce overfitting. The only real risk is choosing split dates after looking at results.
review.expected_effect: It should not directly improve the bot’s trade quality. It will usually make backtest claims look worse, but more believable, and should prevent us from wasting live tests on noise.
review.test_protocol: Retrospectively replay the current recipe and any candidate tweak under two schemes on the same archive: (A) pooled/full-sample fit and (B) strict chronological validation with a 70/30 split, then a rolling monthly walk-forward check. Compare holdout net P&L after costs, profit factor, and t-stat; a tweak only survives if it stays positive on the holdout and does not flip sign across the walk-forward blocks. Minimum sample for the retrospective gate is the current 67 sessions; then require confirmation on the next 20 unseen sessions before promoting anything.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and standard practice. It is not an alpha idea, but it is exactly the right research-control change for this bot, and it uses data we already have.

name: Paper-trade pilot with production-like instrumentation
one_line: Run each new rule in a low-risk paper phase using the same logs, order IDs, and post-trade code path you would use live.
parameter_choices: minimal risk for 10-20 unseen sessions before scaling; compare intended vs actual orders; use the same post-trade infrastructure and regression tests as production.
disagreement: No real disagreement on the principle; some sources emphasize paper trading first, others emphasize production-identical simulation and logging.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources directly recommend paper/forward testing, starting new deployments at the least risk possible, using unique market-facing order IDs, comparing logs to intended orders, and building production-like historical playback. This proposal is basically a synthesis of those validation practices rather than an extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a mandatory deployment gate for every new Midas rule: run it paper-only for 10 unseen sessions at minimum possible size (1 share or the smallest notional the bot can place), using the same live order-routing/post-trade code path, globally unique order IDs, and full intent-vs-fill logging before any promotion to normal size.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha by itself. It reduces implementation drift, duplicate/late orders, look-ahead mistakes, and fill surprises, which is a real leak on a small $1,000 book. It should improve realized results indirectly by catching bad rules and buggy execution before they contaminate live PnL.
review.data_missing: The bar data is enough to generate intended signals, but the key validation metric needs actual order/fill logs, order timestamps, and intended-vs-actual decision records from the paper/live simulator. Those logs are not in the market data archive and must be instrumented.
review.already_tried_note: We already operate a paper-trading research bot, so the general idea of forward testing is not new. But the stricter production-identical logging, unique order-ID discipline, and daily intended-vs-actual diff are not listed as already tried and rejected.
review.overfit_note: Almost no tunable knobs: pilot length and pilot size. This is process validation, not signal fitting. The main risk is false confidence from too short a pilot, not overfitting the 67 archived days.
review.expected_effect: Neutral to short-run PnL, but better plumbing: fewer reconciliation errors, fewer silent execution bugs, tighter backtest-to-paper correspondence, and faster rejection of bad strategy changes. It should reduce wasted tests, not raise expectancy on its own.
review.test_protocol: First replay the full archived history with the new instrumentation turned on and assert the outputs are identical to the baseline: same signals, same order IDs, same intended stops/targets, no look-ahead, no duplicate IDs. Then run the next 10 unseen sessions in paper mode at minimum size. Success metrics: zero unintended order mismatches, zero duplicate/reused order IDs, no side/size/stop/target drift versus the intended order trail, and a small backtest-vs-paper PnL gap after costs. If the paper path diverges, fix plumbing before testing any new alpha idea. If the pilot produces very few trades, extend to 20 sessions before deciding.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible, and directly aligned with the bot's biggest non-alpha risk: live/backtest mismatch. It is not a new trading edge, but it is valuable validation infrastructure and can be implemented immediately without extra market data.

name: Pessimistic execution and cost model
one_line: Stress-test the backtest with harsher fills, explicit costs, and latency/impact assumptions instead of perfect bar fills.
parameter_choices: round-trip commission about 5 bps; slippage $0.02/share; next-bar-open or worse fills; queue/latency delay; missed fills penalized at close; dynamic slippage on fast/high-range opens.
disagreement: Some books treat bar-level backtests as a practical screen, while others want exchange-like matching or book replay; use simple bars for screening and pessimistic fills for final validation.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books clearly argue for realistic execution modeling—latency, FIFO priority, slippage, fees, market impact—and warn that perfect-fill replay is too optimistic. They do not prescribe our exact one-bar-late stress test or close-penalty rule; that part is our conservative proxy because we lack tick/L2 data.
review.exact_rule_change: Not a new trading strategy: add a fixed 1-bar execution latency to the replay. For every ORB entry and exit, fill at the open two 5-minute bars after the signal bar instead of one, while keeping the existing 0.05% round-trip commission and $0.02/share slippage. Any order that cannot be cleanly filled under this delayed model is marked at the session close.
review.mechanism: This is mainly a guardrail, not alpha. It tests whether the current ORB edge survives slower, worse fills on a small book where costs matter a lot. If the edge disappears when we add one bar of latency, the apparent win rate is probably fragile and not worth trusting live; if it survives, we have more confidence that the edge is real.
review.data_missing: We can do the delayed-fill replay from 5-minute OHLCV, but we cannot calibrate true queue priority, bid-ask spread, or real latency/impact without tick data or L2. So this is a coarse stress test, not a microstructure-accurate simulation.
review.already_tried_note: The live recipe already uses next-bar-open fills plus explicit commission and slippage, so the core cost-aware idea is already in place. What has not been tried is the extra latency stress on top of that.
review.overfit_note: Low if the 1-bar delay is frozen before looking at results. The main risk is not classical alpha overfit; it is choosing an arbitrary haircut that is too harsh to be informative. Do not tune the delay to force the strategy to fail.
review.expected_effect: Likely lowers measured P&L, win rate, and profit factor, but that is useful if it filters out fragile breakouts and prevents us from approving rules that only work under optimistic fills.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the delay rule before inspection. Replay the current baseline ORB and the stressed-fill version on all 67 archived sessions, then split the sample in half and check both halves separately. Compare net P&L after costs, profit factor, average $/trade, max drawdown, and the sign of expectancy. Keep the change only if the stressed version remains profitable in both halves and does not materially change the ranking of candidate variants. Then forward-test the accepted variant on the next ~20 unseen trading days; if live results fall outside the stressed-backtest band, reject or tighten the execution assumptions.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible now, cheap to run, and directly relevant to our cost-sensitive setup. It will not create alpha, but it can stop us from trusting optimistic fills. The main caveat is that we already model next-bar fills and costs, so this is a validation overlay rather than a new trading edge.

name: Data-quality gate for bars and timestamps
one_line: Reject symbols or days with bad timestamps, missing bars, weird candles, or unadjusted prices before any test or trade.
parameter_choices: strictly increasing 5-minute timestamps; no missing intraday bars in-session; distinguish expected weekend/holiday gaps from errors; use adjusted daily closes for cross-day calculations; cross-check against a second source when possible.
disagreement: No major disagreement; the only nuance is that some gaps are normal market closures, not data errors.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books directly recommend the component checks: strictly increasing timestamps, auditing gaps, screening out weird candles, using adjusted prices, and verifying live/sim data consistency. Turning those checks into a hard pre-trade gate is a small implementation step, not a new claim.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a hard pre-trade data gate: a symbol-day is tradable only if its regular-session 5-minute bars are complete and strictly increasing for the NYSE session calendar (78 bars on a full day; official half-days exempt), with allowed_missing_bars=0 and allowed_bad_candles=0. A bad candle means any OHLC violation or non-positive price. If any check fails, exclude that symbol for that session; if SPY fails, skip the day. Use adjusted daily closes for yesterday-close, overnight-gap, and $20 close / $20M dollar-volume filters. No imputation or forward-filling.
review.mechanism: This should not create alpha; it should stop garbage inputs from creating fake OR highs/lows, fake relative-volume ranks, and bad overnight-gap filters. That can prevent a few false breakout trades and reduce live/backtest mismatches, but on clean data the effect is likely small.
review.data_missing: We can do the timestamp, missing-bar, and candle-sanity checks from the existing 5-minute OHLCV archive. To make the daily-cross-day filters robust, we need adjusted daily closes or split/dividend factors; a second-source cross-check would also require an additional feed not currently in the stack.
review.already_tried_note: Nothing in the rejected list is a data-integrity gate. This is new hygiene, not a rehash of pet-stock ORB or exit logic.
review.overfit_note: If frozen as a zero-tolerance rule, there are essentially no fit knobs. Overfit only appears if we start inventing ad hoc exceptions for specific symbols/days after looking at results.
review.expected_effect: Small to neutral on PnL in the average case, but better data integrity and fewer bogus signals. The main benefit is robustness: fewer spurious breakouts and cleaner backtests/live alignment. If the archive is already clean, expect almost no change.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the gate with no threshold tuning, then replay all 67 archived sessions side by side with baseline. Compare: trade count, net PnL, profit factor, max drawdown, and the number of symbol-days rejected by the gate. Also inspect every rejected case to confirm it was a real anomaly, not a normal market closure or half-day. Require it to be non-worse in both halves of the archive (no meaningful PnL deterioration and no systematic drop in trade quality), then shadow it on the next ~20 unseen trading days. Because this is hygiene, not alpha, it is acceptable if it is neutral; it should not introduce false positives or material trade loss on clean days.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, feasible with our existing bar archive, and directly addresses a real source of false signals and backtest/live mismatch. It is not an alpha idea, but it is exactly the kind of guardrail that can stop us wasting tests on bad data.

name: Regime and symbol-group slicing
one_line: Report every candidate separately by regime and by symbol group instead of pooling the whole universe.
parameter_choices: mega caps vs $20-$80 play batch; high-vol vs low-vol days; trending vs choppy SPY; month-of-year; January vs non-January; event days or special-session clusters.
disagreement: Books differ on whether to segment by symbol, group, month, or volatility regime; there is no consensus on one regime definition.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: The books do support the *general* idea of splitting results by regime, subperiod, symbol, or group instead of pooling everything. They do not, however, give this exact mega-cap vs play-batch / SPY trend-vs-chop slicing as a proven trading rule. So the support is for the validation method, not for a guaranteed edge.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not pool Midas ORB results across the full universe. Pre-register two slices only: (1) symbol group = existing mega caps vs existing $20–$80 play batch; (2) regime = SPY high-vol if its 9:30–10:30 range is above its prior-20-session median, otherwise low-vol. Report performance separately for each slice, and only consider a slice-specific live rule if it beats the pooled baseline in both archive halves. Do not add month-of-year or event-day slicing in the first test.
review.mechanism: Pooling likely hides concentration: the ORB edge may live in the play batch, or only on trendier/higher-vol SPY days, while mega caps or choppy days dilute it. Slicing can show where breakouts actually follow through and where they fail, so we can stop trusting weak segments and reduce failed-breakout stops and flat closes. The segmentation itself does not improve execution; it only helps us avoid trading the wrong slice.
review.data_missing: Mega-cap vs play-batch and SPY regime slices are computable from the 5-minute OHLCV we already have. Month-of-year is also feasible. Event-day/special-session slicing would need an earnings/news/macro calendar that we do not currently have.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly. We already use SPY direction inside the entry rule and already have a fixed universe split, but we have not calibrated or validated the ORB separately by symbol group or regime.
review.overfit_note: This idea invites many possible cuts: group, volatility, trend/chop, month, January, event days, and combinations of them. With only 67 sessions / 53 trades, it is easy to find one lucky cell. Pre-registering only one group split and one regime split is essential.
review.expected_effect: Mostly diagnostic, not a direct edge. Best case: we find the ORB edge is concentrated in one group or regime, which could cut failed-breakout trades and reduce flat closes. Worst case: no slice shows durable lift, and the live bot stays unchanged.
review.test_protocol: Retrospective only first: replay all 67 archived sessions with the baseline ORB, then report pooled vs slice results for the two pre-registered slices. Compare net PnL per session, profit factor, win rate, and max drawdown with the same fees/slippage. Require the better slice to outperform the pooled baseline in both halves of the archive and have at least 10 trades per half before any live change. If that holds, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions side-by-side with baseline; otherwise keep the pooled bot and treat slicing as a diagnostic only.
review.verdict_reason: As a standalone bot change this is not an edge, just a way to look at the data. It also opens a large p-hacking surface if we start slicing by month/event/day on only 67 sessions. Use it offline to audit where the current ORB works, but do not spend scarce live-test capacity on it until one pre-declared slice already shows durable out-of-sample lift.

name: Minimum sample size before promotion
one_line: Do not accept a tweak until it has enough out-of-sample trades to separate luck from edge.
parameter_choices: 30-50 theoretical trades for an early screen; 100+ out-of-sample trades before decision; hundreds total for comfort; around 1000 signals if using raw accuracy.
disagreement: Exact thresholds vary a lot across sources, but all warn against judging from tiny samples.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)

review.source_support_note: The sources repeatedly say small samples are not reliable for trading decisions, that 30-50 theoretical trades is only an early screen, that you need hundreds / 100+ out-of-sample trades before confidence, and that raw accuracy-style evaluation should wait for very large signal counts (~1000). The exact 50/100 gate is our synthesis, but the underlying principle is directly supported.
review.exact_rule_change: Adopt a formal promotion gate: a candidate tweak may be screened after 50 theoretical trades, but it cannot replace the baseline until it has at least 100 out-of-sample trades and positive net expectancy after full costs.
review.mechanism: This reduces false promotions from noise. On a 67-session bot with only 53 trades so far, a lucky streak can easily look like edge; the gate keeps fragile entry/exit tweaks from reaching live capital, which should reduce future bad days and research churn.
review.data_missing: None for the gate itself; we can count trades from the existing replay history and future sessions.
review.already_tried_note: We already do replay-style validation and compare against baseline informally, but we have not enforced a hard minimum-trade promotion rule.
review.overfit_note: Few knobs if fixed in advance; the main risk is moving the threshold after seeing results. The threshold should be set once, not tuned to the same data.
review.expected_effect: Indirect but useful: fewer weak tweaks get promoted, so forward expectancy should be more stable and we should waste less time and capital on false edges. It does not create a new trading edge by itself.
review.test_protocol: Retrospectively apply the gate to all archived candidate tweaks: compare current ad hoc promotion vs the 50-trade screen / 100-OOS promotion rule. Success means a lower false-promotion rate and better forward expectancy among promoted tweaks, without materially rejecting the current baseline. Then lock the rule and confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions. Use net expectancy after full costs as the decision metric.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and directly targets our biggest research risk: overfitting tiny samples. It is a validation-policy change rather than a trading edge, but that is still valuable for this bot because our current sample is too small to trust ad hoc judgments.

name: Multiple-testing and complexity control
one_line: Treat many candidate filters as a joint-hypothesis problem and penalize complexity before picking a winner.
parameter_choices: bootstrap or SPA-style correction; cross-validation; AIC/BIC minimums; sequential lag testing; stop boosting when validation error stops improving.
disagreement: Books propose several tools rather than one standard method: bootstrap/SPA, CV, AIC/BIC, sequential lag tests, and early stopping for boosting.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources directly warn about data snooping and multiple-testing bias, and they explicitly recommend bootstrap/SPA-style checks, cross-validation, and parsimony. The exact 'complexity control' framing is our synthesis, but the underlying validation logic is squarely supported.
review.exact_rule_change: Change the research gate, not the live signal: when testing any batch of new Midas filters/exits, promote only the simplest candidate that still beats the current recipe after a 5% SPA/bootstrap multiple-testing correction; if none survive, keep the baseline unchanged.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha by itself; it prevents us from mistaking one lucky tweak for a real edge. On Midas, the benefit is fewer false-positive filters, less regime-specific fragility, and fewer wasted tests on ideas that only look good in the 67-day sample. It should improve the durability of future rule changes more than the current daily PnL.
review.already_tried_note: The bot already has some discipline (one change at a time), but it has not been using an explicit multiple-testing correction or complexity penalty as the promotion rule for candidate changes.
review.overfit_note: The method itself has few knobs, but it can be abused by redefining the candidate set after looking, changing the correction threshold, or keeping the search alive until something wins. The main risk is process overfit, not signal overfit.
review.expected_effect: Fewer false positives in filter/exit experiments, simpler promoted rules, and better out-of-sample durability. The tradeoff is that some backtest 'winners' will be rejected, so paper stats may look worse while live reliability improves.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the candidate list before looking at results. Re-run the full archived 67-session history and compare two selection procedures: (A) naive best-backtest pick and (B) the 5% SPA/bootstrap gate. Score each candidate by net after-cost PnL, consistency across the two halves of the archive, and how often a candidate would have been promoted under (A) but failed under (B). The method passes if (B) rejects more historical false positives without losing the genuinely positive variants. Then run the promoted rule, with no retuning, on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible with our OHLCV archive, and directly targeted at our biggest small-sample failure mode: cherry-picking a lucky tweak. It is not a trading edge, but it is exactly the right guardrail before we spend more tests on new filters and exits.

name: Monte Carlo and bootstrap robustness
one_line: Perturb prices or resample returns and rerun the full pipeline to see whether the edge survives noise.
parameter_choices: 1% blur on Close; 1000 reruns; bootstrap with replacement; compare max-drawdown clusters; apply an observed live-vs-sim haircut if needed.
disagreement: Some books prefer price blurring, others bootstrap resampling; both are trying to test fragility under small perturbations.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources do support Monte Carlo blurring of prices and bootstrap resampling as backtest-validation tools. They do not show that this creates trading edge; they only justify it as a robustness check / research filter, not as a live-trading rule.
review.exact_rule_change: No live-trading rule change. Use this only as an offline acceptance gate for future Midas tweaks: rerun the full ORB backtest 1,000 times with a 1% normal blur applied to the OHLC-derived trigger/fill prices, and also bootstrap the observed daily trade returns with replacement. Keep a candidate only if its median net PnL and profit factor remain above the unperturbed baseline after a 20% live-vs-sim haircut.
review.mechanism: It does not improve entries, exits, or costs directly. Its only benefit is to reject brittle tweaks whose apparent edge disappears when fills, trigger levels, or day order are nudged. So the bucket it moves is 'fewer bad tests / fewer false positives,' not better live performance.
review.data_missing: None for the stress test itself. We have 5-minute OHLCV and trade logs sufficient to blur prices and bootstrap returns. If we wanted true microstructure realism (spread, L2, tick fills), that data is missing, but it is not required for this validation gate.
review.already_tried_note: Not among the rejected trading rules. This is a research-validation method, not one of the live entry/exit variants already tested.
review.overfit_note: Very easy to tune the blur size, distribution, resampling unit, and acceptance threshold until a favored tweak 'passes.' With only 67 archived sessions, this can easily become a story-confirmation tool rather than a genuine robustness check.
review.expected_effect: No direct uplift in live PnL. At best it reduces wasted development time and may stop us from promoting fragile tweaks; at worst it rejects good but noisy edges. It does not address failed breakouts, flat exits, or transaction costs by itself.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend scarce unseen trading days on the method itself. Use it only as an offline gate: replay the current baseline and each future candidate on all archived days, generate 1,000 perturbed runs with 1% normal price blur, and bootstrap daily returns with replacement. Compare candidate vs baseline on median net PnL, profit factor, max drawdown, and the 25th/5th percentile outcomes after the standard costs plus a 20% haircut. Minimum sample for the gate is the full archived history we already have; if a candidate passes, then test the actual trading rule on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: This is not a trading change, so it cannot improve the bot's live edge by itself. It is a useful internal validation procedure, but allocating the bot's change budget or scarce unseen-day test budget to it would not tell us anything new about execution, costs, or alpha.

name: Stationarity-aware overlays
one_line: If you add regime or volatility overlays, build them from lagged, differenced, or residualized series rather than raw levels.
parameter_choices: first differences; seasonal differences; regression residuals; lagged volatility only; ADF checks; ACF/PACF screens with ±2/sqrt(T) bands.
disagreement: Books broadly agree raw levels are dangerous, but differ on whether to start with differencing, residualization, or a unit-root test.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books support the statistical principle: use returns/differences/residuals and lagged volatility instead of raw price levels, and treat stationarity diagnostics as a validation step. They do not provide direct evidence that this improves ORB PnL; that trading link is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add one pre-entry market-regime gate: compute SPY’s 60-session EWMA of close-to-close volatility using only data through yesterday; if that lagged volatility is below its 20-session median, skip all ORB trades for the day. Otherwise keep the current rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is meant to keep us out of quiet, choppy days where ORB tends to fake out and then flatten or stop out. High-volatility days should have better breakout follow-through and a better chance of reaching 2.5R. Because the filter uses only lagged returns/volatility, it avoids look-ahead and raw-level nonstationarity.
review.data_missing: None; SPY daily closes and our existing 5-minute bars are enough to compute the filter.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact gate. But the bot already uses return-based SPY confirmation and relative-volume normalization, so this is an incremental regime overlay rather than a brand-new signal family.
review.overfit_note: Only two knobs, but with 67 sessions it would be easy to tune the window/threshold after the fact. Freeze 60 and 20 before replay; do not search a grid.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades and lower costs, with fewer failed-breakout stopouts and fewer dead-flat exits on low-volatility days. If it helps, the gain should come from higher average trade quality, not more activity.
review.test_protocol: Replay baseline vs gated version on all 67 archived sessions with no parameter search. Compare net PnL after costs per session, max drawdown, and trade count, split into the first 33 and last 34 sessions. Accept only if both halves improve net PnL/session and drawdown is not worse, while trade count does not fall by more than about 20%. If it passes, run unchanged on the next 20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: This is the only concrete, data-feasible instantiation of the idea, and it is cheap to replay. It is not a guaranteed edge, but it is simple, uses only lagged data, and targets the bot’s chop/failed-breakout problem directly enough to justify one controlled test.

name: Forward-label and outcome-distribution tests
one_line: Test each setup by forward-labeling future returns and comparing outcome distributions, not just raw trade PnL.
parameter_choices: average of next N closes or mids, with N=10 in one example; classify up/down/flat using 1-2% thresholds; ANOVA on mean forward return; chi-square on 3 bins; compare calendar-day vs active-day PnL.
disagreement: Some books prefer mean-comparison tests, others contingency tables, and others expectancy-based journaling; they are complementary rather than contradictory.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The books directly support the ingredients: forward labels from the next N candles, 3-way threshold binning, ANOVA, chi-square, and active-day vs calendar-day scoring. But they present these as validation tools, not as a trading rule for Midas, so the link to a live bot change is an adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: No live entry/exit rule changes. As an offline research gate, label each entry by the average close of the next 10 five-minute bars (N=10) and classify it as up/down/flat using ±1.0% thresholds, then compare candidate variants with one-way ANOVA on forward R and a 3-bin chi-square table before any live deployment.
review.mechanism: It would help only indirectly: forward labels tell us whether an entry is producing real post-entry drift or just a noisy one-bar pop that fades into the flat exit. That can stop us from promoting filters or exits that look okay in terminal PnL but do not actually improve follow-through. It does not itself add edge or reduce costs in live trading.
review.data_missing: No extra data needed for the close-based version. If you insist on mid-price labels, we would need quote or bid-ask data, which we do not have.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. We do already inspect raw trade PnL, win rate, profit factor, and flat/stop/target breakdowns, so this is mainly a more formal way to score the same trades rather than a brand-new edge.
review.overfit_note: Low risk if N and threshold are fixed once. High risk if we search N, threshold, bin edges, and test choice on the same 53-trade sample. The method itself can become a p-hacking machine very quickly.
review.expected_effect: No direct live PnL improvement. Best case, it helps us reject weak variants sooner by showing which setups produce sustained forward drift instead of random post-entry noise. Think of it as research hygiene, not alpha.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend live unseen days on the method itself. Fix one label scheme up front: N=10 future 5-minute closes, ±1.0% bins. Replay all 67 archived sessions and compare the current ORB baseline against any candidate variant using: (1) mean forward R at the label horizon, (2) ANOVA across signal groups, and (3) a 3-bin chi-square table. Require the effect to keep the same sign in both halves of the archive and to remain visible after costs. If it only looks good on one half, discard it. Only after that should any actually changed trading rule get about 20 unseen days.
review.verdict_reason: This is a valid research and validation tool, but it is not a bot change and cannot be used as a live decision rule because the labels require future prices. With only about 53 trades, it is also easy to overfit the bins and statistical test. Use it offline if you want, but do not count it as one of our scarce live experiments.

name: Standardized performance dashboard and trade journal
one_line: Replace raw PnL-only judging with a fixed diagnostics pack and a structured trade journal for every change.
parameter_choices: net PnL after costs; trade count; exposure; expectancy; profit factor; Sharpe; Sortino; Calmar; max drawdown; win/loss sizes; exit-type breakdown; day-of-week slices; calendar-day and active-day scores.
disagreement: Books disagree on which ratio should be primary first, but they all say raw PnL alone is insufficient.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources strongly support the components: journaling, trade-level diagnostics, and risk-adjusted metrics (Sharpe/Sortino/Calmar/max drawdown), plus separate calendar-day vs active-day scoring. But none of them prescribes this exact locked dashboard package or a single fixed ranking order; that part is our synthesis.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace ad hoc PnL-only review with a locked post-run report for every replay/live day: log one structured journal row per trade (date, symbol, setup, relative-volume rank, gap, entry time, exit reason, entry/exit prices, R, costs) and emit the same diagnostics table every time: net PnL after costs, trade count, exposure, expectancy, profit factor, Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, max drawdown, win/loss sizes, exit-type breakdown, day-of-week slices, and calendar-day vs active-day scores. Do not change the metric set after seeing results.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha directly; it reduces research noise. The dashboard should show whether any tweak is really improving after-cost expectancy, whether gains come from a few target hits versus many small flats, and whether a change is just shifting PnL around while drawdown worsens. That is useful on a small book where costs already eat a big chunk of the edge.
review.data_missing: None for the dashboard itself. 5-minute OHLCV plus the replay-generated trade log are enough; no pre-market, news, L2, float, or borrow data is required.
review.already_tried_note: You already report some aggregate stats (net PnL, win rate, PF, max DD, exit counts), but not a fixed per-trade journal or a locked standardized diagnostics pack for every tweak.
review.overfit_note: There are effectively no tuning knobs if the report format is pre-committed. The only risk is metric-shopping after the fact; lock the metric order and the pass/fail rules before reviewing results.
review.expected_effect: No direct improvement to the current trading edge. The likely benefit is better decision quality on future tweaks: fewer false positives, clearer attribution of edge to targets/flats/exits, and less wasted testing.
review.test_protocol: Adopt it immediately on the 67 archived sessions and lock the metric order before inspecting any future tweak. Success criterion for the process change is completeness (all fields filled), plus the ability to reproduce the known baseline story: small number of target winners, many flat exits, and a visible August failure cluster by exit type and day-of-week. For future strategy changes, require the same dashboard to show improvement in both halves of the archive, then confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions. No extra live-trade sample is needed to adopt the dashboard itself because it does not change execution.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with the data we already have, cheap to implement, and useful as a research control. It will not itself generate alpha, but it can stop us from misreading the small sample and overvaluing tweaks on raw PnL alone.

name: Opening-bar anchoring filter
one_line: Skip days where the opening 5-minute bar is abnormally large, because the first print can anchor the rest of the session.
parameter_choices: Flag if the first 5-minute bar range or volume is above a rolling threshold, e.g. >2x the 20-day median range or above the 90th percentile.
disagreement: Whether a very large opening shock is more likely to continue or to fade.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book’s quote supports the general idea that the open can influence the rest of the day, but it does not specifically recommend filtering out large opening bars. Turning that warning into a skip rule is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00 New York, before ranking the in-play list, exclude any stock whose 9:30–9:35 range is greater than 2.0x its rolling 20-session median 9:30–9:35 range; leave the rest of the ORB rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: Large opening bars are the days where the morning shock is already extreme; on this bot those names are most likely to whipsaw back into the opening range or produce late, low-quality breakouts with wide stops. Skipping them should reduce failed-breakout stops and some flat-at-close losers, with a side benefit of slightly lower costs from fewer trades.
review.data_missing: Nothing material; 5-minute OHLCV is enough to compute the opening-bar range and the 20-session rolling median.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact pre-entry filter. We have tried stricter entry confirmation and a morning-fade idea, but not a size filter on the opening bar.
review.overfit_note: One visible knob, but the cutoff is easy to tune against only 67 sessions and the filter can quickly turn into a data-mined way of deleting bad days. If 2.0x does not work, do not start searching percentiles and multiple thresholds.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades and a modest drop in stop-outs on days with violent opens; may also cut some of the best trend days. Net effect is uncertain, but if the bad opening-shock days are the main source of reversals, the average trade should improve a bit.
review.test_protocol: Replay the baseline and the filtered version on all 67 archived sessions with the threshold fixed at 2.0x before looking. Compare after-cost net PnL/day, profit factor, max drawdown, win rate, and trade count, and require the filter to improve both the Jul–Aug and Sep–Oct halves rather than only the full sample. Because this is a skip filter, also require that it leaves at least about 40 trades in the archived sample; otherwise it is too sparse. If it passes, run the same fixed rule on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, fully computable from existing data, and it targets a real failure mode of this bot. The support is only a general anchoring warning, so it is not strong evidence, but it is worth one fixed test. Do not tune the cutoff after the fact; kill it if it does not improve both halves.

name: Bar-aggregation ablation
one_line: Compare 5-minute ORB with 10- and 15-minute aggregated bars and keep the bar size that survives costs best.
parameter_choices: Test 5 vs 10 vs 15 minute bars; compare net expectancy, win rate, and late-day fills.
disagreement: Coarser bars may cut false breakouts, but they also delay entries and may miss fast moves.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books support the *general* idea that time aggregation can smooth microstructure noise and that 5–30 minute bars are a practical intraday compromise. They do **not** specifically endorse switching an opening-range breakout system from 5-minute to 10/15-minute bars, so the link is an extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current 5-minute ORB signal with a 10-minute aggregated-bar ORB: build 10-minute bars from the existing 5-minute OHLCV, define the opening range from 9:30–10:00 NY as usual, trigger on the first 10-minute close above OR high (long) or below OR low (short), and fill at the next 10-minute bar open. Keep all other rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could help by filtering out one-bar fakeouts that are visible on 5-minute bars but do not persist for 10 minutes. On this bot, the likely gain is fewer failed-breakout stops and fewer flat-at-close trades that never really got going. The trade-off is later entries and possibly missing some fast winners, so the main question is whether the reduction in noise beats the loss of speed after costs.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. The closest prior rejection was a stricter entry rule (two consecutive closes beyond the range), but that is not the same as changing the bar aggregation.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob, but choosing among 5/10/15-minute bars on roughly 53 trades is still easy to overfit by noise. The risk is selection bias: the best-looking bar size on 67 days may not hold up once the market regime changes.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer false-breakout entries and a higher win rate, but also fewer trades and later fills. Net P&L could improve if the current edge is mostly coming from noisy 5-minute breakouts that reverse; if the bot already needs speed to capture its winners, performance may worsen.
review.test_protocol: Run a side-by-side replay on all archived days for 5-minute, 10-minute, and 15-minute bars with every other rule frozen. Judge by net expectancy after costs first, then win rate, profit factor, max drawdown, and trade count. Also inspect the mix of outcomes (stops vs targets vs flats) because this idea is about filtering noise, not just raw P&L. Before looking at unseen days, require the winner to beat the 5-minute baseline in both halves of the archived sample (first ~33 days and last ~34 days) on net expectancy after costs, not just on total profit. If one bar size clearly wins, lock it and confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully feasible with the data we already have, cheap to replay, and plausible for this bot’s main problem (false breakouts after costs). The evidence is weak and the overfit risk is real, but this is exactly the kind of low-cost ablation worth running before spending live days on it.

name: Gap-robust volatility sizing
one_line: Size positions with a simple rolling volatility estimate that treats gap days separately, instead of trusting GARCH or naive close-to-close vol.
parameter_choices: Use 10- and 20-day rolling vol/ATR, split out gap days above 1%-2%, and compare against a GARCH proxy.
disagreement: Whether the extra model complexity of GARCH helps after costs, or whether a simpler gap-aware proxy is more stable.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books support the ingredients, not this exact Midas rule. B1-c011-05 warns that GARCH often looks good in-sample but forecasts poorly out-of-sample, which supports avoiding a fancier volatility model. B1-c018-04 says OHLC volatility estimators are biased when gaps/jumps are present, which supports a gap-aware proxy. B1-c017-06 reminds us realized vol depends on sampling interval, so keep the estimator simple. None of them prove that gap-aware ATR sizing improves ORB after costs on our book.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace raw stop-distance sizing with a 20-session gap-aware ATR cap. At 10:00, for each candidate compute ATR20 from the last 20 daily sessions reconstructed from the 5-minute bars; define a session as a gap day when |open / prior_close - 1| > 1.5%, and include that gap separately in the ATR estimate instead of using close-to-close volatility. Keep the existing 1% of equity risk budget, but set shares = floor((0.01 × equity) / max(OR_stop_distance, ATR20_gapaware)). Before a symbol has 20 sessions of history, fall back to the current sizing.
review.mechanism: This would shrink positions on noisy, gap-heavy names/days where the OR stop is most likely to get tagged by random movement and slippage. If it helps, the win should show up as smaller bad days and a lower max drawdown, with a side benefit of slightly lower dollar costs. It is not an alpha filter; it only tries to stop us from betting too large when the setup is statistically ugly.
review.data_missing: None for the test. We can reconstruct daily OHLC from the 5-minute bars and use the daily closes as backup. No pre-market, L2, news, or float is needed. Need a 20-session warm-up per symbol.
review.already_tried_note: Not on Midas. The rejected list has signal/exit ideas, not a volatility-based sizing overlay. The closest thing is the generic volatility-adjustment claim in B4, but that is not a prior test on our bot.
review.overfit_note: Only two knobs, but the effect will come from a small number of volatile days, so it is easy to tune the 20-day lookback and 1.5% gap cutoff to the first 67 sessions. Fix the parameters before looking and require out-of-sample confirmation.
review.expected_effect: Most likely a small reduction in drawdown and maybe a mild reduction in cost drag, with flat-to-lower raw PnL. It will not fix failed breakouts; it only makes the losers smaller on the days that are hardest to trade.
review.test_protocol: Fix the parameters now: 20-session lookback, 1.5% gap threshold. Replay all 67 archived sessions side by side against baseline. Primary metric: after-cost equity curve and max drawdown; secondary metrics: net PnL, profit factor, win rate, and average trade size. Require improvement in both halves of the sample (first 33 vs last 34 sessions), and do not accept a version that improves DD only by cutting PnL hard or reducing trade count by more than 10%. If the replay is better, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting it.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our data, cheap to replay, and the thesis is at least plausible: gap-heavy volatility can make the OR stop too optimistic. The expected gain is probably modest, but this is a valid sizing overlay worth a quick deterministic replay; if it does not improve after-cost replay PnL and drawdown, kill it.

name: Kalman intraday drift filter
one_line: Estimate a slowly varying intraday drift with a simple state-space/Kalman filter and only take breakouts aligned with that filtered state.
parameter_choices: Set process-noise vs measurement-noise ratio, update every 5 minutes, and optionally require drift sign to agree with the breakout.
disagreement: Whether trend drift is stable enough intraday to filter bad breakouts, or whether the filter just chases noise.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the statistical mechanism, not the trading rule. It says Kalman/state-space models can handle slowly varying parameters, which is enough to justify testing an intraday drift estimate, but using that estimate to gate breakouts is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a 1-state Kalman filter on each stock's 5-minute log returns (local-level drift model). Fix the process-noise / measurement-noise ratio at q/r = 0.01. From 10:00 onward, only take a long ORB entry if the filtered drift estimate is > 0 at the signal bar close; only take a short if it is < 0. Otherwise skip. No other entry, stop, target, or time rules change.
review.mechanism: This is just an entry gate. It should skip breakouts when the recent intraday drift is flat or pointing the wrong way, which could cut failed-breakout stop-outs and some flat-at-close trades, and slightly lower commissions because fewer trades fire. The tradeoff is fewer entries and a real chance of filtering out strong reversals, so any edge is likely to be small.
review.data_missing: None. It can be computed from the 5-minute regular-session OHLCV we already have; SPY is optional, not required.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact model, but it is the same family of trend-confirmation overlays. We already tried a SPY/QQQ half-hour predictor and a stronger breakout-confirmation rule (two closes beyond the range), and both hurt. This is just a smoother version of that idea.
review.overfit_note: One smoothing knob (q/r) is enough to fit the 67-session archive if we let it, and the filter is a lagging confirmation layer that can look good in-sample simply by shrinking trade count. Small sample + discretionary threshold = high overfit risk.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer bad breakouts and a slightly better win rate / target rate, with lower costs from skipped trades. More likely: fewer trades and only a marginal change in net P&L. I would not expect a large edge from this alone.
