review.test_protocol: Fix q/r = 0.01 before looking at results. Replay the filter side by side with the frozen baseline on all 67 archived sessions. Compare after-cost net P&L, profit factor, max drawdown, and trade count using the paired daily delta; require improvement in both chronological halves of the archive, not just overall. If the archive passes, run the next ~20 unseen sessions in parallel and keep it only if the live delta stays positive after costs.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully testable with the OHLCV we already have and cheap to replay, so there is no reason to spend live days before checking. But the support is only conceptual and the idea is a high-overfit trend filter, so it should be archived first and dropped fast if it only reduces trade count without improving after-cost P&L.

name: Adaptive volume baseline and event-day handling
one_line: Smooth intraday volume profiles, avoid early remaining-volume estimates, and treat event-like volume spikes as special cases.
parameter_choices: Use a smoothed rolling intraday volume profile; do not use remaining-volume forecasts before noon; flag event days when early volume or turnover exceeds a threshold.
disagreement: Whether a static profile is good enough, or whether adaptive profiles and event-day flags produce cleaner in-play selection.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book supports the general mechanics: smooth noisy intraday volume profiles, do not trust early remaining-day volume forecasts, and expect static profiles to miss event-day spikes. That is related to our in-play volume screen, but it is still an adaptation from execution/benchmarking into breakout selection, not a direct trading rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current 10-session 9:30–10:00 volume lookback, but compute the baseline from a smoothed 5-minute intraday profile: for each symbol, average the last 10 regular sessions’ 5-minute volumes and apply a 3-bin moving average across the six 5-minute bins in the first half-hour. Use that smoothed expected 9:30–10:00 volume for the existing in-play RVOL screen (still 1.5x, still top 8). Add one event-day override: if realized 9:30–9:45 volume is at least 2.5x its smoothed expected volume, widen that day’s shortlist to the top 12 names. Do not add any full-day volume forecast before noon.
review.mechanism: This is meant to make the volume filter less jumpy and less hostage to one weird session. The hoped-for gain is fewer false in-play names on ordinary days and better retention of true catalyst/high-activity names on abnormal-volume days. If it works, it should slightly reduce failed-breakout entries and improve the chance that the one daily trade is chosen from a genuinely active name.
review.data_missing: True catalyst/news labeling would make event-day identification better, but for this test we can proxy event-like days from realized early volume only. No pre-market, L2, or float data is strictly required for the proposed rule.
review.already_tried_note: We already use a static early-volume RVOL gate, so this is a mild variant of the current selection logic. The specific smoothing plus event-day override has not been tried.
review.overfit_note: Only two real knobs here, but the sample is small and event-spike days are rare. It would be easy to tune the threshold to the last 67 sessions if we let ourselves.
review.expected_effect: Small and uncertain positive. Best case, it trims a few bad selection days and slightly improves continuation on high-activity names. More likely it is a modest change rather than a step-change in edge.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the parameters before replay: 3-bin smoothing and a 2.5x early-volume event threshold. Replay all archived days side by side with the frozen baseline. Primary metric: after-cost net PnL per session and per trade. Secondary metrics: stop rate, target rate, flat-at-close contribution, trade count, and max drawdown. Require the modified rule to improve in both halves of the sample (early and late) and not reduce trade count by more than 15% or worsen drawdown. If it passes replay, paper it on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, computable from the data we already have, and the source support is at least directionally relevant. The expected edge is small, so this should be treated as a quick A/B, not a big thesis.

name: Matched exposure comparison
one_line: Compare strategy variants only after matching notional, holding time, and leverage so sizing changes do not masquerade as alpha.
parameter_choices: Keep notional and holding duration fixed across variants; test low vs high leverage as a separate sensitivity run.
disagreement: Raw PnL alone mixes signal quality with exposure and execution size, so it can reward the wrong variant.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: B1 explicitly argues that strategy effects should be calibrated on the same amount of stock over the same amount of time, and B2 explicitly recommends low-vs-high leverage backtests. Neither source says "use matched-exposure scoring to choose Midas variants," so this is a close extrapolation rather than a direct quotation of the exact rule.
review.exact_rule_change: No live-trading rule change. Change the evaluation rule: when comparing any Midas variant, replay it with fixed comparison exposure of $500 notional per entry (baseline median) and the existing 15:45 flat time, then rank variants only by normalized performance (net P&L per dollar risked, plus max drawdown), with a separate leverage sensitivity run at 0.5x and 1.0x equity risk. Do not pick a variant on raw dollar P&L alone.
review.mechanism: This removes the biggest confound in our tests: a variant can look better just because it takes bigger positions, stays in trades longer, or uses more leverage. Matching exposure should reduce false winners, make cost effects easier to see, and keep us from adopting a rule that only works by swinging more size rather than by improving breakout quality.
review.data_missing: None needed for the core comparison. We can compute entry price, exit price, holding time, notional, leverage, and net P&L from the existing 5-minute OHLCV replay plus the current sizing rules. We cannot measure true implementation shortfall or order-book impact, but this idea does not require that.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list, and I do not see an earlier exposure-normalized comparison pass in the brief.
review.overfit_note: The rule is fixed ex ante and adds almost no free knobs. The main risk is choosing the normalization after seeing results; if we lock the metric before the replay, overfit risk is low.
review.expected_effect: No direct alpha boost by itself. The main effect is better model selection: fewer false positives from size/leverage/holding-time confounding, lower chance of selecting a variant that looks good only on raw P&L, and a cleaner read on whether a real edge survives costs.
review.test_protocol: Run a deterministic replay of baseline and each candidate on all 67 archived sessions using the same fixed exposure rule ($500 notional) and the same 15:45 flat time. Compare: (1) average net P&L per trade, (2) average net P&L per unit of risked dollar, (3) max drawdown, and (4) results separately in the first half vs second half of the archive. Declare the method useful if the ranking of variants is stable across both halves and does not flip when switching from raw P&L to normalized P&L. Then, for only the best variant, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions before letting it guide live choices.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, computable with our existing replay data, and directly attacks a real selection bias. It will not create edge by itself, but it is worth adopting immediately as the standard way to judge future changes.

name: Bin the noisy fit, then recheck raw
one_line: Estimate execution or cost effects on binned data, but validate promising rules again on the rawest available series to make sure the result survives aggregation choices.
parameter_choices: Bin by relative volume, time of day, volatility, or similar low-dimensional buckets; then rerun on raw unsmoothed bars.
disagreement: A pure raw-trade workflow is too noisy, but a pure smoothed-bin workflow can hide fragility; use both for different stages.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general method: smooth/bin noisy market data for empirical estimation, then check that the result still holds on raw unsmoothed data. They do not state this exact two-stage protocol for Midas, so the link is adapted rather than direct.
review.exact_rule_change: This is a process change only, not a live trading rule change: for any proposed tweak, fit it first on coarse bins of the 5-minute archive (relative volume × time-of-day, 3 buckets each; no third learned axis), then rerun the exact same tweak on the raw 5-minute bars. Keep the tweak only if the raw replay preserves the sign and at least 50% of the binned improvement.
review.mechanism: It reduces false discoveries from noisy, sparse trade data. Coarse bins can reveal whether an effect is concentrated in a real regime, while the raw replay checks that the effect is not just a smoothing artifact. For Midas, that mainly means fewer fragile tweaks shipped, and a better chance of finding regime-specific filters that cut failed breakouts or cost-heavy exits.
review.data_missing: None required for this protocol; tick/spread/pre-market data would improve execution-cost realism, but the bin-then-raw robustness check itself works on our current 5-minute archive and daily closes.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. The closest analogue is the SPY/QQQ first-half-hour overlay, but that was a predictive live filter, not a bin-then-raw robustness gate.
review.overfit_note: Low-dimensional bins are safer than free-form fitting, but with only 67 sessions it is still easy to create sparse cells and then tune the buckets until something looks good. Keep the binning coarse and precommit it before looking.
review.expected_effect: Mostly a research guardrail: fewer fragile tweaks accepted, less chance of overestimating edge from smoothed summaries, and a better shot at finding regime-specific filters. By itself it will not change live P&L.
review.test_protocol: Retrospective meta-test first: lock the bucket definitions now, then run the gate on all 67 archived sessions for 3-5 historical candidate tweaks (include at least one known loser and one near-winner). Compare bin-then-raw screening versus raw-only screening on out-of-sample net P&L, profit factor, max drawdown, and whether the sign survives in both halves of the archive. If the gate rejects the losers without rejecting the known good ones, adopt it for future idea screening. For any future promoted tweak, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions before making it live.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible with the current archive, and genuinely aimed at reducing overfit. It will not create alpha by itself, but as a pre-commit research gate it is worth using now because the main cost is discipline, not capital.

name: No chase after a missed breakout
one_line: If the breakout trigger is missed or delayed, skip the trade rather than chasing the next bar after the edge has likely decayed.
parameter_choices: Do not enter on bars after the trigger bar unless the original signal is still active by the same rule; no catch-up entries.
disagreement: Chasing the next bar feels safer, but it often pays up after the setup has already weakened.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: B1 is the right general warning: unconditional catch-up is a drag. B4 adds the latency/fee caution for momentum systems. But neither source states this exact Midas rule, and Midas already enters on the first breakout close with next-bar-open execution, so the books support the intuition more than the specific change.
review.exact_rule_change: Make breakout signals one-shot: after the first 5-minute close outside the OR, the setup is valid only for the immediately following bar open; if that open is missed, cancel the setup and do not enter on any later bar even if price remains beyond the OR. New parameter: max_entry_delay_bars = 0.
review.mechanism: If the live engine is currently re-arming a missed breakout and paying up later, this should avoid late, weaker momentum entries that tend to stop out or flatline. That would mainly reduce bad days and costs, at the expense of fewer fills. But if the bot already only takes the first breakout and enters next bar open, the rule changes nothing.
review.data_missing: 5-minute OHLCV is enough to simulate a coarse bar-late catch-up rule, but not to know whether an order was truly missed, partially filled, or delayed at the quote/tick level. We do not have order-status, tick, or bid-ask data.
review.already_tried_note: The frozen recipe already says 'first close above/below OR' and 'fill at the NEXT bar's open,' which is effectively no catch-up. So this idea is mostly already implemented, not a new edge.
review.overfit_note: There is essentially one binary knob (max_entry_delay_bars), so overfitting risk is low. The bigger issue is not overfit but that the rule is probably already the baseline and may not change anything measurable.
review.expected_effect: If anything, fewer late entries and slightly lower slippage/costs; possibly fewer failed-breakout losses if the code currently chases. In the current written bot, likely no material effect because the behavior is already baked in.
review.test_protocol: First, audit the code to confirm whether delayed catch-up entries are actually possible. If yes, replay the 67 archived days with a strict max_entry_delay_bars=0 variant versus the current implementation. Compare net PnL after costs per session, trade count, win rate, and max drawdown; require the strict version to beat baseline in both historical halves, not just overall. If the archived replay produces no differing trades or fewer than ~20 differing setups, stop: the rule is not a real testable change on this data.
review.verdict_reason: This is basically already in the live recipe, so it is not a new alpha lever. Also, 5-minute OHLCV cannot tell us whether a real missed order was chased or merely delayed, so the only test would be a code-audit/implementation check rather than a meaningful performance experiment.

name: Graded filters, not hard intraday switches
one_line: Use condition scores or ranks instead of binary switches, and avoid swapping exit or regime templates once the session has started.
parameter_choices: Convert filters to continuous scores where possible; if a day mode is chosen, lock it until the close.
disagreement: Hard switches are simpler, but they can reset state and create brittle all-or-nothing behavior.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: B1-c042-04 explicitly argues against using a predictive condition as a blunt binary switch and favors integrating it more smoothly; B1-c042-05 warns that frequent switching can lose state. But neither source is a direct ORB study, and Midas already has one fixed intraday exit template, so only the graded-filter part really applies.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the hard 'sit out if fewer than 2 names qualify' rule with a fixed day-risk multiplier m = min(1.0, qual / 4.0), where qual is the number of universe names that meet the existing 1.5x 9:30–10:00 relative-volume test at 10:00. Keep the rest of the ORB entry/exit recipe unchanged for the full session; do not add any intraday template switching.
review.mechanism: This turns an all-or-nothing breadth gate into a throttle. On thin mornings we still take the best setup but smaller, which could reduce bad full-day skips and smooth P&L; if the filter is informative, it should work as a continuous input rather than a binary on/off switch.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: We have already tried adjacent selection changes like top-5 only and price caps, but not a graded day-risk multiplier. This is related, but it is not the same test.
review.overfit_note: The formula itself is simple and can be frozen up front, but if we start tuning the divisor or adding more buckets/ranks on only 67 sessions, it will overfit quickly.
review.expected_effect: Likely modest at best: possibly fewer zero-trade days and a little less variance, but no reason to expect a big lift in breakout quality or after-cost edge.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the multiplier formula before looking. Replay all archived days and compare paired daily results against the baseline on net P&L after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just overall. If it only helps by taking more weak days or by one lucky month, reject it. If it survives archive, forward-test on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: This is feasible with the data we already have, adds no new data dependency, and has no live-state complexity. The evidence is weak, but the concrete version is cheap to falsify in replay, so it is worth one disciplined test rather than a broad philosophical debate.

name: Versioned research/live pipeline
one_line: Keep one shared code path for backtests and paper/live, version every scenario, and backfill analytics so results are reproducible.
parameter_choices: Store per-scenario outputs, version calibration inputs, run CI/regression on every change, and generate T+0 analytics when possible.
disagreement: Separate notebooks and split research/TCA stacks feel faster at first, but they drift and become hard to reproduce.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The sources directly argue for this exact plumbing pattern: modular pipeline, versioned calibration data, shared research/production infrastructure, regression tests on every change, separate scenario outputs, backfilling analytics, T+0 reporting, and avoiding disconnected TCA/research stacks. This is not an extrapolation; it is essentially the source material turned into an implementation rule.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to trade logic. Change the Midas stack so every backtest, paper run, and live trade uses one shared signal/fill/cost/logging code path; assign each run an immutable scenario_id; run a fixed regression suite on every code or parameter change; and backfill any new analytics or filters across the full historical archive before they can be used in selection. Defaults: regression_suite = every code/parameter change; backfill_scope = full archive.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha directly. It reduces false confidence from buggy backtests, cost-model drift, fill-rule drift, and notebook/live divergence. For Midas that means fewer bad days caused by hidden implementation errors, faster attribution when a tweak helps or hurts, and less wasted testing on tweaks that only look good in one stack. The bucket moved is mostly 'better validation / fewer bad decisions,' not 'more targets' or 'fewer failed breakouts' by itself.
review.data_missing: None for the core change. It only needs the same 5-minute OHLCV, daily closes, and paper/live logs you already have. If you want the T+0 dashboard, you also need intraday bars during the session, which you already have.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the rejected list. You have not already standardized research/live code paths or implemented the versioned scenario and regression/backfill discipline described here.
review.overfit_note: There are basically no tunable trading knobs here. The only real risk is process bloat, not overfitting to the 67-day sample. The implementation should be fixed and boring, not optimized to history.
review.expected_effect: Indirect but worthwhile: cleaner attribution, reproducible reruns, fewer accidental look-ahead/cost bugs, and faster detection of whether a trading tweak genuinely improves the bot. It should improve research quality more than raw P&L.
review.test_protocol: Implement on a branch, then run a full deterministic replay of all 67 archived sessions through both the old path and the new shared path. Success metric: identical trade timestamps, directions, sizes, fills, fees, slippage, and end-of-day P&L within machine tolerance; zero unexplained divergences. Then keep the new pipeline live for the next ~20 unseen sessions and audit any discrepancy daily. This is an engineering acceptance test, not an alpha test.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with current data, cheap to validate, and directly protects you from wasting time on false edges. It will not by itself generate trading edge, but it is the right plumbing to have before you keep testing strategy tweaks.

name: Replay-clock backtest engine
one_line: Drive the simulator off historical timestamps, not wall clock time, so session cutoffs and halts trigger exactly when they would live.
parameter_choices: Replay the market-data clock bar by bar; all timers read the latest processed timestamp.
disagreement: Wall-clock scheduling is easy to code, but it hides timing bugs in entry cutoffs and end-of-day flattening.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: B1 explicitly recommends an internal time service whose `now()` is the latest processed timestamp, and B4 recommends bar-by-bar/event-based backtesting. That is essentially the proposed change, not a loose analogy.
review.exact_rule_change: Implement a single replay-clock time service in the simulator: `now()` always returns the timestamp of the latest processed 5-minute bar, and the 15:15 no-new-entry cutoff, 15:45 forced flat, and -3% day-loss halt are evaluated only against that replay time. No strategy parameters change.
review.mechanism: This is not an alpha idea; it reduces backtest/live divergence. It prevents session cutoffs and halts from firing early or late because of wall-clock scheduling, which can distort the many end-of-day flat exits and any stop/target near the close. The likely gain is cleaner accounting and fewer timing bugs, not higher raw trade expectancy.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. If the current engine already uses bar timestamps internally, this is a no-op; otherwise it is a real implementation fix.
review.overfit_note: No tuning knobs and no strategy degrees of freedom. The only risk is accidentally introducing a bug while refactoring the time service, not statistical overfit.
review.expected_effect: Neutral to slightly negative on measured P&L if the current backtest is optimistic, but materially better realism. Trade count should be unchanged; exit timing and day-halt behavior become trustworthy.
review.test_protocol: Run the replay-clock engine and the current wall-clock engine side by side on all 67 archived sessions. For every trade, compare signal time, entry time, stop/target time, forced-flat time, and day-halt time, plus final P&L. Success metric: zero unintended timing mismatches on archived days, or any mismatch is traced to a genuine bug and fixed before any further strategy testing. Then shadow the corrected engine on the next ~20 unseen sessions and require no new cutoff/flatten/halt bugs before promoting it.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, data-feasible, and directly protects the validity of every later strategy test. It does not create alpha, but if the current simulator uses wall time anywhere, you should fix that before trusting any results.

name: Shock-day entry halt
one_line: Pause new ORB entries on abnormal open-range or extreme SPY shock days.
parameter_choices: Define a shock threshold on opening-range size, OR expansion, or SPY move; if breached, no new trades that day.
disagreement: Always trading through shock days keeps the sample large, but it also invites the worst false-breakout regimes.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: Both books warn that abrupt events and noisy/special-event sessions can break a system, but neither gives a measured rule for a SPY shock-day halt. This is a regime-filter extrapolation, not a quoted trading rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current ORB rules, but add a daily shock gate: from 10:00 NY time onward, if SPY's open-to-current return at any 5-minute close has |return| >= 1.0%, do not initiate any new ORB trades for the rest of that session.
review.mechanism: This tries to skip the mornings where the broad market is already making an outsized move and our breakouts are most likely to whipsaw or fail. On this bot, the main gain would be fewer stop-outs and fewer low-quality flat holds; the main cost is that we will also miss some big trend days.
review.data_missing: None for the proposed SPY-only version; 5-minute regular-session SPY OHLCV is enough.
review.already_tried_note: We have not tested a hard entry halt. The closest prior idea was a SPY/QQQ first-half-hour overlay that tried to forecast later returns and it hurt, but that is not the same as a binary shock-day skip filter.
review.overfit_note: One threshold is simple, but with only 67 sessions the number of true shock days is small. If we start tuning 0.6/0.8/1.0% after the fact, or add OR-width plus SPY in the same test, it becomes easy to fit noise.
review.expected_effect: Likely a modest reduction in the worst losing days and in commission/slippage drag, with a possible small drop in total trades and some missed target days. I would expect the effect to show up more in lower drawdown and better session-level expectancy than in win rate.
review.test_protocol: Lock the 1.0% threshold before looking at results. Replay the baseline and the shock-gated version on all 67 archived sessions side by side. Primary score: cost-adjusted daily P&L and max drawdown; secondary: trade count, stop rate, target rate. Accept only if the gated version improves primary P&L and drawdown in both halves of the archive and does not cut trade count by more than about 20%. If it passes, run unchanged on the next ~20 unseen paper days and keep it only if the live result stays in the same direction.
review.verdict_reason: It is computable from our existing 5-minute SPY data, adds no execution cost, and targets a known bad-regime failure mode. The evidence is weak, but the test is cheap and the rule is simple enough to reject quickly if it starves the bot or misses too many trend days.

name: No-trade on choppy MA crossover mornings
one_line: Treat rapid moving-average crossovers as a no-trade regime for ORB entries.
parameter_choices: Use a short/long MA pair and skip days where crossovers flip more than once before the trigger window ends.
disagreement: A moving-average filter can help trend days, but in ranges it often just adds whipsaws.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general warning, not the exact rule: it says moving averages can cross repeatedly in short, directionless ranges, which is consistent with using crossover churn as a warning sign. But it does not propose an ORB no-trade filter or any specific crossover-count threshold; that part is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a SPY morning regime filter: on 5-minute regular-session bars, compute EMA(5) and EMA(13) from 9:30 to 10:00. If the sign of (EMA5 - EMA13) flips more than once before 10:00, take no ORB trade that day and stand aside. Otherwise run the frozen ORB rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This only helps if the bad ORB days are the choppy ones. The filter is meant to avoid failed breakouts and stop-outs when the market is whipping around, which should also cut some cost drag and drawdown. The trade-off is fewer trades and possibly missing some good trend days that start messy.
review.data_missing: None; the existing 5-minute SPY bars are enough.
review.already_tried_note: Not the same rule, but it is in the same family as the rejected SPY/QQQ first-half-hour overlay: an early-session regime filter on a momentum-style strategy. That prior test hurt profit, so this should be treated skeptically.
review.overfit_note: There are many hidden knobs: SPY vs stock, short/long EMA lengths, flip threshold, and whether the EMA state is carried across days or reset. With only 67 sessions, it is easy to tune the filter to a few failed-breakout mornings and mistake that for edge. Because the filter uses the same opening bars that define the trade, in-sample improvement may be mostly self-referential.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer stop-outs and fewer bad days, with slightly better profit factor and lower drawdown. Likely side effect: fewer trades and some missed target days. Any net edge would probably come from skipping a small number of ugly mornings, not from improving the average trade.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule before testing: SPY EMA(5)/EMA(13), no trade if the spread flips more than once from 9:30 to 10:00. Replay all 67 archived sessions side by side with the frozen baseline. Judge first on after-cost net P&L, then on stop rate, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in both chronological halves of the archive and no more than a 25% drop in trade count; if fewer than about 15 archive sessions are filtered out, the signal is probably too weak to trust. If it passes the archive, paper it on the next 20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, computable from data we already have, and aimed at a real weakness of the bot: failed breakouts on choppy mornings. The evidence is weak and the overfit risk is high, but this is still worth one fixed-parameter replay before we dismiss it.

name: Confirmed past-pattern filters only
one_line: Use pivots, channels, triangles, engulfings, and similar patterns only after they are fully confirmed by past bars, with explicit lag and short windows.
parameter_choices: Delay pivot/fractal signals by the full confirmation window; keep engulfing spans to 1-2 candles; require pivot alternation for patterns.
disagreement: Pattern signals feel stronger when they include the current bar or long confirmation chains, but that is where look-ahead and lag creep in.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: The sources do support the mechanics of confirmed patterns: lag pivots/fractals so future candles are not used, fit channels/triangles only on completed bars, reject non-alternating pivot triangles, and keep engulfings short. They do not provide evidence that these confirmed patterns create trading edge; they mainly warn against look-ahead bias and subjective overfitting.
review.exact_rule_change: If any pattern-based filter is used at all, it must be computed only from completed bars: set confirm_lag=3 bars for pivots/channels/triangles, cap engulfing patterns at engulf_span=1 bar, and reject any triangle unless pivot highs and lows alternate. No current bar may enter the pattern fit.
review.mechanism: This is mostly a hygiene rule. It prevents impossible live signals and may cut some noisy false breakouts before they become entries. Best case, that lowers stop-outs and commissions a bit; more likely, it just delays entries and reduces trade count, which can hurt on a small, already-low-sample bot.
review.data_missing: None; 5-minute regular-session OHLCV is enough to compute confirmed pivots, channels, triangles, and engulfings with explicit lag.
review.already_tried_note: We already tested the same general direction of 'more confirmation before entry' with two consecutive closes beyond the range, and it got worse. This idea uses a different pattern family, but it is still more lag/confirmation, so the precedent is not encouraging.
review.overfit_note: There are multiple discretionary pattern families plus confirmation lag, window length, and alternation rules. With only 67 sessions and few trades, it is easy to find a pattern that looks good by chance after costs.
review.expected_effect: Best case: slightly fewer failed-breakout stops and a cleaner backtest. More likely: fewer signals, later entries, lower trade count, and no durable edge by itself.
review.test_protocol: Do not send this live as a standalone alpha. If you still want to sanity-check it, freeze the parameters above and replay baseline vs filter on all 67 archived sessions. Compare net PnL after costs, stop rate, max drawdown, and trade count. It only earns a live unseen test if it improves both archive halves (Jul-Aug and Sep-Oct) and does not cut trade count by more than about 20%. Then confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: The sources support only no-lookahead implementation hygiene, not a profitable edge. We already have evidence that adding confirmation before ORB entries hurts, and this idea adds lag/complexity without showing it can beat the current breakout logic after costs.

name: Breakout buffer around the OR
one_line: Allow a small buffer around the opening-range boundary instead of requiring a strict close beyond the exact high or low.
parameter_choices: Test a small absolute or percent buffer around OR high/low; keep the rest of the ORB logic unchanged.
disagreement: Exact closes are clean, but they can be too strict and miss legitimate moves.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: B2 explicitly suggests loosening an ORB condition by allowing a small buffer around the range boundary instead of requiring a strict close beyond it. B7 is also broadly consistent with using confirmed closes and, if testing earlier triggers, adding a buffer before entry. The support is direct, but it is still anecdotal/opinion rather than statistical evidence.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the ORB logic unchanged except for the trigger: long only if the first 5-minute candle closes at least 0.10% above OR high (close >= OR_high * 1.001); short only if it closes at least 0.10% below OR low (close <= OR_low * 0.999). Fill remains at the next bar open; all other filters, stop, target, sizing, and time exits stay frozen.
review.mechanism: This is meant to filter borderline pokes through the opening range that often snap back. If the breakout is real, price should clear the boundary by a bit; if it only barely closes outside, it is often noise. Best case: fewer failed-breakout stops and a small reduction in costs from smaller size on wider stops. Worst case: later entries, fewer trades, and missed winners.
review.data_missing: none; the trigger can be computed from the existing 5-minute regular-session OHLCV and OR high/low.
review.already_tried_note: Not the same rule, but it is in the same family as the already-rejected 'two consecutive closes beyond the range' confirmation idea and the baseline already uses a strict close trigger. So this is adjacent, not brand-new.
review.overfit_note: Only one knob, but with 67 sessions and ~1 trade/day it is still easy to tune a tiny buffer to noise. The effect will probably show up in only a handful of trades, so do not sweep multiple buffer values.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small drop in false-breakout stopouts, but also later entries and fewer fills. The net effect is probably modest at best and could easily be negative if the buffer is too wide; it is not a fix for the much larger flat-exit drag.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the buffer at 0.10% before looking at results. Replay the buffered version against the baseline on all 67 archived sessions. Compare after-cost net P&L per session, profit factor, max drawdown, stopout rate, and trade count. Require the buffered version to improve in both archive halves and not reduce trade count by more than 20%. If it passes the archive test, paper it on the next 20 unseen sessions without retuning. If it only wins in one half or by a hair, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully data-feasible, and the source directly suggests the tweak. That said, it is only a mild confirmation filter, so do exactly one fixed-buffer test and expect a small or zero effect; if the archive does not improve in both halves, kill it.

name: Higher-resolution intraday validation
one_line: Add 1-minute data and compare signal timing and fill quality against the current 5-minute ORB.
parameter_choices: Run the same setup on 1-minute and 5-minute bars, keeping the rest of the rules fixed.
disagreement: 5-minute bars are simpler and cheaper to work with, but they may hide timing and fill effects that matter in fast breakouts.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general principle that intraday strategies need minute/hour data rather than coarse bars. It does not specifically argue for 1-minute-vs-5-minute validation of this ORB, so that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Validation-only change: rerun the existing ORB on 1-minute regular-session OHLCV instead of 5-minute bars, with all other rules unchanged (9:30–10:00 OR, 10:00 in-play filter, first breakout, next-bar-open fill, same stop/target/time exit). This is not a new live strategy, just a higher-resolution replay.
review.mechanism: This would tell us whether 5-minute candles are hiding timing and fill effects on fast breakouts. If the edge disappears on 1-minute replay, the current backtest is likely overstating realism. If it survives, we get a cleaner estimate of true entry timing and execution cost. The main bucket is better measurement of fills and a check on whether some breakouts are being entered too late or on misleading candle closes.
review.data_missing: We do not have 1-minute regular-session OHLCV for the 55 names and SPY. If the goal is true fill-quality realism, bid/ask or tick data would also help; with only 1-minute bars we can improve timing resolution but not fully model spread/slippage.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. Nothing listed here is the same as the existing ORB or the previously rejected overlays/filters.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob (bar resolution), but it is easy to cherry-pick the cleaner-looking backtest from just 67 sessions. As a pure diagnostic it is fine; as a basis for changing live timing, the sample is still small.
review.expected_effect: Mostly diagnostic, not a direct alpha improvement. It may show that the current 5-minute backtest is slightly too optimistic or that a few fast names need finer timing, but I would not expect a big standalone P&L gain. Best case: cleaner entry timing and a more honest cost estimate; worst case: we learn the current edge is an artifact of coarse bars.
review.test_protocol: Acquire 1-minute OHLCV, then replay the exact current strategy on all archived days in two versions: 5-minute baseline vs 1-minute variant. Compare net P&L after the same commissions/slippage model, win rate, profit factor, max drawdown, and how often the trade entry changes. Require the 1-minute version to beat the 5-minute baseline in both halves of the archive (Jul-Sep and Oct+) on net expectancy per trade after costs, with no worse drawdown and no major trade-count collapse, before considering any live switch. Then paper-trade the chosen resolution for the next 20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: Useful as a measurement upgrade, but we cannot run it now with the current dataset because we only have 5-minute bars. It is not a live edge by itself, and without 1-minute OHLCV it is not testable today.

name: Time stop on stalled breakouts
one_line: Close ORB trades that fail to follow through after a short, fixed window instead of waiting all the way to the session flat.
parameter_choices: Test a time stop of 2, 3, or 4 bars after entry; also test an invalidation rule that exits if price re-enters the opening range or fails to extend by at least 0.5R.
disagreement: A time stop can cut off the rare slow-burning trend, so it may help chop but hurt the biggest winners.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The book/example warns that fixed support/resistance exits can trap you in a trend and says levels should move with the market. That is related to managing a breakout that stalls, but it is not a direct recommendation for a time stop on ORB trades; the link is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current ORB entry, stop, and 2.5R target, but add an early exit: if a position has not reached +0.5R of favorable excursion by the close of the 3rd completed 5-minute bar after entry, exit at the next bar's open; also exit at the next bar's open on the first 5-minute close that re-enters the opening range.
review.mechanism: This should mainly cut dead-money breakouts that go nowhere after the trigger, which is the part of the book that lost you money in August. It could reduce the number of trades that drift back to flat or stop, and lower max drawdown from stalled moves. The downside is that some of your rare slow-burning winners will be cut before they can become 2.5R targets, and because you only get one trade per day, an early exit does not create a second chance.
review.data_missing: None for a close-based rule using 5-minute OHLCV. If you want intrabar wick/touch re-entry into the opening range, you would need tick or L1 data.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exit. You have tried a different entry filter (two closes beyond the range) and a failed-breakout fade, but not a fixed time stop or an OR-reentry invalidation on the open breakout trade.
review.overfit_note: If you precommit to one combo (3 bars, +0.5R) the rule is simple, but it is still easy to mine the 67-session archive by trying 2/3/4 bars and toggling the 0.5R gate. Do not sweep and pick the best; that would push this to high overfit risk.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer stalled-breakout givebacks and slightly lower drawdown, but probably fewer full-target wins and possibly no net P&L gain. The most realistic upside is a modest improvement in average trade quality, not a large new edge.
review.test_protocol: Precommit now to the single rule above and replay it on all 67 archived sessions side by side with the frozen baseline, with identical entries, stops, target, costs, and no retuning. Judge by net $/day after costs, profit factor, max drawdown, and average trade, and require the modified rule to improve both the early and late halves of the archive before you believe it. If it passes, paper it on the next 20 unseen sessions; if it does not beat baseline there too, reject it. Do not choose among 2/3/4 bars after looking.
review.verdict_reason: This is feasible with your data and costs, cheap to replay, and directly aimed at a known failure mode. The support is only indirect and the edge is likely small, so I would not spend time sweeping parameters, but a single fixed replay is worth doing before you dismiss it.

name: Baseline-benchmarked model gate
one_line: Only promote a learned filter if it beats a simple baseline on unseen days and does not show negative out-of-sample explanatory power.
parameter_choices: For model filters, require out-of-sample R² > 0 against a naive baseline; for strategy changes, require after-cost performance to beat both the unfiltered ORB and SPY on untouched sessions.
disagreement: R² can be too strict or unstable on small samples, so some useful filters may fail this gate even if they improve live trading.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the two ingredients separately: (1) negative out-of-sample R² as a rejection signal, and (2) benchmarking against a relevant yardstick such as an index or another strategy. They do not explicitly say to require both SPY and the unfiltered ORB to pass, so the combined promotion gate is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: No live trading rule change. For any future learned filter or overlay, only promote it if a pre-fixed walk-forward replay on archived days shows out-of-sample R² > 0 versus a naive baseline and after-cost performance beats both the unfiltered ORB baseline and SPY; otherwise discard it.
review.mechanism: This is a research-quality gate, not a signal. It would mainly prevent us from adding overfit filters that look good in-sample but add no real edge after costs. That can reduce bad overlays and research churn, but it does not directly improve the current breakout logic, exits, or costs.
review.data_missing: None for the gate itself; archived 5-minute OHLCV plus SPY are enough. A specific learned filter would still need a pre-fixed target/label.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list, and we have not yet built a learned filter to which this gate would apply.
review.overfit_note: The gate itself has almost no knobs, but with only 67 sessions OOS R² will be noisy, and the real danger is cherry-picking among many candidate models until one passes.
review.expected_effect: No direct P&L edge. As a governance rule it should reduce false-positive model additions and keep us from worsening the bot with overfit overlays, but it will not by itself improve hit rate, targets, or costs.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend a standalone bot test on the gate itself. If we later build a learned filter, pre-register the model and target, replay it walk-forward on all archived days, and require: (1) OOS R² > 0, and (2) after-cost results beat both unfiltered ORB and SPY in the first and second halves of the archive. Only then forward-test on ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: Useful as internal research hygiene, but it is not a trading edge and does not change the current bot’s P&L path. On our small sample, OOS R² is too noisy to be a hard live gate, so do not spend a bot test on this as if it were a strategy idea.

name: Look-ahead-free feature construction
one_line: Build every threshold and filter from completed bars only, with explicit time-of-availability checks for rolling features.
parameter_choices: Shift rolling calculations by one bar before computing highs/lows/means; audit each feature to verify it is available at the decision timestamp; ban any full-sample statistics from live logic.
disagreement: This can slightly worsen backtests if the current implementation is accidentally using same-bar information, but that is the point.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly recommends shifting the input series by one bar before rolling calculations and warns against using whole-sample information before a decision. That is the same look-ahead-free rule, just applied to Midas’ features.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a global availability rule: every rolling/high-low/mean/relative-volume feature used by Midas must be computed only from completed bars, using `shift(1)` before any rolling calculation (`lag = 1 bar`), and any feature that cannot be proven available at the decision timestamp is banned from live logic.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha; it removes impossible information. If the current implementation is leaking the current bar or full-sample stats, the backtest is overstating breakout quality and in-play selection. Fixing that prevents us from deploying a mirage and gives a live-tradable estimate of whether the ORB edge is real. The likely effect is fewer fake winners in the backtest, not better fills or lower costs.
review.data_missing: None for this audit. 5-minute regular-session OHLCV plus daily closes are enough to enforce timestamp availability and to recompute all trailing features with a one-bar lag.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. This is a code/measurement hygiene change, not one of the prior alpha overlays or entry rules.
review.overfit_note: Essentially zero free knobs if we hard-code `shift=1` and a strict decision-time audit. The only real risk is making ad hoc exceptions after seeing the results.
review.expected_effect: If there is hidden look-ahead, the audited version will usually have lower PnL, fewer apparent winners, and more realistic trade timing. If results barely move, the current implementation was likely clean. Either way, the audited version is the one we should trust live.
review.test_protocol: Do a deterministic replay on all 67 archived days with the current code and with the audited version. Compare feature timestamps, signal times, entries, trade counts, and day PnL day-by-day. Success criterion is zero timestamp violations and no unexplained trade differences; if the audited version is worse, keep it anyway because that means the old code was leaking future information. Then shadow the audited code on the next ~20 unseen days and require live-vs-replay parity within normal slippage. Do not wait for 100+ unseen trades; this is a correctness check, not an alpha significance test.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible, and necessary. This is not a speculative edge idea; it is a mandatory audit for backtest validity. If the current bot is clean, nothing changes. If it is not, we need to know before trusting any of the reported edge.

name: Pre-trade safety checks and kill switches
one_line: Reject orders that violate size, price, side, or position limits, and hard-stop the bot on day-loss or order-logic anomalies.
parameter_choices: Add checks for cash-based max notional, nonsensical stop distance, wrong-side orders, excessive outstanding position, max order count, and a kill switch tied to the existing day-loss halt.
disagreement: Hard rejects can be annoying during live trading, but they are safer than silent bad orders.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The cited book excerpts directly recommend pre-trade order validation and kill-switch style safeguards: rejecting malformed/invalid orders, checking size/side/price/position limits, and stopping after dangerous anomalies. They support the safety mechanism, not a trading edge.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a pre-submit OMS validator: reject any order if required cash > available cash (cash cap = 100% of cash), if the stop price is not strictly on the correct side of entry / stop distance <= 0, or if the order would create more than one open position; if one validation failure occurs in a session, hard-disable new entries for the rest of the day (keep the existing -3% day-loss halt unchanged).
review.mechanism: This does not change breakout behavior or expected trade quality. It only prevents fat-finger, logic, or sizing bugs from sending bad orders or compounding into a bad day, which matters on a tiny $1k book where one bad order can dominate results. The benefit is lower tail risk and cleaner execution logs, not higher average edge.
review.data_missing: OHLCV is enough to compute whether a planned order would violate cash/stop-side/position rules, but not to measure whether the guardrail ever mattered in practice. To evaluate usefulness you need historical order-generation/execution logs or fault-injection replay; market bars alone cannot reveal logic bugs.
review.already_tried_note: The bot already has a -3% day-loss halt, which covers part of this idea. The new OMS reject rules for bad size/side/price/position are not in the rejected-alpha list, but they are operational safeguards rather than a new market signal.
review.overfit_note: Almost no free knobs if kept as a hard validator. The risk is not overfitting the market; it is wasting time pretending an engineering safeguard is a PnL hypothesis.
review.expected_effect: No meaningful change to historical edge on clean data. Big reduction in operational blow-up risk if a bug, duplicate submit, wrong-side order, or oversize order appears. It should not improve win rate, target rate, or costs in normal trading.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend scarce live trading days on this as an alpha test. First, replay all 67 archived sessions with the validator enabled and require identical fills/PnL on all historical valid orders. Second, run fault-injection tests on the replay: oversized orders, stop on wrong side, zero/negative stop distance, duplicate submits, unsupported order types, and cash overuse; success is 100% rejection of injected bad orders and 0 false rejects on valid historical orders. If you want live confirmation, run it in shadow/logging mode for the next ~20 unseen sessions, but treat that as an engineering audit, not a strategy test.
review.verdict_reason: This is a worthwhile safety patch, but it is not a tradable edge and cannot be validated as a PnL-improving change with our OHLCV sample. It should be implemented directly for operational safety, not consumed as one of our scarce strategy experiments.

name: Strategy code unit/regression tests
one_line: Test the ORB engine at the component level and replay fixed sessions after every code change to catch logic drift.
parameter_choices: Unit-test OR high/low calculation, gap filters, sizing, stop/target logic, and forced-flat handling; regression-test a saved set of historical sessions and compare trades, timestamps, and PnL decomposition to baseline outputs.
disagreement: This adds engineering overhead, but it is cheaper than debugging a live trading error.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The cited book sections explicitly recommend unit tests and regression tests for algorithmic trading software. They support this QA gate directly, though they do not claim any market alpha.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a pre-deploy quality gate: run unit tests for OR high/low calculation, gap filters, sizing, stop/target logic, and forced-flat handling, then replay the full frozen archive of historical sessions (currently 67 days) and require the new code to match the baseline trade list exactly on count, side, timestamps, sizes, and exit reasons, with PnL matching to the nearest cent.
review.mechanism: This does not create edge; it protects the existing edge. It should catch silent logic drift in the parts most likely to break this bot: opening-range math, gap filters, position sizing, stop/target placement, and end-of-day liquidation. On a small-cost, small-edge system, a hidden bug can easily look like a real strategy result, so regression testing reduces false confidence and prevents accidental PnL leakage.
review.data_missing: None for this change; the existing archived 5-minute OHLCV and daily-close data are enough for deterministic replay.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the rejected list. This is engineering validation, not a trading overlay or entry/exit rule already tested.
review.overfit_note: There are essentially no tunable trading parameters if the fixture set is frozen. The only real risk is cherry-picking test sessions; avoid that by freezing the suite now and appending any bug-triggering session permanently.
review.expected_effect: Near-zero direct effect on returns if the code was already correct. If there are hidden bugs, this can recover lost PnL and prevent live/backtest divergence. The main benefit is protecting the current edge, not adding new alpha.
review.test_protocol: This is an engineering gate, not a market hypothesis. Freeze the current baseline outputs, then run every archived session through the revised code. Pass only if the full trade log matches: same trade count, entries, exits, sizes, timestamps, and exit reasons; any difference is a bug unless explicitly intended and reviewed. Keep at least a couple of hand-picked edge-case fixtures forever (for example: OR high/low ties, gap threshold boundaries, and forced-flat near 15:45). After adoption, monitor the next ~20 live sessions for any intended-vs-actual order mismatches, but no unseen-trade sample is needed to approve the harness itself.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible, and directly useful. It will not generate alpha, but on a small book with a weak statistical edge it is worth doing immediately because silent implementation errors can swamp the strategy and invalidate every later test.

name: Bear case checklist and disconfirming evidence
one_line: Before adopting a rule change, write the bearish case and require at least one explicit disconfirming signal in the review log.
parameter_choices: For every candidate change, record the conditions under which it should fail, plus one concrete bearish argument or counterexample before promotion to paper or live testing.
disagreement: This is slower than intuition-led iteration, but it reduces confirmation bias and narrative trading.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly recommends a pre-mortem: imagine how the idea could fail and look for contrary evidence before deciding. That is essentially this checklist, just formalized into a review gate.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a mandatory pre-test gate: every proposed Midas change must come with exactly 1 bearish case and 1 concrete disconfirming example from archived replay; if either is missing, the change does not advance to paper/live testing.
review.mechanism: This does not create market edge by itself. It is meant to reduce confirmation bias and stop weak narrative tweaks from consuming our scarce unseen days. The expected gain is fewer bad rule changes and less overfitting, not better entries, exits, or lower execution costs directly.
review.data_missing: The checklist is a human research process, not a signal computable from 5-minute OHLCV. To evaluate its value we would need a log of candidate changes, their pre-mortems, and an objective label for whether the bearish case was actually disconfirming.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the rejected list. The team may already do informal review, but this explicit bearish-case-plus-counterexample gate has not been tested as a formal rule.
review.overfit_note: There are no market parameters to tune, so classic overfitting risk is minimal. The real risk is subjective hindsight and checkbox theater, not data snooping.
review.expected_effect: Good research hygiene, but no direct PnL lift on the current bot. At best it filters out weak future rule changes before they waste tests.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend a bot replay on this as if it were a trading edge. If adopted, use it prospectively as an internal research gate for the next 10 candidate changes and audit whether it blocks at least one change that later would have failed on archived replay. No meaningful unseen-trade sample is applicable.
review.verdict_reason: This is a process safeguard, not a tradable rule. It cannot be validated with our OHLCV archive or costs, and it does not change entries, exits, or sizing. Useful discipline, but not worth a bot test.

name: Volatility-adjusted stop width / narrow-OR skip
one_line: Widen the stop or skip the trade when volatility or the opening range is too tight for the default OR stop to make sense.
parameter_choices: Test an ATR- or prior-day-range-based stop cap; alternatively skip trades when OR width is below a minimum fraction of price or ATR.
disagreement: Wider stops can lower position size and may reduce expectancy if the market does not actually need the extra room.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The source says stops that are too close get shaken out in volatile markets, and gives anecdotal examples of traders using wider percentage stops. That supports the general concern, but it does not specifically argue for an opening-range-width filter or for this exact rule, so this is an adaptation rather than a direct citation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a narrow-OR filter: at 10:00, compute today's opening-range width W = OR_high - OR_low from the 9:30-10:00 bars, and compute the symbol's trailing 10-session average OR width M from prior regular-session 5-minute bars. If W < 0.60 × M, skip that symbol for the day; otherwise keep the current ORB entry, stop, size, and exit rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This should cut the worst whipsaw days: when the morning range is unusually tight, breakouts often have little room to run and can flip back into the stop. Skipping those setups should reduce failed-breakout stop-outs, avoid oversized share counts on tiny stops, and lower the amount of commission/slippage spent on low-quality trades.
review.data_missing: None for the proposed skip rule. The widening-stop variant would need daily high/low or a true ATR feed, which we do not have stored.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tried. The rejected two-close confirmation rule is different: that was extra breakout confirmation, while this is a pre-entry volatility filter that skips very tight openings.
review.overfit_note: Only one threshold, but 67 archived sessions and one trade per day is still a small sample, so it would be easy to tune a cutoff that flatters backtest results. Keep the cutoff global and fixed before looking at the archive.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades and fewer immediate stop-outs on compressed mornings. Best case: modestly higher win rate, better profit factor, and lower drawdown. Worst case: it just cuts the sample and removes some good breakouts, with little net improvement.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the 0.60 threshold now. Replay the full archive side by side with the baseline using identical fill/cost assumptions. Primary metric: net $ per session after costs; secondary metrics: max drawdown, stop-out rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive (first and second half of the 67 sessions), or at minimum no meaningful deterioration in one half while improving the other, and keep total trades high enough to be informative (roughly 35+ trades if the filter is not too restrictive). If it passes the replay, run it unchanged on the next ~20 unseen sessions before considering any further tweak.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully computable from the data we already have, and directly targets a known failure mode of this bot. The evidence is weak and the effect may be small, but this is exactly the kind of one-parameter filter worth replaying before spending live trades on it.

name: Directional exhaustion filter
one_line: Avoid buying fresh intraday lows and avoid shorting names that are already too extended down without renewed downside follow-through.
parameter_choices: For longs, require the signal bar not to make a fresh intraday low; for shorts, require continued downside follow-through and reject names that are already deeply extended or reversing.
disagreement: This can filter out some strong continuation moves that begin from extreme prints.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: Both quotes are generic anti-'catch a falling knife' warnings. They support a long-side rule that avoids buying a breakout bar that is also the day's low, but they do not validate an ORB-specific threshold, and they say nothing about the short-side 'too extended' cutoff.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a long-entry exhaustion filter only: when the first 5-minute close above OR high triggers a long, skip that trade if the signal bar's low is the lowest low of the regular session so far (a fresh intraday low). Leave the short rules unchanged for now.
review.mechanism: This can cut some of the nastier long failures: breakout attempts that are really panic-reversal bars being bought into a still-weak tape. It may reduce stop-outs and a few bad days, but it will also remove some of the best V-shaped longs, so the benefit is likely small and the trade count may fall.
review.data_missing: None; the rule can be computed from 5-minute regular-session OHLCV alone.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact filter, but it lives in the same neighborhood as the already-tried 'two consecutive closes beyond the range' confirmation overlay and the failed-breakout ideas. The short-side exhaustion cap was not previously tested.
review.overfit_note: Only one boolean rule, but the sample is still tiny (67 sessions / ~53 trades) and the effect could easily be sample-specific. If you start tuning any extension threshold, the risk jumps to high.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer long stop-outs and slightly better cost-adjusted expectancy. More likely: a small reduction in losers at the cost of fewer trades and some missed momentum winners. It is not a solution to the bot's flat-at-close problem.
review.test_protocol: Fix the rule before looking. Replay all 67 archived sessions side-by-side with baseline. Primary metric: cost-adjusted net PnL per session; guardrails: max drawdown and trade count should not collapse. Require the modified rule to improve both halves of the archive (first 33 vs last 34 sessions) or at least not lose badly in one half while winning in the other. If it survives the archive, forward-test unchanged on the next ~20 unseen sessions before calling it real.
review.verdict_reason: The long-side version is cheap, computable from our data, and directly matches the 'don't catch a falling knife' warning. I would not bundle the short-side 'already too extended down' cap yet, because that needs an arbitrary threshold and is more likely to delete good momentum shorts than fix a real problem.

name: Intrabar fakeout tolerance
one_line: Treat a very quick break-and-recover through the OR as noise instead of instantly assuming the breakout failed.
parameter_choices: If price briefly breaks the OR but closes back inside within the same bar or the next bar, test a hold-or-ignore rule before stopping out; tune the tolerance window to 1 bar or less.
disagreement: Tolerating fakeouts can turn a real breakdown into a larger loss, so the window must stay small.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The book’s tree-shake warning supports the general intuition that brief spikes and reversals can be noise, so you should not overreact mechanically. But it does not state a quantified stop-grace rule for ORB breakouts; the link to this exact exit change is our adaptation, not direct evidence.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a 1-bar fakeout grace to the ORB stop: for the first 5-minute bar after entry, if price touches the stop intrabar but that bar closes back on the breakout side of the opening range, do not exit. Keep the original stop active after that. Parameter: grace_window = 1 bar.
review.mechanism: This could turn a few wick-only stop-outs into surviving trades, which might improve the failed-breakout bucket and reduce a little drawdown. The downside is that it can also delay exits on real failures and make losses larger. Because Midas already has many flat-at-close exits and only a handful of stops, the expected benefit is small.
review.data_missing: We can backtest a bar-close proxy from 5-minute OHLCV, but we cannot know the true intrabar sequence inside a 5-minute bar, so a stop-and-recovery that happens within the same bar is ambiguous without tick data.
review.already_tried_note: Not the same as the previously rejected entry-side rule requiring consecutive closes beyond the range. This is a post-entry stop-grace change, not an entry filter.
review.overfit_note: Only one knob, but it will be judged on a tiny number of affected trades. With about 7 stops in 67 sessions, it is easy to mistake noise for edge and to tune the grace window to the archive.
review.expected_effect: Likely slightly fewer immediate stop-outs, but also slightly larger losers and longer holds. Net effect is probably flat to mildly negative unless most current stops are pure wick noise.
review.test_protocol: Fix grace_window = 1 bar before looking. Replay the full archive side by side with baseline on all available sessions. Compare after-cost net P&L per session, max drawdown, profit factor, and the number of trades changed from stop to non-stop. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just overall. Because this idea only affects a small number of stops, do not trust it unless at least 10 affected stop events are observed in aggregate; with the current archive, that is probably underpowered, so treat any result as exploratory unless the next ~20 unseen sessions confirm it.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible to compute from our bars, but the effect is rare and sample-starved. This is exactly the kind of tweak that can look good on a handful of stop events and then vanish. Also, our current bottleneck is not obviously premature stops, so I would not spend an unseen-day live test on it yet.

name: Point-in-time ticker stitching
one_line: Stitch ticker changes through a point-in-time symbology map so historical series remain continuous when a symbol changes.
parameter_choices: Historical mapping keyed both backward and forward through time; no numeric parameters.
disagreement: No disagreement; this is data hygiene rather than a market rule.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly recommends point-in-time symbology mapping that handles ticker changes both backward and forward in time. This is the same implementation idea, just not a market signal.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace raw ticker history with a point-in-time symbology map (effective-date keyed). When a symbol changes, stitch the predecessor and successor tickers into one continuous underlying-name series before computing daily close history, 10:00 relative volume, OR highs/lows, and signal eligibility. No other trading-rule changes.
review.mechanism: Prevents false resets or gaps from corrupting volume averages, yesterday-close checks, and breakout statistics when a held name changes ticker. That can stop missed entries or wrong in-play ranks, but it is correctness plumbing, not an alpha source.
review.data_missing: Point-in-time ticker-change / issuer identifier map with effective dates. OHLCV + daily closes alone cannot tell us when symbol A became symbol B.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected-strategy list; also not something we have tested because it requires a symbology table.
review.overfit_note: No tunable market parameters. The only risk is hand-filling mappings after seeing outcomes.
review.expected_effect: Tiny to none on P&L. Best case it prevents a handful of bad rankings/signals around ticker changes and keeps the replay aligned with live. It will not address failed-breakout losses, costs, or flat exits.
review.test_protocol: Do this as a data QA audit, not a live alpha test. Replay the archive before/after stitching and compare trade lists, OR levels, and relative-volume ranks on any names that actually changed tickers. Success = identical outputs on all non-event days and continuous history across event days. Minimum sample before drawing a conclusion: at least 1 real ticker-change event; if none exist in our archive, there is no strategy verdict to make.
review.verdict_reason: This is worthwhile data hygiene, but it is not a market rule and it has no realistic chance of improving Midas P&L on the current 67-day sample unless a ticker change is already present. We also cannot compute it from the data we have without an external point-in-time symbology map, so it should be treated as an engineering prerequisite, not a test queue item.

name: Short-horizon trend confirmation
one_line: Only enter the breakout when the stock's immediate trend agrees with direction, using a short EWMA drift or a slower SMA-based deviation check.
parameter_choices: EWMA one-step drift on recent bars/session returns; or close-vs-SMA(20) deviation on 5-minute bars.
disagreement: EWMA is faster but noisier; SMA(20) is slower and may lag. The no-repeat band in the StatArb example is redundant here because Midas already does one trade per day.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the *ingredients* of the idea, not the exact ORB rule. B1 supports short-horizon EWMA-style forecasting, B4 shows a 20-bar SMA/deviation signal in a trading example, and B6 warns that extra trading costs matter. None of them says "only take breakout entries when the stock's short-term trend agrees," so this is our adaptation, not a direct sourced rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a single entry filter to the existing ORB: for the first valid breakout signal after 10:00, take a long only if that signal bar's 5-minute close is above its 20-bar SMA of 5-minute closes; take a short only if that signal bar's close is below its 20-bar SMA(20). Otherwise skip the trade. Keep every other Midas rule unchanged. Do not add any no-repeat band; Midas already trades at most once per day.
review.mechanism: This should cut out breakouts that are fighting the short-term tape. If the stock is already trading above its recent average, a long breakout is more likely to be real continuation rather than a one-bar poke and reverse; same logic for shorts. The hoped-for improvement is fewer failed-break stops, fewer low-quality flat exits, and less cost drag from marginal trades. The trade-off is later entries and some missed winners.
review.data_missing: none; this uses only regular-session 5-minute OHLCV closes that we already have.
review.already_tried_note: We already rejected a different confirmation filter: requiring two consecutive closes beyond the range before entry. This is not the same rule, but it is close in spirit because it tries to be more selective before entry. So this is adjacent, not a fresh area.
review.overfit_note: If we fix the lookback at SMA(20), there is only one real knob. But with 67 sessions and only 53 trades, the effect can still be noise, and it will be tempting to cherry-pick 10/20/30-bar versions if we let ourselves.
review.expected_effect: Fewer trades, slightly higher win rate if the filter is real, fewer stop-outs, and likely lower commission/slippage drag. Best case: the losers shrink more than the winners do. Worst case: it simply delays entries and kills some of the good breakouts.
review.test_protocol: Replay baseline vs. the SMA(20) filter on all archived days side by side, with the parameter fixed before looking. Primary metric: after-cost expectancy per trade and total net P&L. Secondary metrics: stop rate, flat-at-close P&L, profit factor, and max drawdown. Split the archive into two time chunks (for example first 33 sessions vs last 34) and require the filter to help in both halves, not just one lucky streak. If it wins on the archive and does not collapse trade count to useless levels, forward-test it on the next ~20 unseen sessions before promoting.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully computable from the data we already have, cheap to replay, and only adds one simple filter. The source support is indirect, but the idea is plausible, directly aimed at failed breakouts, and low-cost to falsify.

name: Multivariate regime filter
one_line: Gate ORB entries with a small multivariate regime score from recent price, volume, and SPY features.
parameter_choices: Lagged stock returns, volume, volatility, and SPY/market factors; if the feature set is wide or collinear, compress it to the first r PCA components.
disagreement: Direct lag models are more transparent; PCA is less interpretable but may stabilize the filter.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source books support the building blocks—PCA for compressing correlated inputs and multivariate models that can include lagged price/volume/market factors—but they do not give trading evidence that a PCA-based regime gate improves ORB. This is a method extrapolation, not a cited trading edge.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current SPY open-to-now direction check with a single regime gate. At 10:00, compute six 9:30–10:00 features for the candidate stock and SPY: return, high-low range divided by close, and volume divided by that symbol’s average 9:30–10:00 volume over the last 10 sessions. Standardize the features on a trailing 60-session walk-forward fit, take PC1 only (r=1), and flip its sign so higher values correspond to a stronger candidate-stock return. Allow the first ORB long only if the score is > 0 and the first ORB short only if the score is < 0. No other rules change.
review.mechanism: This tries to keep trades only when the stock and the market are both showing an early, coherent regime instead of noisy opening churn. If it works, it should mainly reduce failed-breakout stops and some flat-at-close trades, and maybe lift average trade quality. The likely trade-off is fewer trades and possibly lower gross PnL if the gate is too strict.
review.data_missing: None required. Everything is derivable from the existing regular-session 5-minute OHLCV for the stocks and SPY, plus the 10-session same-window averages already available from that archive.
review.already_tried_note: We already rejected a simpler SPY first-half-hour predictive overlay. This is not the same rule, but it is the same family of market-regime gating, so it should be treated as an adjacent idea rather than a fresh direction.
review.overfit_note: The PCA itself is not the problem; the search space is. Feature choice, fit window, and cutoff can all be tuned to 67 days very easily, and with only ~53 trades a gate can look good simply by deleting losers. If you sweep parameters, you will almost certainly overfit.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer bad entries on choppy days, fewer stopouts, and a modest drawdown reduction. More likely than not, the main effect will be fewer trades; if the gate is too strict, it may also cut away some winners and leave the bot flat.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the specification before looking: 6 features, 60-session walk-forward PCA fit, sign flipped by stock-return loading, threshold fixed at 0. Replay the gated version against the frozen baseline on all 67 archived sessions, with no parameter sweep. Primary metric: after-cost net PnL per session; secondary metrics: expectancy per trade, win rate, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just overall, and require trade count to stay at least ~70% of baseline. If it passes the archive, paper it on the next ~20 unseen sessions; reject it if the live confirmation fails to preserve at least half the archive uplift.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with the data we already have, cheap to replay, and plausibly targeted at the bot’s main failure mode. The evidence is weak and overfit risk is high, so it must be tested once, frozen, and judged on walk-forward archive results plus a short unseen confirmation—not swept until it looks good.

name: ORB bar-size retest
one_line: Retest the opening-range breakout on different aggregation windows and pick the bar size that survives frictions best.
parameter_choices: 5-minute baseline plus coarser 10- and 15-minute bars from our existing data; 1- and 2-minute bars would require higher-resolution data.
disagreement: The source encourages scanning many windows, but our current archive cannot test the sub-5-minute options.
