books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book excerpt supports the general idea of choosing an aggregation window by comparing frictions versus information content. It does not specifically validate this ORB variant, and the 1-2 minute options are outside what we can test with the current archive.
review.exact_rule_change: Change the ORB signal/entry aggregation from 5-minute to 10-minute bars (`bar_size_minutes = 10`); keep the 9:30-10:00 opening range, stop, target, sizing, and flat-time rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: Coarser bars may filter intrabar noise and reduce head-fake breakouts, which is the failure mode that hurt the bot in August. If the move is real, the delayed confirmation still gets you in; if it is fake, you avoid some stop-outs and cut marginal commission/slippage on tiny trades.
review.data_missing: You can test 5-, 10-, and 15-minute bars from the existing 5-minute archive. You cannot test 1- or 2-minute variants without higher-resolution intraday data. If you want to measure the friction argument more realistically, bid/ask or spread data would help, but they are not required for the reduced test.
review.already_tried_note: This exact bar-size sweep has not been tried. The rejected ideas on the list were different filters/exits, not a re-aggregation of the same ORB signal.
review.overfit_note: Only one knob, but the search can still fit 67 sessions if we let the winner emerge after the fact. The sample is small, the edge is weak, and the feasible windows are highly correlated, so pre-register the candidates and require holdout confirmation.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer false breakouts, a slightly better win rate, lower trade count, and a bit less cost drag. Common case: later entries give back some upside and the change does little. This is a noise-filtering tweak, not a new alpha source.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register only the feasible candidates: 5-minute baseline, 10-minute, and 15-minute bars. Replay all 67 archived sessions with every other rule unchanged. Score each variant by post-cost expectancy per session, profit factor, max drawdown, and exit mix (stop/flat/target). Require the same winner to beat the 5-minute baseline in both halves of the archive and not cut trade count by more than 25%. If one window passes, freeze it and run it on the next 20 unseen sessions before promoting it.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible from the current 5-minute archive for 10/15-minute aggregation, cheap to replay, and directly aimed at the bot's failed-breakout problem. Do not waste time on 1- or 2-minute variants until higher-resolution data exists. This is only worth a narrow, pre-registered parameter test, not a broad search.

name: Opening volatility filter
one_line: Stand down or size down when range-based volatility at the open is too high, since those days may be more likely to stop out.
parameter_choices: 0.5[ln(H/L)]^2 - 0.386[ln(C/O)]^2 computed on daily and 30-minute bars; threshold set by cutoff or quantile.
disagreement: The source gives the estimator but not the cutoff; the hypothesis is that high opening volatility is a bad ORB regime.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the volatility estimator formula, not the trading rule. Using opening range-based volatility as a stand-down filter for ORB is our extrapolation, not something the book states as a performance claim.
review.exact_rule_change: At 10:00 New York, for each in-play name compute the 9:30–10:00 range-based volatility estimate on the 30-minute opening bar: σ²_open = 0.5[ln(H/L)]² − 0.386[ln(C/O)]². If σ²_open is above the 80th percentile of that stock’s prior 20 sessions’ σ²_open values, skip that name for the day; otherwise keep the existing ORB rules unchanged. No other entry/exit rules change.
review.mechanism: This is a regime filter meant to avoid the wildest, choppiest openings, where our current bot is most likely to get a breakout, then stop out or drift to a flat close. If it works, it should reduce failed-breakout stops and bad low-expectancy trades. It will probably also cut some good trend days, so the main hope is better net expectancy and lower drawdown, not more targets.
review.data_missing: We can compute the 30-minute opening σ²_open from our 5-minute regular-session bars. What we cannot do literally is the book’s daily-vs-30m comparison, because we do not have daily OHLC, only daily closes. So the testable version is the 30m opening-bar proxy plus a trailing 20-session history.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly. The rejected SPY/QQQ half-hour overlay was a directional timing rule, not a volatility regime filter. The failed-breakout fade is conceptually related but not the same test.
review.overfit_note: One free threshold is enough to cherry-pick 67 sessions, and the effect could be very unstable. The symbol-specific 20-session percentile adds another layer of noise, so this needs a fixed cutoff before looking at results.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trades, fewer stop-outs, and possibly lower drawdown on noisy open days. Best-case it removes the worst regime; worst-case it just skips some of the few large winners and leaves costs/edge unchanged.
review.test_protocol: Fix the rule first: 80th percentile cutoff, 20-session lookback. Replay baseline vs filter on all 67 archived sessions, side by side, with identical fills/costs. Judge on net P&L after costs, profit factor, stop rate, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in both halves of the archive, not just overall. A reasonable pass is: higher net P&L, lower stop rate by at least ~10%, and no worse than ~20% trade-count reduction. If it passes the archive, paper-trade the next 20 unseen sessions before trusting it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, computable from our 5-minute data, and directly targets the bot’s main weakness (failed breakouts on ugly mornings). The source support is weak, so I would not sell it as well-founded, but it is simple enough to test without wasting much time or data.

name: Intraday channel gate
one_line: Skip ORB entries when price is still trapped in a clean intraday channel and only trade after a channel break.
parameter_choices: Rolling intraday high/low channel definition; lookback and width threshold to be tuned.
disagreement: Channel trading and breakout trading are opposing uses of the same structure; here we choose the breakout side only after a channel break.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The book supports the general notion that once a channel is identified you can either trade inside it or wait for a breakout in the breakout direction. It does not specify an intraday gate, a lookback, or any threshold, so this is our extrapolation rather than a stated rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a pre-entry channel gate to the existing ORB: after the 10:00 opening range is set, compute the high-low span of the last 6 completed 5-minute bars. If that span is <= 1.0× the opening-range width, classify the name as still in a channel and ignore the first ORB trigger. Re-arm only after a later 5-minute close breaks above that 6-bar high for longs or below that 6-bar low for shorts, then enter on the next bar open if the existing SPY direction filter still passes.
review.mechanism: This tries to keep us out of the chop days where the stock is still oscillating in a tight band after the open and the first OR break is likely to fail or round-trip into a flat exit. In theory it could cut failed-break stops and some flat churn, but it will also delay good entries, widen stops, shrink size, and may reduce the already modest trade count.
review.data_missing: None needed for the basic rule; 5-minute regular-session OHLCV is enough.
review.already_tried_note: We already tried the same family of idea in the form of extra breakout confirmation (two consecutive closes beyond the range) and it was worse. This channel gate is not identical, but it is another delay/confirmation filter on the same entry logic.
review.overfit_note: The channel definition is arbitrary and easy to tune to 67 sessions. With only OHLCV and a small sample, a 6-bar lookback plus width cutoff can be optimized to past noise, and the filter may simply starve trades.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer failed-break stops and fewer flat/churn trades. More likely: fewer trades, later fills, and potentially worse target capture. Any gain would have to come from higher expectancy per trade, not more activity.
review.test_protocol: If tested at all, fix the spec before looking: 6-bar lookback, width threshold = 1.0× OR width. Replay all archived days side by side with baseline, with no parameter sweeps. Compare net P&L after costs per session, max drawdown, stop rate, flat rate, and trade count. Require improvement in both chronological halves and no material trade-count collapse (e.g. at least 80% of baseline trades) before considering the next ~20 unseen days. If it does not clear that bar, stop.
review.verdict_reason: This is a weakly supported, highly parameterized variant of a confirmation filter we have already tried in spirit. It is likely to reduce sample size and delay fills more than it improves expectancy, and the channel definition is too easy to overfit on our 67-day sample.

name: Ex-dividend gap hygiene
one_line: Exclude ex-dividend names on the ex-date, or adjust the overnight gap reference, so mechanical dividend drops do not contaminate the gap filter.
parameter_choices: Block trades on ex-dividend days, or subtract the dividend amount from the gap calculation.
disagreement: This is a calendar effect, not a sentiment signal; it matters mainly for long entries and gap-based filters.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly says ex-dividend dates create a mechanical price drop and suggests exactly this kind of hygiene fix: block entries on those days or adjust the gap reference. It is support for the rule, but only as a calendar/mechanical filter, not as proven alpha.
review.exact_rule_change: Add an ex-dividend calendar. If a symbol is ex-dividend on the trade date, skip all new ORB entries in that symbol for that session (ex-div filter = ON). Do not change any other Midas rule.
review.mechanism: This would keep the overnight-gap filter from treating a mechanical dividend drop as real bearish pressure. That can prevent a few bad shorts and a few misclassified gap days, so it mainly targets bad entries and a small amount of avoidable drawdown. It is not likely to fix the bot’s bigger issue of failed breakouts.
review.data_missing: We do not currently have ex-dividend dates/corporate actions data, and if we choose to adjust the gap numerically we would also need the dividend amount. Our 5-minute OHLCV and daily closes are not enough to identify ex-div days reliably.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list, and no similar corporate-action or dividend calendar filter has been tested yet.
review.overfit_note: Almost no tuning knobs if implemented as a hard block, so it is not an overfitting trap. The problem is not flexibility; it is that the event is rare and currently unobservable in our data.
review.expected_effect: At best a small improvement: fewer false gap-based decisions on a handful of dividend dates. In our universe this is likely too sparse to move daily equity materially, though it could shave off an occasional bad trade.
review.test_protocol: Do not test with the current dataset. If we add a corporate-actions feed, replay baseline vs. ex-div block on all archived days and only compare sessions where at least one candidate was ex-dividend. Success metrics: higher net PnL after costs, lower max drawdown, and no meaningful drop in trade count. Require at least ~10 affected ex-div sessions in the archive before trusting the result; otherwise it is too sparse to judge. Then confirm on the next ~20 unseen days.
review.verdict_reason: This cannot be implemented or validated with the data we currently have. The needed ex-dividend calendar is missing, and the effect is too sparse in a 55-name universe to justify a standalone test on a 67-day sample.

name: Mechanical execution with review log
one_line: Keep the bot fully mechanical during the session and require a written review of every loss and flat day.
parameter_choices: No manual overrides; checklist for setup, entry, stop, exit, and regime on each session.
disagreement: No direct disagreement; this is process discipline rather than a market rule.
books: How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: One source explicitly warns against manual intervention in live trading; the other argues for post-loss diagnosis and having help to figure out what went wrong. Neither source specifically supports a written review log for every loss/flat day, so this is an extrapolation rather than a stated rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Operational rule only: manual_override_allowed = no during the session, and review_required_on = every losing or flat day. After each such day, complete a standardized log for every trade with setup, entry, stop, exit, and regime note. No entry/exit logic changes.
review.mechanism: At best this reduces human-induced drift from the frozen rules and creates a cleaner feedback loop for future rule changes. It does not alter the opening-range breakout edge, the cost structure, or the failed-breakout problem directly, so any P&L lift would be indirect and delayed.
review.data_missing: Structured manual-override timestamps and the actual review logs. OHLCV plus daily closes can show losses and flat days, but cannot measure whether the review process changed anything causal.
review.already_tried_note: The live recipe is already frozen and deterministic, so 'fully mechanical' is already mostly baked in. The genuinely new piece is the written review log, and that has not been tested as an alpha change.
review.overfit_note: There are no numeric market knobs, but the process is easy to rationalize after the fact and impossible to attribute causally from 67 days of P&L.
review.expected_effect: No direct edge; maybe fewer operator mistakes and faster identification of weak rules in future iterations.
review.test_protocol: Do not evaluate this as a P&L alpha test. If you adopt it, treat it as an ops audit: over the next 20 unseen sessions, require zero discretionary overrides and 100% completion of the review log on every loss/flat day. Success is compliance, not return uplift. If the bot is already fully mechanical and the logs are filled anyway, the idea adds no measurable signal.
review.verdict_reason: This is process discipline, not a market edge. It is mostly already implicit in a mechanical bot, cannot be validated from the available OHLCV data, and has no direct path to improving the failed-breakout and flat-exit profile that actually hurts Midas.

name: One-change-at-a-time validation
one_line: When testing an improvement, change only the entry or only the exit logic in a given experiment, never both.
parameter_choices: Separate entry-only and exit-only tests; keep the untouched side fixed.
disagreement: The source warns that weak signals may still work with better trade management, so exit tests should be separated from signal tests.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The source gives a related principle: weak indicators can still work if paired with better trade management, and it explicitly suggests keeping the entry fixed while testing exit management. It does not explicitly say "never change entry and exit together," so our rule is an operational extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to live trading logic. New research rule: when evaluating any candidate improvement, run only one side at a time. Either (A) entry-only test: freeze the current exit/stop/target/flat rules and change just the entry logic, or (B) exit-only test: freeze the current entry rule and change just the exit logic. Do not alter both sides in the same experiment.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha by itself; it prevents us from fooling ourselves. By isolating entry and exit changes, we can tell whether improvements come from better signal selection, fewer failed-breakout stops, better target capture, or just a lucky interaction between two knobs. That is especially important on a 67-day sample, where combined changes can look good while being impossible to diagnose or reproduce.
review.data_missing: none for the method itself; it uses the same archived 5-minute OHLCV and daily closes we already have.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. This is a validation protocol, not a prior trading rule.
review.overfit_note: There are no free trading parameters here. It actually lowers overfit risk by preventing confounded tests and reducing the temptation to fit a two-knob combination to 67 sessions.
review.expected_effect: No direct PnL change from the protocol itself. Indirectly, it should reduce false positives, make exit tests and entry tests interpretable, and stop us from promoting confounded combinations that only work in-sample.
review.test_protocol: Adopt this as the default research workflow immediately. For every future idea, create two separate replays: one where only entry is changed and one where only exit is changed. Compare each candidate against the frozen baseline on all 67 archived sessions, then confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions. Decision rule: if the improvement only appears when both sides are changed together, reject the idea or split it into separate entry-only and exit-only hypotheses. Minimum sample to decide on a candidate: at least a clean result in both halves of the archive plus the 20-session forward check; no need to wait for 100+ unseen trades.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible, costs nothing, needs no new data, and directly addresses the biggest small-sample risk on this bot: confounded experiments. It will not itself improve the live bot, but it is the right way to test the next ideas without wasting the archive.

name: Cost-anchored auxiliary signal threshold
one_line: If we add any side-filter or overlay, require its expected edge to clear estimated commission and slippage instead of just beating zero.
parameter_choices: Set the minimum expected edge at about 1.0x-1.5x estimated round-trip cost; only take the trade if the filter's projected benefit exceeds that floor.
disagreement: A stricter floor reduces trade count and may miss some real edges if cost estimates are noisy.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book supports using transaction cost as the benchmark c in a return decomposition. That is adjacent to anchoring a threshold on costs, but it does not prescribe a pre-trade activation rule or a 1.0x-1.5x floor; those parts are our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to the base ORB. For any future auxiliary overlay/filter, estimate its rolling 20-session out-of-sample expectancy in dollars per trade and only turn it on when expectancy is at least 1.25x the estimated round-trip cost (0.05% commission on entry notional round trip + $0.04/share slippage round trip); otherwise ignore the overlay.
review.mechanism: This would block marginal add-on signals whose apparent edge is smaller than friction. On a $1,000 book with small position sizes, that mainly protects us from paying costs for weak overlays and can reduce bad days from low-quality extras, but it does not create edge by itself.
review.data_missing: A specific overlay or score that can be estimated walk-forward from past bars only. Our 5-minute OHLCV can measure realized outcomes and costs, but not a generic ex-ante expected edge for an undefined signal.
review.already_tried_note: We already evaluate changes on net P&L after costs, so the cost-awareness part is not new. What we have not tried is a formal cost-floor gate on a specific auxiliary overlay.
review.overfit_note: The only practical way to operationalize this is to invent an expectancy estimator and a threshold, both of which can be tuned on the same short archive. With only 67 sessions, that is very easy to overfit.
review.expected_effect: At best, fewer marginal overlay trades and slightly better average P&L per trade. Likely lower trade count and only a small effect unless the overlay itself has genuine edge above costs.
review.test_protocol: Do not live-test this as a free-floating idea. First define one specific overlay that outputs an out-of-sample expectancy estimate from past data only. Freeze cost_floor_multiple=1.25 and lookback=20 sessions before inspecting results. Replay on all archived days with walk-forward estimation only; compare baseline ORB vs ORB+overlay-gated-by-cost-floor on net $ P&L, trade count, win rate, profit factor, max drawdown, and % negative days. Require the gated version to beat baseline in both halves of the archive. Only if that holds, forward-test on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: As written this is a vetting principle, not a standalone, testable change to the current bot. Without a specific overlay and a robust ex-ante expectancy model, there is nothing to replay cleanly on our data, and any threshold can be tuned to the 67-day archive.

name: Magnitude-aware prediction labels for overlays
one_line: When building any predictive overlay on top of ORB, label outcomes with both direction and return size rather than using a binary up/down target alone.
parameter_choices: Use next-bar or next-two-bar return as a regression target, or classify into down/flat/up buckets with a flat band sized to costs.
disagreement: Magnitude-aware labels are more informative, but they can be harder to model and may overfit if the sample is small.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The source directly supports the *mechanics* of using regression or multi-class targets that encode future move size, but it does not claim this improves ORB trading. The link to Midas is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: No direct change to the live ORB rules. If we add a predictive overlay, replace any binary up/down target with a 3-class label on the next 10 minutes of return from the signal bar: +1 if return > +0.12%, 0 if between -0.12% and +0.12%, and -1 if return < -0.12%. Keep the model/features fixed when comparing against the binary-label version.
review.mechanism: A cost-aware 3-class target could teach an overlay to ignore tiny post-breakout wiggles and focus on moves large enough to matter after commission and slippage. Best case: fewer low-quality breakout entries and slightly better trade selection. Worst case: same edge, less sample, more noise.
review.data_missing: none; 5-minute regular-session OHLCV is enough to compute next-10-minute returns and labels.
review.already_tried_note: We have not tried this exact label scheme. But we did try a nearby predictive overlay ('first half hour predicts last half hour' on SPY/QQQ), and it cut profit, which makes me cautious about generic overlay ideas.
review.overfit_note: There are multiple easy knobs to tune (horizon, flat band, model class, decision threshold), and the live sample is still small. It is very easy to fit the 67 archived days without learning a durable effect.
review.expected_effect: Likely modest at best. If it helps, it should mostly reduce false positives on tiny moves and slightly improve entry quality. More likely, it either does little or lowers trade count without meaningfully improving net P&L.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the overlay model/features before looking at results. Compare binary-label vs 3-class-label versions on all archived sessions with the same walk-forward retraining scheme. Score after-cost net P&L, profit factor, max drawdown, and trade count. Require the candidate to improve in both the early and late halves of the archive and not cut trade count by more than 10%. Only if it wins there, confirm on the next ~20 unseen sessions.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, but this is only a label-construction tweak, not a standalone edge. Without a frozen overlay/model, it is too generic and too easy to tune to the 67-day archive. I would not spend scarce unseen days on it until there is a concrete overlay candidate to evaluate.

name: One-minute volume profile bins
one_line: If higher-resolution data is added later, build intraday volume profiles in 1-minute bins rather than 5-minute bins.
parameter_choices: Use 1-minute bins for the open and close profile, then compare against the current 5-minute aggregation on the same dates.
disagreement: More granularity may improve normalization near the open, but it can also add noise and data-management complexity.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source directly supports the general practice of using 1-minute bins for intraday volume profiles, but it does not show that this improves ORB performance, costs, or slippage for Midas. The link to our bot is still an extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Not testable with the current 5-minute archive. If we later add 1-minute regular-session bars, compute any intraday volume-profile feature with 1-minute bins instead of 5-minute bins; keep the existing ORB rules, thresholds, and sizing unchanged.
review.mechanism: Finer bins would stop the 9:30 burst from being smeared across a 5-minute bar, so a future profile-based filter could tell a real opening participation spike from noise. That might slightly improve an in-play selector or a future time-of-day filter, but it does not directly fix failed breakouts, exits, or trading costs.
review.data_missing: We only have 5-minute regular-session OHLCV. To do this properly we need 1-minute intraday OHLCV for the same universe and SPY; trade/quote data would be even better.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list, but also not something we have actually tested on the current 5-minute bot.
review.overfit_note: Bin size is a classic data-snooping knob. With only 67 sessions, any apparent lift from finer granularity would be easy to fit to noise and unlikely to be stable.
review.expected_effect: At best, a small improvement in any future volume-profile-based filter from better open/close normalization. For the current bot, the effect is likely negligible.
review.test_protocol: Only after 1-minute data exists: run a paired replay on the same archived days with all other ORB rules frozen, comparing bin_size = 1 minute versus 5 minutes for the profile module. Pre-fix all thresholds before looking. Primary metric: net P&L after costs per day and per trade. Secondary metrics: stop rate, target rate, flat-at-close P&L, and trade count. Require the 1-minute version to beat 5-minute in both halves of the archive and to hold up over the next ~20 unseen trading days before promoting it.
review.verdict_reason: Plausible as a data-resolution upgrade, but it cannot be tested with the data we have now and it does not directly address the bot's known weak spots. Do not spend a test slot on it until 1-minute bars are available.

name: Correlation-weighted signal ensemble
one_line: When combining multiple confirmations, weight each signal by its rolling absolute correlation to forward breakout success instead of simple voting.
parameter_choices: Estimate 20-60 day rolling absolute correlations, normalize weights to sum to 1, and drop any signal whose weight stays near zero.
disagreement: Correlation weights can become unstable and may overweight a noisy signal that only looks good in-sample.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The book supports the general idea of weighting multiple predictors by correlation magnitude, but only as a static ensemble in currencies. It does not support rolling weights, a breakout-success label, or anything specific to our ORB bot.
review.exact_rule_change: This is a new entry framework, not a tweak to the frozen ORB: replace the current hard entry gating with a weighted score built from the existing confirmations (relative volume, SPY alignment, and the overnight gap cap). Set each weight to the 30-session rolling absolute correlation between that confirmation and the realized post-cost trade outcome, normalize weights to sum to 1, drop any weight below 0.05, and enter only if the weighted score is above 0.50. Leave exits, sizing, and time stops unchanged.
review.mechanism: In theory this could reduce failed-breakout entries by downweighting whichever confirmation is currently noisy, so fewer stop-outs and fewer bad days. It does not touch costs or holding time, so any gain would have to come from better entry quality, not cheaper execution.
review.data_missing: No extra market data are needed; the blocker is model design, not data. The current recipe just does not have a rich, clean set of independent confirmations to ensemble.
review.already_tried_note: We have already tried the same family of 'more confirmation' ideas: two closes beyond the range, the SPY overlay, and a morning-fade variant. This is more sophisticated, but it is still the same direction.
review.overfit_note: With 67 sessions and about one trade per day, rolling correlations will be noisy and regime-dependent. The lookback, the weight floor, and even the choice of component signals are all easy to fit to the archive.
review.expected_effect: Best case: a small reduction in false-breakout trades and a modest lift in win rate. More likely: the weights chase noise, trade count falls, and the edge does not survive costs.
review.test_protocol: Archive-only first. Fix the parameters up front at 30 sessions and a 0.05 weight floor, then replay all 67 archived days side by side with baseline. Compare paired daily net PnL after costs as the primary metric, plus trade count, profit factor, max drawdown, and the number of stop-outs from failed breakouts. Require the ensemble to improve both halves of the archive, not just the full sample, and to keep trade count within about 80% to 120% of baseline. Only if it clears that gate should you paper it for the next 20 unseen sessions. Do not tune the signal list or thresholds on the archive after the first pass.
review.verdict_reason: This is a meta-method, not a concrete edge for our current bot. We do not yet have a stable, independent signal stack to ensemble, and the only family related to this idea - more entry confirmation - has already been tried and hurt. With 67 days of data, rolling correlation weights are more likely to fit noise than to survive.

name: Loss-streak size throttle
one_line: After a losing streak, cut position size sharply for the next few sessions instead of relying only on the daily loss halt.
parameter_choices: Reduce size to 25%-50% after 3 consecutive losses or after a day below about -1.5R; restore only after a green session.
disagreement: This can reduce drawdown, but it may also slow recovery after a normal losing streak.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: Burns is giving general risk/emotional control advice ('cut stakes dramatically or get out' when you hit a tipping point). He is not proposing a quantified loss-streak sizing rule. Turning that into '3 losing sessions then halve size' is our own extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: If the bot records 3 consecutive losing trading sessions, reduce size on all new entries to 50% of normal until the next net green trading session, then restore full size. Keep the existing -3% daily loss halt unchanged. Do not count no-trade days in the streak.
review.mechanism: This is a capital-preservation overlay, not an edge source. It could trim damage when Midas enters a bad breakout regime and slightly lower commissions/slippage during those bad patches by trading smaller. But because Midas already has a daily loss halt and only one trade per day, the extra room for improvement is likely small; if the losses are mostly random, the throttle will just shrink both losers and the few big recovery winners.
review.data_missing: Nothing extra. The streak and the post-throttle PnL can be computed from the existing replayable 5-minute bars and daily closes; no L2, news, or pre-market data is needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not this rule specifically, but it lives in the same risk-control bucket as the existing -3% daily loss halt.
review.overfit_note: Only 2 real knobs here (streak length and size cut), but the trigger will probably fire only a few times in 67 sessions. A couple of streaks can dominate the apparent result, so it is easy to fool ourselves.
review.expected_effect: Best case: a modest reduction in max drawdown and day-to-day volatility. More likely: little change in expectancy, with some reduction in upside because size is cut precisely when the bot may be about to mean-revert back to normal. It is a smoother-equity rule, not a direct fix for failed breakouts.
review.test_protocol: Replay baseline vs throttle on all archived sessions with identical signals, entries, exits, commissions, and slippage. Fix the rule before looking. Judge on session-level equity, not just trade count. Primary success metric: lower max drawdown; secondary: net PnL and profit factor. I would only call it a pass if archive replay shows at least ~15% lower max DD and no worse than ~10% lower net PnL, with improvement in both halves of the sample (early and late periods). Minimum sample: at least 3 throttle activations and about 10 throttled sessions in the archive; if the trigger is too rare, treat the result as inconclusive and do not spend a live-day slot on it. If it passes archive, confirm on the next ~20 unseen trading days.
review.verdict_reason: It is computable and cheap, but it is mainly a safety overlay, not a direct fix for Midas's real problem (failed breakouts plus cost drag). With only 67 sessions, the trigger will likely be rare, so the result will be sparse and easy to overread. I would prioritize a rule that changes entries/exits before spending scarce live-test attention on this.

name: Staged partial-profit exit
one_line: Test taking partial profits before the full target and trail the remainder instead of always holding the whole position to 2.5R.
parameter_choices: Take 50% off at 1.0R-1.5R, move the stop to breakeven or the OR midpoint, and let the rest run to 2.5R or a trailing stop.
disagreement: This may smooth equity and reduce emotional exits, but it can lower expectancy if the current full-target winners drive most of the edge.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The book quote supports having predefined stops and profit targets in general, but it does not argue for staged partial-profit exits or trailing the remainder. That is our extrapolation, not the source's rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the single full 2.5R exit with a staged exit: when price first reaches +1.25R from entry, sell 50% of the position; immediately move the stop on the remaining 50% to the entry price; keep the remaining half's take-profit at +2.5R and still flatten any open position at 15:45.
review.mechanism: Best case, this could turn some trades that spike and then fade into a realized partial gain, which might smooth equity and slightly reduce bad days. But it does not address failed-breakout entries, and on this bot the real edge seems to come from a few full-target winners. Splitting exits also adds an extra leg, which increases slippage/commission drag on a small book. So the likely effect is fewer big winners, maybe a bit less variance, and probably lower net expectancy.
review.data_missing: We can compute the levels from 5-minute OHLCV, but we do not know intrabar sequence inside a 5-minute candle. If the partial target and the moved stop are both touched in the same bar, the exact fill order is ambiguous without tick data.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the rejected-idea list. This is an exit-management change, not the prior failed fade or multi-close overlays.
review.overfit_note: Only two tunable knobs here, but the sample has very few true winners (3 full targets in 67 sessions). That makes it easy to optimize the partial level/fraction to the tiny archive and accidentally kill the real edge.
review.expected_effect: Most likely slightly worse expectancy after costs, with a possible small reduction in drawdown/variance. It may rescue a few give-back trades, but the current edge is concentrated in the rare full-target winners, and partial exits tax those winners while adding execution cost.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule before looking: 50% off at +1.25R, stop the remainder at entry, final target still +2.5R. Replay it on all 67 archived days side by side with baseline. Primary metric: net PnL after costs per day and max drawdown. Secondary: profit factor, average trade, and fraction of days that would have been losers. Require improvement in both halves of the archive (Jul-Aug and Sep-Oct) before considering it live. If the archived replay is only marginally better or gets better only by sacrificing the few large winners, do not promote. If it clears the archive, confirm on the next ~20 unseen days without changing the parameters.
review.verdict_reason: This is a psychological-style exit tweak applied to a deterministic bot, so the main mechanism from the source is weak here. The bot's edge is currently coming from a tiny number of full-target winners, and this change would likely cap those while adding another costly exit leg. With only 67 sessions and 3 full targets, the sample is too thin to justify a partial-profit scheme as a likely improvement to this specific system.
